Seeds of EpTFIIAγ transgenic wheat plants and wild-type controls were sown in 7 cm × 10 cm pots containing a nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture and grown in a growth chamber. At the three-leaf stage, seedlings were exposed to 42 °C for 36 h and allowed to recover at 23 °C for 4 days. Seedling survival rates were calculated based on the number of individual plants with green, viable shoots. At least nine seedlings per genotype were analysed per assay, with three independent experiments. Maximum photochemical efficiency of photosystem II (Fv/Fm) was measured using a FluorPen FP110 fluorometer (PSI). Electrolyte leakage was determined using a conductivity meter (DDSJ-307F, Shanghai INESA Scientific Instruments). Relative electrolyte conductivity (%) was calculated as (C1 – C0)/(C2 – C0) × 100%, where C1 represents initial conductivity before boiling, C2 is the final conductivity after boiling and C0 is the conductivity of deionized water.

Industry observers note that wild-type Fielder and EpTFIIAγ transgenic wheat plants were cultivated in a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m−2 s−1, 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod at 14 °C and 12 °C (day and night) with 60% relative humidity. Three-week-old seedlings were inoculated with Pst urediniospores and maintained in darkness at 12 °C and 100% relative humidity for 24 h, after which plants were returned to standard growth conditions. Disease phenotypes were evaluated following the development of stripe rust symptoms. Relative fungal biomass was quantified by qPCR analysis of the ratio of Pst-specific PstEF transcripts relative to that of the wheat reference gene, TaEF64, in CTAB-extracted genomic DNA.

Recent findings suggest that for histological analyses, reactive oxygen species accumulation was visualized by staining infected leaves with 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (1 mg ml−1). Stained samples were examined using a BX-51 microscope (Olympus). Stomata associated with haustorial mother-cell formation were defined as successful infection sites, and the 3,3′-diaminobenzidine-stained area at each site was quantified using CellSens Entry software (Olympus). At least 30 infection sites were analysed for each time point. Fungal infection structures were visualized by WGA–Alexa Fluor 488 staining (20 μg ml−1; Amresco) following tissue clearing and alkali treatment. Samples were mounted in 50% glycerol and examined using an Olympus BX-53 fluorescence microscope equipped with a GFP filter set. Substomatal vesicles, infection hyphae and other fungal structures were observed, and hyphal length and fungal colonization area were quantified using CellSens Entry software. At least 30 infection sites were analysed for each time point.

Wheat drought resistance at the maturity stage was evaluated under full-irrigation (that is, control) and water-limited conditions in the field. Each plot measured 5 m × 2 m and consisted of 25 rows, with 20-cm spacing between rows and 10 cm between plants. Control plots were irrigated regularly throughout the entire growing season, and water-limited plots were isolated using a 1.5-m-deep underground waterproof barrier and covered with a rain-out shelter to exclude natural precipitation. After the initial irrigation at sowing, water-limited plots received approximately 30% of the water volume applied to the well-watered plots for the remainder of the season.

Photosynthetic parameters of wheat were recorded with a LI-6400XT portable photosynthesis system (LI-COR) at four Zadoks growth stages from tillering (Z25) to milk development (Z75). Net photosynthesis rate (Pn), transpiration rate (Tr), stomatal conductance (Gs) and instantaneous water use efficiency (calculated as Pn/Tr) were measured from at least 15 plants per line. Light-response and CO2-response curves were fitted using the Farquhar–von Caemmerer–Berry model to estimate maximum carboxylation rate (Vcmax) and maximum electron transport rate (Jmax). Chlorophyll fluorescence (Fv/Fm) and SPAD values were measured using a hand-held chlorophyll-fluorescence measurement instrument (FluorPen FP 110, FluorCam) and chlorophyll meter (SPAD-502, Konica Minolta), respectively. Leaf area of the main tiller was measured using a leaf-area meter (Yaxin-1242, Dianjiang Technology). Agronomic traits, including plant height, spike number, spike length, spikelet number, grain number per spike, grain length, grain width, 1,000-grain weight, yield per plant, biomass and harvest index were measured from 50–100 plants per line. Grains were oven-dried at 37 °C before yield quantification.

Rice agronomic traits were evaluated in the field at maturity. Seeds were sown in a seedling nursery and transplanted into the field at 25 days after sowing. A wide–narrow row-planting pattern was adopted in the field, with 5 rows × 10 plants per plot. Each line was randomly assigned to three plots (that is, three biological replicates). Water-limited plots were covered with a rain-out shelter to exclude natural precipitation, and drought stress was initiated at booting stage by withholding irrigation and opening drainage valves to remove standing water. Drought treatment was terminated and followed by a rewatering recovery phase once either the experimental or control plants showed irreversible leaf-rolling symptoms that persisted for 5 consecutive days. At maturity, each plant was harvested individually. Traits assessed included plant height, grain size, 1,000-grain weight and grain yield per plant.

Recent findings suggest that maize field trials were conducted at the three abovementioned locations under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions. Drought treatment was applied through artificial irrigation control using a drip irrigation system equipped with underground Watermark 200SS sensors to monitor and maintain soil water potential. Each treatment included four replicate plots (2.6 m wide; 0.4 m row spacing), with four rows per line. Agronomic traits, including plant height, grain number per ear, yield per plant and 100-grain weight, were measured following open pollination.

Wheat lodging resistance was evaluated using the second basal internode of the main tiller. Stem breaking strength was measured at 10 days after anthesis using a plant stem strength tester (IN-JG2, Shandong Holder Electronic Technology). Stem diameter was measured on the same internode using a digital caliper. Each stem was measured three times, and 20 biological replicates were analysed for each genotype.

For stem histology, the middle region of the peduncle internode was collected at 15 days post-anthesis and fixed in formalin alcohol acetate solution at 23 °C for 48 h. Following dehydration through a graded ethanol series (75–100%, v/v) and clearing in xylene, samples were embedded in paraffin. Sections (6–8 μm) were cut using a rotary microtome (Leica RM2235; Leica Biosystems) and subjected to safranin–fast green double staining. In brief, sections were stained with safranin, differentiated in 90% ethanol, counterstained with fast green, cleared in a 1:1 (v/v) xylene–ethanol mixture and mounted. Panoramic images were acquired using SlideViewer software (v2.9.0), and stem diameter, vascular bundle number and mechanical tissue thickness were quantified using ImageJ (v1.53).

Recent findings suggest that for seedling-stage stress experiments, germinated wheat seedlings were grown in 7 cm × 7 cm × 10 cm pots with Hoagland’s modified nutrient solution for 3 days under a 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod at 14 °C and 12 °C (day and night) with 60% relative humidity. Subsequently, the control group was continuously cultured in modified Hoagland’s nutrient solution, whereas the drought-stress group was cultured in modified Hoagland’s nutrient solution containing 20% (w/v) PEG6000. Seedlings in both groups were grown for 3–4 weeks, with the culture solution replaced every 3 days, after which root parameters were scored. The root system of each seedling was excised, lateral roots were separated from nodes, evenly spread in a transparent plastic tray with 0.5 cm of deionized water, and intertwined fine lateral branches were gently separated with forceps to avoid overlap. Primary root length, root fresh weight and root dry weight were measured manually.

Industry observers note that wheat plants were grown in PVC columns (150 cm × 15 cm) filled with soil under well-watered and water-limited (water supply terminated at the jointing stage) conditions, with one plant per column. When wheat reached the grain-filling stage, the soil and root system were carefully removed from the columns. Roots were rinsed with running water to remove adhering soil and impurities, then excised from shoots. Root length was measured immediately after cleaning. Subsequently, roots were placed in paper envelopes and dried in a forced-air drying oven at 65 °C for 7 days, after which root dry weight was determined.

Water loss assays were performed on 4-week-old wheat seedlings as previously described25. Fully expanded third leaves were excised and immediately weighed to record their initial fresh weight (FW0). Leaves were then placed on dry filter paper under ambient room conditions (22–25 °C, 40–60% relative humidity, with light exposure) without covering. Fresh weight (FWt) was recorded at regular intervals. Water loss was expressed as a percentage of the initial fresh weight using the formula: Water loss rate (%) = [(FW0 − FWt)/FW0] × 100. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

In a recent development, water loss assays on Arabidopsis were carried out as previously described65. In brief, fully expanded rosette leaves from 3-week-old plants were detached at the same time of day to minimize circadian effects. The initial fresh weight (FW0) was recorded immediately using a precision analytical balance. Leaves were then placed on dry filter paper in a controlled environment (22 °C, 50–60% relative humidity, no direct airflow). Fresh weights (FWt) were measured at specified time intervals, typically every 30 or 60 min for 6 h. Water loss rate was calculated using the same formula as for wheat. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Infrared thermography was performed on 4-week-old greenhouse-grown seedlings that were subjected to 15 days of water withholding, during which soil water content was maintained at approximately 50% of well-watered capacity. Leaf surface temperatures under different treatments were recorded using a FLIR A655sc infrared camera (Teledyne FLIR). Thermal images were analysed using FLIR ResearchIR Max (v4.40) to quantify temperature differences and assess drought-induced physiological responses.

Sources indicate that to evaluate photosynthesis-related changes, multispectral imaging was conducted using the PhenoBox live-plant multispectral imaging analysis system (LemnaTec GmbH). Five-leaf-stage wheat seedlings were individually cultivated in plots filled with nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture under controlled growth-chamber conditions. Imaging was performed under three distinct soil-moisture regimes, including well watered (soil water content maintained at approximately 90%), mild drought (soil water content reduced to approximately 50%) and severe drought (soil water content reduced to approximately 30%). Four surface multispectral images were captured for each plant. Standardized imaging protocols were applied to ensure consistent lighting and sensor calibration. Two spectral values, normalized water index and normalized difference vegetation index, were used to assess plant water status and physiological responses under drought stress: normalized water index = (R970 – R850)/(R970 + R850) and normalized difference vegetation index = (R800 – R670)/(R800 + R670), with R representing reflectance and numbers referring to wavelength (nm).

In a recent development, for chlorophyll fluorescence measurements, imaging was performed using the live-plant imaging system CV-200 produced by Beijing Feizhi Technology and controlled by CropVision_Controller_v2 software. Fluorescence images were captured under stable-lighting conditions at the same time points used for multispectral imaging. The effective ΦPSII was automatically extracted using the software and was used to evaluate photosynthetic performance and drought-stress responses in wheat seedlings across the different water treatments.

Stomatal density measurements were performed following a published protocol66. To determine stomatal density in wheat, the middle region of the abaxial surface of the fully expanded second leaf of seedlings was selected for analysis. The abaxial epidermis was carefully adhered to a piece of transparent adhesive tape. The upper epidermis and mesophyll tissue were then gently scraped off using a razor blade. The tape carrying the intact abaxial epidermal cells was subsequently mounted on a standard microscope slide (75 mm × 25 mm) for microscopic observation. A minimum of ten slides were prepared for each wheat line. Stomata were observed and photographed using compound microscope (Olympus IX71) under a ×10 objective lens, and stomatal density was calculated as the number of stomata per unit area of the field of view.

For Arabidopsis, fully expanded and healthy functional leaves (typically the fifth or sixth true leaf) were selected. The abaxial surface of each leaf was gently pressed onto clear adhesive tape. The upper epidermis and mesophyll were carefully removed using a razor blade, leaving the lower epidermis adhered to the tape. The tape carrying the epidermal imprint was then mounted smoothly onto a standard glass slide (75 mm × 25 mm), avoiding air bubbles. At least ten slides were prepared per line for analysis.

Stomatal aperture measurements in wheat and Arabidopsis were determined following established protocols65. For wheat, a fully expanded second leaf was excised and incubated in stomatal opening buffer containing 0.05 M KNO3, 10 mM MES and 50 μM CaCl2 (pH 6.15) under light conditions (200 μmol photons m–2 s–1, 25 °C) for 1.5 h or in darkness for 1 h. Leaves were then exposed to drought treatment under ambient air for 10 min, followed by incubation in continuous light, continuous dark or a light-to-dark transition for 30 min. The abaxial surface was carefully blot dried and adhered to transparent tape, and the adaxial epidermis and mesophyll cells were gently removed using a razor blade. The exposed abaxial epidermal layer on the tape was then mounted on a microscope slide for imaging. For Arabidopsis, the fifth or sixth rosette leaves were harvested and incubated in MES buffer (10 mM MES-KOH, pH 6.15, 10 mM KCl and 50 μM CaCl2) in a light incubator for 2.5 h to induce stomatal opening. The leaves were subsequently transferred to MES buffer containing 20% w/v PEG6000 and incubated for 2 h. Epidermal strips were prepared and imaged using a compound microscope (Olympus IX71). Stomatal aperture was defined as the width of the pore between the two guard cells, and the stomatal aperture ratio (width:length) was measured using ImageJ (v1.8.0). Data for each ecotype were collected from a minimum of 100 stomata.

Wheat seedlings were grown under controlled conditions until the three-leaf stage. Once soil moisture content declined below 30%, leaf samples were collected at designated intervals. Each genotype comprised three biological replicates, with each sample weighing no less than 1.5 g. Samples were placed in dry envelopes and dried in a constant-temperature forced-air oven at 60 °C until completely desiccated. The dried tissue was then ground into a fine powder for carbon isotope analysis using the stable-isotope ratio mass spectrometry method. Ground samples were treated with 4 mol dm−3 HCl for 24 h, then washed with deionized water until neutral, dried, ground and sieved through a 60-mesh screen. Approximately 0.4 mg of the solid sample was accurately weighed, placed into a tin cup and hermetically sealed, and placed in a 96-well plate. Isotopic measurements were conducted using a Flash 1112 Elemental Analyzer coupled to a Delta V Plus Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Finnigan). The carbon isotope ratio (δ13C) was calculated relative to the Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB) international standard using the formula: δ13C (‰) = [(Rsample/RVPDB) – 1] × 1,000, where R is the ratio of 13C to 12C. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Recent findings suggest that uniform wheat seeds were germinated at room temperature for 3 days and subsequently grown in half-strength Hoagland’s nutrient solution for 1 week. Seedlings were then subjected to either control conditions or drought stress induced by 15% (w/v) PEG6000. After 10 days of treatment, leaf and root tissues were harvested, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Three independent biological replicates were collected for each treatment. Hormone quantification was performed by Metware Biotechnology using an AB Sciex QTRAP 6500 LC–MS/MS system.

Industry observers note that wheat seeds were sown side by side in plastic boxes (32 cm × 24 cm × 12 cm, length × width × height) filled with a nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture. Seedlings were cultured under a 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod, 14 °C and 12 °C day and night temperature and 60% relative humidity for approximately 30 days (three-leaf stage). Drought stress was imposed by withholding water for approximately 20 days until leaf wilting was observed. Leaves were collected from at least three individual plants under well-watered and drought-stressed conditions. The activity of RuBisCO, along with the contents of chlorophyll, soluble sugars, sucrose, glucose and starch were measured using commercial assay kits all obtained from Solarbio: BC0445 for RuBisCO activity, BC0995 for chlorophyll, BC2460 for sucrose, BC0030 for soluble sugars, BC2500 for glucose and BC0700 for starch, all following the manufacturer’s instructions. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

It has been revealed that to evaluate wheat grain development and filling dynamics, main tiller spikes were tagged before anthesis. Under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions, grains from the six central spikelets of each tagged spike were sampled at 5-day intervals from anthesis to physiological maturity, with a minimum of nine spikes collected per genotype per time point. Grain length, width and thickness were measured in 60–100 grains with a digital caliper (0.01-mm resolution); fresh weight was determined for 100-grain samples. Dry weight was obtained by drying samples at 80 °C to a constant weight following a 30-min pre-treatment at 105 °C. The mean grain-filling rate was calculated as the final grain dry weight divided by the grain-filling duration, expressed as mg per grain per day.

Sources indicate that flag leaf sheaths and developing grains were harvested at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 days after flowering. Soluble sugars (sucrose, fructose and glucose) and starch contents were quantified using commercial assay kits from Solarbio (BC2460 for sucrose, BC6360 for fructose, BC2500 for glucose and BC0700 for starch). Enzymatic activity assays were conducted using kits for sucrose synthase (SUS; BC0585), cell-wall invertase (CWI; BC4325) and ADP-glucose pyrophosphorylase (AGPase; BC0435) following the manufacturer’s protocols. All assays were performed with at least three independent biological replicates.

For grain histology, developing grains were collected from central spikelets at 15 days after flowering, then fixed in formalin alcohol acetate solution (G2355, Solarbio) at 23 °C for 48 h. Following dehydration through a graded ethanol series (75–100%, v/v) and xylene clearing, samples were embedded in paraffin. Sections of 6–8 μm thickness were cut using a rotary microtome (Leica RM2235; Leica Biosystems). For histological analysis, sections were stained with toluidine blue, whereas starch granules were visualized using periodic acid–Schiff reagent. Images were acquired using SlideViewer panoramic scanning software (v2.9.0). Grain cell size, cell number and starch granule number were quantified using ImageJ (v1.53).

It has been revealed that total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. First-strand complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized from 1 μg of DNase-treated RNA using the HiScript reverse transcription kit (R223-01, Vazyme). RT–qPCR was performed in a 20-μl reaction volume containing 1.4 μl cDNA (pre-diluted to a concentration of 200 ng μl−1), 0.4 μM primers and 10 μl of SYBR Green Mix (Q121-02/03, Vazyme), using a CFX96 real-time PCR system (Bio-Rad). Gene-expression levels were calculated using the \({2}^{-\Delta \Delta {{\rm{C}}}_{{\rm{T}}}}\) method67 with TaActin1 (TraesCS1B01G283900) serving as the reference gene for normalization. Primer sequences used for RT–qPCR are listed in Supplementary Table 15.

In a recent development, the Saccharomyces cerevisiae Δhog1 mutant, which is sensitive to osmotic stress and lacks a functional copy of a gene encoding a high osmolarity glycerol 1 protein kinase (HOG1)68, was used to assess the drought-resistance function of TFIIAγ proteins. Coding sequences of EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were amplified via PCR using primers with flanking attB sites. These fragments were first cloned into the pDONR221 entry vector (Invitrogen) via BP recombination using the Gateway cloning system and subsequently transferred into the pGAD426 destination vector (Addgene) through an LR (attL and attR) recombination reaction. Recombinant plasmids were transformed into Δhog1 cells using the Frozen-EZ Yeast Transformation Kit (Zymo Research). Transformed strains were selected on synthetic dropout medium lacking uracil (SD−Ura). The pGAD426-GUS plasmid was used as a control.

For stress-tolerance assays, 10 μl of yeast culture (OD600 nm = 0.6) was spotted onto SD−Ura solid medium supplemented with 0.75 M sorbitol and incubated at 28 °C for 3 days. Growth in SD−Ura liquid medium containing 0.75 M sorbitol was monitored by measuring OD600 nm at 24-h intervals.

In a recent development, the full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ (excluding translational stop codons) were cloned in-frame into the N-terminal region of the pJIT163-GFP expression vectors64, both driven by the CaMV 35S promoter. The resulting fusion constructs were introduced into wheat protoplasts (pJIT163-TFIIAγ-GFP). Transformed wheat protoplasts were incubated for 16 h to permit transient expression. GFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) with an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and an emission wavelength range of 500–530 nm. Nuclei were labelled with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI), and fluorescence signal was verified to originate solely from intact fusion proteins via anti-GFP western blot.

According to recent reports, fluorescence imaging was conducted in wheat protoplasts and N. benthamiana epidermal cells transiently expressing EpTFIIAγ–GFP. To induce drought-stress-related or osmotic stress-related cellular responses, cells were treated with 10% (w/v) PEG8000, 1.5 M sorbitol, 50 μM ABA or 250 mM NaCl as indicated. Imaging was performed with an FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus). GFP fluorescence was excited at 488 nm and emission was captured at 491–535 nm. Image acquisition and processing were performed using FV31S-SW software.

According to recent reports, molecular dynamics of EpTFIIAγ–GFP condensates were characterized through FRAP assays. Selected condensates were photobleached using a 488-nm laser, and fluorescence recovery was monitored by timelapse imaging. Recovery curves were normalized to both pre-bleach intensity and the fluorescence of adjacent unbleached regions to correct for background photobleaching; data were analysed with FV31S-SW software. Molecular mobility of EpTFIIAγ and the IDR deletion variant was assessed by FCS analysis in wheat protoplasts. Autocorrelation curves were acquired from multiple cells and fitted to appropriate diffusion models using CorTector NanoX FCS software to obtain diffusion coefficients and molecular concentrations.

It has been revealed that to identify proteins that can potentially physically interact with EpTFIIAγ, a yeast two-hybrid screen was performed. The full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ was cloned into the pGBKT7 vector and served as the bait construct, fused to the binding domain of GAL4. The resulting pGBKT7-EpTFIIAγ plasmid was co-transformed with a pGADT7-based cDNA library (from wheat cv. Chinese Spring seedlings) into S. cerevisiae strain AH109 using the lithium acetate method, according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Clontech). Positive clones were selected on selective dropout media, and candidate-interacting proteins were identified by PCR amplification and subsequent DNA sequencing.

According to recent reports, to validate putative physical interactions between EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ with candidate partners, the coding sequences lacking translational stop codons of TaAKS1, TaWRKY46, TaARF6, TaVOZ1, TaTFIIAαβ and AtTFIIAαβ were individually cloned into the pGADT7 vector to form prey constructs. The coding sequences of EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were used as bait in the pGBKT7 vector. Bait and prey constructs were co-transformed into S. cerevisiae AH109 using the lithium-acetate method. Protein–protein interactions were assessed by spotting serial tenfold dilutions of co-transformed yeast cultures onto SD/–Trp–Leu and SD/–Trp–Leu–His–Ade selective media.

It has been revealed that to perform luciferase-complementation imaging assays, the coding sequences of TaWRKY46, TaARF6, TaAKS1, TaVOZ1, TaTFIIAαβ and AtTFIIAαβ were cloned upstream of the nLUC in the pCAMBIA1300-nLUC vector, whereas EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were cloned downstream of the cLUC in the pCAMBIA1300-cLUC vector. These constructs were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 and cultured overnight. The bacterial suspensions were adjusted to an OD600 nm of 0.6 in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 150 μM acetosyringone and 10 mM MES, pH 5.6). Equal volumes of Agrobacteria carrying pairs of nLUC and cLUC constructs of interest and controls were co-infiltrated into 4-week-old N. benthamiana leaves. Forty-eight hours post-infiltration, 150 μg ml−1 D-luciferin potassium salt (ST196, Beyotime) was sprayed onto the abaxial surface of tobacco leaves, followed by a 3-min dark reaction. Chemiluminescent signals were detected using a PlantView100 multispectral dynamic fluorescence microscope system (BLT Photon Technology).

Recent findings suggest that for bimolecular fluorescence complementation assays, the full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ lacking the translational stop codon was amplified and cloned into the cYFP vector pSm35s-cYFP (BioRun), whereas the coding sequences lacking the translational stop codons of TaAKS1, TaWRKY46, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 were amplified and cloned into the nYFP vector pSm35s-nYFP (BioRun). The resulting constructs were introduced into A. tumefaciens GV3101 and subsequently infiltrated into the leaves of 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants. The infiltration buffer contained 10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM 2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid and 150 μM acetosyringone, adjusted to pH 5.6. The bacterial suspension was diluted to an OD600 nm of 0.4 before infiltration. Forty-eight hours post-infiltration, YFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) with an excitation wavelength of 514 nm and an emission wavelength range of 525–555 nm.

The same constructs were transformed into wheat protoplasts, which were incubated for 20 h to allow transient expression. YFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus), with nuclei labelled using DAPI. Total proteins were extracted using RIPA complete lysis buffer (P0045, Beyotime) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail for plant cell and tissue extracts (P0040, Beyotime). The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000g for 15 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants were obtained for SDS–PAGE and western blotting. Western blotting (described below) was performed using the primary antibody anti-GFP tag mouse monoclonal antibody (1:1,000; A02020, Abbkine), followed by horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibody (1:500; P0946, Beyotime).

Full-length cDNAs of EpTFIIAγ, TaAKS1, TaARF6, TaVOZ1 and TaWRKY46 were amplified by PCR and cloned into the pMAL-c5X vector (for MBP tagging), pET32a (Novagen; for His or HA tagging) or the pGEX4T-1 vector (Merck; for GST-tagged expression) using the ClonExpress II One-Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme) following the manufacturers’ instructions and lacking the respective translational start or stop codons as required. The resulting recombinant plasmids were transformed into Escherichia coli Rosetta and cultured in LB medium supplemented with ampicillin at 37 °C. When the culture reached OD600 nm of 0.4–0.6, protein expression was induced by adding 0.5 mM isopropyl-β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside, followed by incubation at 16 °C for 14–16 h. The expressed proteins and corresponding controls were subsequently purified using the GST-tag Protein Purification Kit (P2253, Beyotime), anti-HA affinity gel (P2287, Beyotime) or Dextrin beads 6FF (SA026100, Smart-Lifesciences) according to the respective manufacturer’s protocols. The proteins were separated by 10% SDS–PAGE and detected with anti-HA (AH158-IgG1, Beyotime), anti-GST (AM926, Beyotime) and anti-MBP (66003-1-Ig, Proteintech Group) antibodies, respectively.

According to recent reports, MBP-tagged EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were individually incubated with GST, GST–TaAKS1, GST–TaWRKY46, GST–TaARF6, HA–TaVOZ1, GST–TaTFIIAαβ or GST–AtTFIIAαβ at 4 °C for 3 h. Protein complexes were immunoprecipitated using BeyoGold GST-tag purification resin (P2253, Beyotime) or anti-HA affinity gel (P2287, Beyotime) at 4 °C for 4 h. After incubation, complexes were collected by centrifugation at 300g for 5 min, followed by five washes with phosphate-buffered saline. Proteins were separated by 10% SDS–PAGE and detected by western blotting (described below) using anti-GST antibody (1:1,000 dilution; AM926, Beyotime), anti-HA antibody (1:1,000 dilution, AF2305, Beyotime) and anti-MBP antibody (1:1,000 dilution; 66003-1-Ig, Proteintech Group), and HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (H + L) or goat anti-rabbit IgG (H + L) secondary antibodies (diluted 1:1,000; A0216 and A0208, respectively, Beyotime).

Sources indicate that for co-immunoprecipitation assays, fusion constructs including EpTFIIAγ–GFP, TaAKS1–GFP, TaARF6–mCherry, TaWRKY46–mCherry, EpTFIIAγ–mCherry and TaVOZ1–GFP were prepared in pCAMBIA1302 and pICH86988 vectors, respectively. Combinations of these constructs were co-transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101, which was subsequently infiltrated into the leaves of N. benthamiana in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM 2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid and 150 μM acetosyringone, pH of 5.6). After 48 h of transient expression, total proteins were extracted using RIPA complete lysis buffer (P1015, Beyotime) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail for plant cell and tissue extracts (P0040, Beyotime). The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000g for 15 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants were incubated with GFP-Trap beads (GTA-20, ChromoTek) at 4 °C for 3 h with gentle rotation. Corresponding protein complexes were obtained after a series of washing steps and elution steps. Input and eluted proteins were then resolved by SDS–PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. Western blotting was performed using primary antibodies to GFP (1:2,000; AE012, Abclonal) or mCherry (1:1,000; ABM40125, Abbkine), followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:500; P0946, Beyotime).

In a recent development, epTFIIAγ and SEUSS69 were cloned into the pET-15b expression vector (for His tagging) and heterologously expressed in E. coli Rosetta cells. The recombinant proteins were purified using NTA-Ni magnetic agarose beads with the His-Tag Protein Purification Kit (P2247S, Beyotime) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For phase-separation assays, purified proteins were diluted to 10 μM in phase-separation buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM dithiothreitol). 10% PEG8000 was included as a molecular crowding agent to promote condensate formation. Samples were gently mixed and equilibrated at room temperature before imaging. Condensates were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) equipped with a ×60 oil-immersion objective (NA = 1.42) and images were processed using FV31S-SW software.

Protein concentration was determined using a BCA assay kit (PA115-02, Tiangen Biotech). SDS–PAGE was performed with a PAGE Gel Fast Preparation Kit (EpiZyme). Protein samples (obtained from either prokaryotic expression, in vitro and in planta validation) were mixed with 5× SDS loading buffer at a 4:1 ratio, boiled at 95 °C for 5 min and cooled on ice. Ten micrograms of protein sample and 5 μl of 10–180 kDa molecular-weight marker (WJ103, EpiZyme) were loaded onto gels. Electrophoresis was run at 80 V until samples entered the separating gel, then adjusted to 120 V until bromophenol blue reached the gel bottom. For wet transfer, the gel, 0.45-μm PVDF membrane and filter papers were soaked in transfer buffer (PS109, EpiZyme) for 15 min to equilibrate. A transfer stack was assembled, and transfer was conducted at a constant current of 300 mA at 4 °C. Post-transfer, the PVDF membrane was blocked with 5% w/v non-fat milk (prepared in transfer buffer; PS109, EpiZyme) on a shaker at room temperature for 2 h. The membrane was then incubated with primary antibody (1:1,000 dilution in 5% w/v non-fat milk, adjusted per antibody instructions) on a shaker at 4 °C overnight. After three washes with TBST (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl and 0.1% (v/v) Tween-20), the membrane was incubated with 1:1,000 HRP-labelled secondary antibody (diluted in 5% w/v non-fat milk) at room temperature for 1.5 h. The membrane was washed three times with TBST and once with TBS for 5 min. Chemiluminescent signals were detected using ECL substrate (34098CN, Thermo Fisher Scientific) after 2 min of dark incubation, and images were captured with a chemiluminescent imaging system.

In a recent development, transgenic wheat, rice, maize and Arabidopsis plants, along with non-transgenic controls, were used for the assay for EpTFIIAγ abundance. The anti-EpTFIIAγ antibody was generated by Genecreate via rabbit immunization with EpTFIIAγ-specific short polypeptides, and its specificity was verified by western blotting. Seedlings of rice, maize and wheat were grown to the three-leaf stage under the aforementioned culture conditions; Arabidopsis seedlings were grown for 2 weeks. For each plant, 2 g of leaves were weighed, quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen and ground into powder in a pre-cooled mortar. The powder was transferred to a pre-cooled 50-ml centrifuge tube, and 5 ml of plant RIPA lysis buffer (P0045, Beyotime) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (50×; P1055, Beyotime) was added. After resuspension, the mixture was incubated on ice for 30 min, then centrifuged at 12,000g for 15 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was collected for subsequent experiments. Protein concentration was determined by the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) method. A total of 15–20 μg of protein was mixed with 5× SDS–PAGE sample loading buffer (P0015, Beyotime) at a 4:1 ratio, boiled at 95 °C for 5 min and cooled on ice. SDS–PAGE was performed with a 12% separating gel: electrophoresis at 80 V until samples entered the separating gel, then adjusted to 120 V until bromophenol blue reached the gel bottom. A 10–180-kDa molecular-weight marker (WJ103, EpiZyme) was used as a reference. Proteins were transferred to a 0.45-μm PVDF membrane by wet transfer (constant current of 300 mA at 4 °C for 90 min). The membrane was blocked with 5% w/v non-fat milk (prepared in TBST) at room temperature for 2 h, then incubated overnight at 4 °C with the anti-EpTFIIAγ antibody (1:500 dilution in 5% w/v non-fat milk). After three washes with TBST, the membrane was incubated with HRP-labelled goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (A0208, Beyotime) at 1:5,000 dilution for 1 h at room temperature. Following three additional TBST washes, the membrane was developed with ECL chemiluminescent substrate, and images were captured with a chemiluminescent imaging system. The target protein expression level was analysed based on the presence of the target band. Actin was used as a loading control, detected with an anti-actin antibody (AA128, Beyotime) and HRP-labelled goat anti-mouse secondary antibody (A0216, Beyotime).

Total protein was extracted from seedling leaves using plant protein extraction buffer (AS08300, Agrisera). Equal amounts of protein (10 μg) were resolved by 12.5% SDS–PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Amersham, GE Healthcare). Membranes were probed with primary antibodies to Cyt b6 (AS184069, Agrisera), PsbA (AS05084, Agrisera), PsbD (AS06146, Agrisera), AtpB (AS05085, Agrisera), RbcL (AS03037, Agrisera), RbcS (AS07259, Agrisera), Lhca2 (AS01006, Agrisera) and Lhcb2 (AS01003, Agrisera) at the recommended dilutions, followed by incubation with a goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (1:10,000; AS09602, Agrisera). Actin (AA128, Beyotime) served as the loading control, and protein signals were visualized using the standard chemiluminescence detection described above.

Sources indicate that three-leaf-stage seedling leaves of transgenic wheat expressing EpTFIIAγ–HA in the cv. Fielder background were collected and used for ChIP as previously described70. In brief, 2 g of plant tissue was washed twice with cold phosphate-buffered saline buffer and crosslinked with 1% v/v formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature. The crosslinking was quenched by adding glycine to a final concentration of 125 mM. Samples were then lysed in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 10 mM EDTA, 1% w/v SDS and protease inhibitor cocktail. Chromatin was extracted on ice and sonicated to obtain soluble, sheared fragments with an average DNA length of 200–500 bp. A 20-μl aliquot was reserved as the input control and stored at –20 °C, whereas 100 μl of the sheared chromatin was used for immunoprecipitation with 10 μg of anti-HA antibody (ChIP grade, ab9110, Abcam) overnight at 4 °C. Subsequently, 30 μl of protein A/G magnetic beads was added, followed by incubation for 3 h. Beads were sequentially washed with low-salt buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.1, 50 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 1% v/v Triton X-100 and 0.1% w/v SDS), twice with high-salt buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.1, 250 mM LiCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% v/v NP-40 and 1% w/v deoxycholic acid), and twice with TE buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 and 1 mM EDTA). Chromatin was eluted in 300 μl of elution buffer (100 mM NaHCO3 and 1% w/v SDS), treated with RNase A (8 μg ml−1) at 65 °C for 6 h, followed by proteinase K (345 μg ml−1) digestion overnight at 45 °C. Immunoprecipitated DNA was then used to prepare sequencing libraries using the NEXTFLEX ChIP–seq Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NOVA-5143-02, Bioo Scientific) and sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using a paired-end 150-bp strategy.

Low-quality sequencing reads were filtered using Trimmomatic (v0.36)71. Clean reads were aligned to the wheat reference genome (IWGSC RefSeq v1.1) using bowtie2 (v2.5.4)72. SAMtools (v1.3.1)73 was used to remove PCR duplicates from the aligned data. MACS3 (v3.0.3)74 was used for peak calling using default parameters (bandwidth = 300 bp; model fold = 5, 50; q value = 0.05). Each peak was assigned to the gene for the TSS of which was closest to the peak midpoint. Motif analysis within the peaks was conducted using HOMER (v3)75 with default settings and a maximum motif length of 12 bp. Gene Ontology functional enrichment analysis was performed using the clusterProfiler package in R76. Statistical significance was determined using a hypergeometric test with a P value threshold of 0.05.

Industry observers note that to validate ChIP–seq results, ChIP–qPCR was performed. One microlitre of purified ChIP DNA was used as template in a 20-μl qPCR containing SYBR Green Master Mix (Q121-02/03, Vazyme). Amplification was carried out using a Bio-Rad CFX96 real-time PCR system. Primers were designed to amplify genomic regions containing predicted binding sites based on ChIP–seq results. Each qPCR was conducted in four times. Enrichment values were calculated as mean ± s.d. from three biological replicates and are presented. Non-specific IgG and primers targeting intergenic regions were included as negative controls. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 15.

It has been revealed that total RNA was extracted from leaves of wild-type Fielder and two EpTFIIAγ–HA transgenic lines (TL4 and TL7) using TRIzol reagent (15596026, Invitrogen). Genomic DNA was removed by DNase I treatment following extraction. RNA concentration and purity were determined using a Nanodrop OneC Spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) by examining the A260:A280 ratio. RNA integrity was confirmed through 1.5% w/v agarose gel electrophoresis and quantified using a Qubit 3.0 fluorometer with the Qubit RNA Broad Range Assay kit (Q10210, Life Technologies). For library construction, 2 μg of total RNA was used to prepare strand-specific RNA-seq libraries with the KC Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (DR08402, Wuhan Seqhealth), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Libraries were enriched for fragments ranging from 200 to 500 bp, quantified and sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform using paired-end reads.

Raw sequencing reads were quality filtered using Trimmomatic (v0.36)71 to remove adapter sequences and low-quality reads. Clean reads were aligned to the wheat reference genome IWGSC RefSeq (v1.1) using GEM (v2.5)77. PCR duplicates were removed, and gene expression levels were quantified using DESeq2 (ref. 78). DEGs were identified using a threshold of |log2 (fold change)| > 1 and P < 0.05. Gene Ontology classification and enrichment analysis of DEGs were conducted using the clusterProfiler package76, identifying statistically significantly enriched terms among upregulated and downregulated genes.

According to recent reports, paired-end CUT&Tag79 reads were quality filtered with fastp80 and aligned to the wheat cv. Fielder reference genome using bowtie2 (v2.5.4)72 in end-to-end, very-sensitive mode. Reads with mapping quality < 20 were removed, and duplicate reads were removed after processing with samtools fixmate and samtools markdup73. Genome-wide RPKM-normalized bigWig tracks were generated with deepTools bamCoverage, and signal enrichment around genes and TSSs was visualized using computeMatrix and plotHeatmap81. Peaks were called for each replicate with MACS3 (v3.0.3)74 using matched IgG/input controls. Reproducible peaks between biological replicates were identified using IDR82 and used as consensus peaks. Consensus peaks were annotated against the Fielder genome annotation83. Promoter-associated target genes were defined at the peak–gene pair level: a gene was retained only when its own signed distance from the peak to the TSS satisfied distance to TSS ≤ 3 kb. Motif enrichment was performed on promoter peak regions using HOMER75 with sequence extraction and shuffled genomic background generation performed using BEDTools84.

EMSA was performed using the Chemiluminescent EMSA Kit (GS009, Beyotime Biotech) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Biotin-labelled DNA probes containing putative binding motifs were synthesized by Sangon Biotech and used at a final concentration of 0.05 μM per reaction. Each 20-μl binding reaction contained 4 μl of 5× EMSA/gel-shift binding buffer, 1 μg of recombinant protein (MBP tagged or GST tagged) and the biotin-labelled probe. Reactions were incubated at 23 °C for 30 min, then separated on a native 8% polyacrylamide gel in 0.5× TBE buffer (R0223, Beyontime) at 100 V for 1 h. DNA–protein complexes were transferred onto a nylon membrane (FFN10, Beyontime) and crosslinked by UV. Detection of biotin-labelled DNA was performed using a streptavidin–HRP conjugate and chemiluminescent substrate according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Negative controls included using MBP or GST. Washing and visualization were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Industry observers note that to assess transcriptional regulation mediated by EpTFIIAγ, 1.5-kb promoter regions of selected target genes were cloned into the pGreenII-0800-LUC vector to produce reporter constructs, whereas the EpTFIIAγ coding sequence was cloned into the pGreenII-62-SK vector to produce an effector construct25. Empty pGreenII-0800-LUC and pGreenII-62-SK vectors were used as negative controls. Effector and reporter plasmids were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 (pSoup-p19), which was subsequently co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves and left to allow transient expression for 2 days. LUC and REN activities were subsequently measured using the Dual Luciferase Reporter Gene Assay Kit (RG027, Beyotime), and relative luciferase activity was calculated as the ratio of LUC-to-REN activity.

To investigate the effect of EpTFIIAγ on the transcriptional activity of its assayed interacting proteins (TaAKS1, TaARF6, TaVOZ1 and TaWRKY46), the EpTFIIAγ coding sequence was cloned into the pCAMBIA1302 vector, whereas the coding sequences of the transcription factors were cloned into the pGreenII-62-SK vector. Promoter regions (1.5 kb) of downstream target genes (TaDREB1C, TaFBH4, TaMYBR1, TaVND7, TaCol-B5, TaCIN2, TaSWEET4, TaSWEET12, TaYCF9, TaCP47, TaCOG1 and TaGAPC1) were cloned into pGreenII-0800-LUC to generate reporter constructs. Effector and reporter plasmids were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 (pSoup-p19), which was subsequently co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves and left to allow transient expression for 2 days. Luciferase activities were measured as described above, and relative transcriptional activity was determined by calculating the LUC:REN ratio. Empty pCAMBIA1302 and pGreenII-62-SK vectors were used as negative controls. All experiments were conducted with at least three biological replicates.

Fungal and plant TFIIAγ candidates were retrieved from the JGI MycoCosm portal85 and the OneKP project86, respectively. Protein-level similarity searches were conducted using EpTFIIAγ and representative TFIIAγ proteins as queries. Partial fragments and sequences with abnormal lengths (outside 70–150 amino acids) were removed. Redundant identical sequences from the same species were collapsed, but distinct isoforms passing the filtering criteria were retained. Ultimately, 3,183 fungal and 1,245 Viridiplantae sequences were included, resulting in a final dataset of 4,428 TFIIAγ proteins (Supplementary Table 7).

Filtered protein sequences were aligned with MAFFT (v7.525)87 using the automatic strategy selection mode. Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic inference was performed with IQ-TREE (v3.0.1)88. The best-fitting amino acid substitution model was selected with ModelFinder, and branch support was estimated using 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates and 1,000 Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like approximate likelihood ratio test replicates. The resulting tree was visualized as a circular phylogeny using custom Python scripts with Biopython (v1.84) and Matplotlib (v3.10.8).

Protein structure prediction for TFIIAγ was conducted using AlphaFold3 (ref. 89) for orthologues from E. pusillum (EPUS02736), wheat (TraesCS1D02G024600), rice (LOC_Os01g73890), maize (Zm00001eb356100) and Arabidopsis (AT4G24440) with default parameters, and the resulting models were visualized using PyMOL (v3.1.0).

It has been revealed that statistical tests were conducted using two-tailed Student’s t-tests, Kruskal–Wallis tests, one-way ANOVA, and Brown-Forsythe and Welch ANOVA in GraphPad Prism (v9.5.0). Differences were considered statistically significant at *P < 0.05 or **P < 0.01. Data are presented as the mean ± s.d. from at least three independent biological replicates or independent experiments unless otherwise specified in legends.

Sources indicate that J.W., Z.K. and H.M. conceived the original idea and designed the early experiments. L.D., F.L., X.Q., H.Z., C.F. and C.W. performed the major experimental work. Specifically, L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.F., C.W., B.L., S.W., P.J., Y.H., D.T., S.Y., Q.W., S.T., Z.S., L.S., M.Y., T.X., Y.L., S.Z., P.Z., W.F., J.H., J.Z. and G.Z. contributed to plant cultivation and phenotypic characterization under controlled and field conditions, including stress-resistance phenotyping, agronomic trait assessment, grain-filling analysis and physiological measurements. X.H. generated the transgenic plants. L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.F., C.W., B.L., S.T., Z.S., L.S. and J.H. conducted the microscopy and imaging analyses. F.L., H.Z., B.L., C.W., D.T. and Q.W. performed the biochemical and protein-related experiments. L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.W., S.W., S.L. and D.T. conducted the molecular and transcriptional regulation assays. B.C., Z.Q. and Y.W. performed the genomic, transcriptomic and computational analyses. L.D. and Z.Q. conducted the phylogenetic analysis and protein structure prediction. L.D., F.L., X.Q., H.Z., C.F. and C.W. performed the statistical analyses and data quantification. H.M. and L.D. wrote the manuscript with input from X.Q., J.W. and Z.K. All authors reviewed and approved the final manuscript.

A patent application related to the work described in this article has been filed in China. The patent applicants are the Institute of Microbiology, Chinese Academy of Sciences and Northwest A&F University. The inventors are J.W., Z.K., X.Q., H.M., Xinli Wei, Y.W. and F.L. The application number is 202111602359.2, and the patent application is at the moment under substantive examination. The patent application covers the use of the extremophile gene EpTFIIAγ for improving abiotic stress resistance in wheat, rice and maize. The other authors declare no other competing interests.

(a) Functional co-expression network of EpTFIIAγ target genes. Co-expression relationships among EpTFIIAγ target genes were inferred from published expression data (https://wheat.cau.edu.cn/wGRN/) using the WGCNA signed topological overlap matrix (TOM). Node color denotes functional module, and larger nodes indicate EMSA-validated targets. (b, c) Volcano plots showing up-regulated and down-regulated genes in transgenic EpTFIIAγ line 4 (b) and line 7 (c) versus wild-type Fielder under well-watered conditions. Transcripts with a fold change > 2 or < 0.5 and an adjusted P-value < 0.05 were considered differentially expressed. (d, e) Venn diagram of up-regulated (d) and down-regulated (e) differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in two transgenic EpTFIIAγ lines compared to Fielder controls (|Fold Change| > 2, P < 0.05). (f, g) Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of up-regulated (f) and down-regulated (g) genes identified in transgenic EpTFIIAγ lines. In (b-e), statistical analysis of differentially expressed genes was conducted using the two-sided Wald test within the DESeq2 R package, with subsequent adjustment for multiple comparisons achieved through the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method. In (f) and (g), statistical analysis was assessed using a one-sided hypergeometric over-representation test.

Owner Gerry Cardinale is ready to put his money where his mouth is when it comes to building an AC Milan team that can win trophies.

Industry observers note that cardinale has already spoken publicly about his desire to strengthen the squad available to Ruben Amorim with some further reinforcements in January. While money will not be spent for the sake of it, the American seems infatuated by Endrick, and he certainly will not come cheap.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Corriere dello Sport (via PianetaMilan) confirm this morning that Milan are preparing for ‘significant investment’ in the January window, but they also take a look at the Rossoneri’s financial situation, trying to determine whether these costs are sustainable.

In a recent development, looking at the summer transfer window, €160m was invested on incomings with the club-record signing of Goncalo Ramos as well as the additions of Mario Gila and Diego Moreira. Another €70m could be spent in the winter on Endrick, making it €230m in 2026-27.

Sources indicate that then, two renewals were closed, while work is still underway for Adrien Rabiot. Christian Pulisic went from €3.5m to €5m net per season, while Strahinja Pavlovic went from €1.7m to €3m net per season.

Recent findings suggest that as the newspaper reports, the cost of the squad has already increased by €40m this season. With these investments and without any major sales, the 2026-27 budget could close with a deficit of €140-150m.

The club have room to keep the squad ratio under control, but sporting results will be needed to support it. Otherwise, there’s a risk of ending up under another Settlement Agreement with UEFA, which brings further constraints.

In a recent development, A full-back and centre-back have been tipped to arrive too, which would make things even more precarious. Corriere dello Sport conclude that Cardinale’s move is risky, and it will require almost guaranteed Champions League qualification for the year.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that luciano Spalletti will not hold his eve-of-match press conference before Sunday's trip to Fiorentina.
  • Juventus will travel to Florence without the usual preview from their coach.
  • The run began with a 2-0 win over Napoli at the Allianz Stadium on 1 November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that luciano Spalletti will not hold his eve-of-match press conference before Sunday's trip to Fiorentina. Juventus arrive on two straight wins, chasing fourth place, against a coach Spalletti has never beaten.

Juventus will travel to Florence without the usual preview from their coach. Sunday’s game at the Franchi kicks off at 20:45. The squad got back to Turin overnight from the Netherlands. The reason given is the club’s crowded run of fixtures, TuttoJuve reported. It is the last game before the international break.

The run began with a 2-0 win over Napoli at the Allianz Stadium on 1 November. Kerim Alajbegovic scored in the 70th minute. Aged 19 years and 41 days, no foreign player had ever found the net at a younger age in a Serie A game between Juventus and Napoli.

Four days later, Juventus won 2-1 away at AZ Alkmaar in the Europa League. Teun Koopmeiners and Randal Kolo Muani scored. The result takes them to 10 points from four games in the competition. After the match, Spalletti described himself as very pleased with a solid team display against strong opponents. He felt his side should have added a third goal.

Recent findings suggest that the league position still needs work. The club’s stated aim this season is fourth place, and Como presently hold that spot. The defence gives some grounds for confidence. Going back to last March, no side can match the Bianconeri’s tally of 12 shutouts. Roma are next on 11.

Vanoli and Spalletti have faced each other only twice as coaches. Both meetings were Fiorentina-Juventus fixtures last season. Last November they drew 1-1 at the Franchi. Filip Kostic gave Juventus the lead before Rolando Mandragora equalised with a long-range shot.

The hosts’ struggles on their own pitch offer Juventus an opening against a side yet to find its footing at home.

Industry observers note that the fixture carries plenty of history. Sunday’s game is the 175th Serie A meeting between the sides, according to the club’s statistical preview. Juventus have won 82, Fiorentina 37, and 55 have ended level. Juventus have scored 275 top-flight goals against Fiorentina. Two more would draw them level with Inter’s 277, the highest total by any side against the Viola.

Once the international break is over, Juventus’s next Serie A match is on 22 November.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 13:52.
  • Aiming to remain unbeaten at home in the league this season, promotion-hunting Birmingham City host struggling Bolton Wanderers at St Andrew's @ Knighthead Park in the Championship on Saturday afternoon.
  • Blues were the latest side to take advantage of Burnley's Turf Moor misery on Wednesday night, whilst the Wanderers suffered defeat on their own patch by West Bromwich Albion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 13:52.

Aiming to remain unbeaten at home in the league this season, promotion-hunting Birmingham City host struggling Bolton Wanderers at St Andrew's @ Knighthead Park in the Championship on Saturday afternoon.

Blues were the latest side to take advantage of Burnley's Turf Moor misery on Wednesday night, whilst the Wanderers suffered defeat on their own patch by West Bromwich Albion.

As has been the case after each of their three Championship defeats so far this season, Birmingham City bounced back from last weekend's Stoke City disappointment by claiming three points, this time at the expense of crisis-hit Burnley.

Chris Davies's side have already equalled the number of away victories that they managed across the entirety of last season (6) courtesy of August Priske's seventh league goal of the term and an own goal from Clarets winger Jaydon Banel at Turf Moor.

Following seven wins from their past nine second-tier contests, Birmingham are occupying fourth position in the Championship table, three points behind current pacesetters Middlesbrough and Stoke.

Apart from a 6-1 battering by Brentford in the EFL Cup, Blues have been impressive at St Andrew's this season, with Saturday's hosts unbeaten across their opening eight home league battles (W4 D4).

In fact, Birmingham last experienced Second City defeat in the Championship at the beginning of April, and Davies has lost just three home league games since taking charge during the summer of 2024.

Sliding towards the relegation zone, Bolton Wanderers have now won just one of their past seven Championship contests (D2 L4) after losing to West Brom at the Toughsheet Community Stadium earlier in the week.

A second-half penalty from Ruben Rodrigues levelled the scores momentarily following Albion's opener, however, further strikes from Norwegian duo Aune Heggebo and Felix Horn Myhre sentenced the Wanderers to a fourth defeat in their past six games.

Winless in their past five games (D1 L4) at the Toughsheet, Bolton's last three victories have all arrived on the road, with Saturday's underdog visitors beating Norwich City (4-3), Wolverhampton Wanderers (3-1) and Charlton Athletic (1-0) since late September.

There is no doubting that the newly-promoted side are one of the favourites to suffer relegation this season, with Steven Schumacher's troops at the moment six points clear of the bottom three.

Bolton were defeated on their most recent trip to St Andrew's in October 2024 but were one of only three teams to beat Birmingham during their record-breaking League One title romp of 2024-25.

Birmingham City Championship form:.

Bolton Wanderers Championship form:.

Birmingham defender Ethan Laird missed the Burnley win after picking up a knock at Stoke last weekend, with the right-back a doubt for the Second City match on Saturday.

As a result, Bright Osayi-Samuel is likely to retain his spot in defence, with Dael Fry set to drop out in order to make room for the available-again Christoph Klarer.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Fiorentina went ahead again in the 54th minute. Guglielmo Vicario made the first save, but the Juventus defenders were too slow to clear. Alieu Njie forced in the rebound. Bremer then reached a Douglas Luiz corner in the six-yard box before David de Gea could get to it.

It has been revealed that juventus completed 384 accurate passes to Fiorentina’s 273. Fiorentina still attempted 22 shots to Juventus’s 18, and both sides had 6 on target. The expected goals figures, 2.46 for Juventus and 2.14 for Fiorentina, are consistent with a fairly even contest despite the visitors’ control of the ball.

The closing stages could have gone either way. Former Juventus defender Radu Drăgușin headed in from a corner in the 82nd minute. The goal was ruled out because he pushed Bremer with both hands. Near the end, Vicario saved twice in quick succession to protect the point. Juventus also claimed a penalty when the ball struck João Mário’s arm in the Fiorentina area, but none was given.

Referee Andrea Colombo booked three Juventus players. Juan Cabal was cautioned in the 13th minute and Bremer in the 22nd. Kolo Muani was booked for dissent in the 73rd. Christ Inao Oulaï was Fiorentina’s only booking.

Juventus were without the injured Kenan Yildiz, Andrea Cambiaso, Nico González, Manuel Locatelli, Khéphren Thuram and Kamil Grabara. Weston McKennie and Zeki Çelik returned to the squad. Spalletti made three changes in the 57th minute, sending on Zhegrova for Woltemade, Alajbegovic for Boga and Celik for Cabal. Ekhator replaced McKennie in the 78th minute and Gatti came on for Lucumí in the 89th.

According to recent reports, at his press conference at the Franchi, Spalletti said he was not happy because his team does not play at a steady enough level to aim for anything key. He did praise Kolo Muani, describing him as the player everyone wanted and one he can use as a centre-forward or out wide. Shown a replay of the João Mário incident, he dodged the question and asked, smiling, for a different one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that juventus Next Gen were beaten 4-0 at Lecco in Serie C Girone A, with three of the goals coming after half-time. Coach Massimo Brambilla admitted his young side give goals away too easily, and the table now reflects a long poor run.

At the Stadio Rigamonti-Ceppi, the manner of the defeat was as worrying as the scoreline.

Industry observers note that the opener set the tone. Lecco needed only six minutes to go ahead. Casarotto ran through the middle, got past Corradi and beat goalkeeper Mangiapoco. Lecco held that single-goal lead until half-time.

Sources indicate that next Gen did have one clear opening before the break. In the 40th minute, Grelaud shot from near the penalty spot. Vettorel turned the effort over for a corner.

The second half was one-way traffic. Capello made it 2-0 in the 50th minute, and Manetti added a third in the 56th. Capello struck from close range after the goalkeeper parried Pellegrino’s second attempt. Murillo’s goal in the 72nd minute summed up the match. Mangiapoco erred as Juventus built from the back, and Murillo pounced.

According to recent reports, the hosts are in strong form. This was their second 4-0 win in a row, after beating Dolomiti Bellunesi by the same score. Lecco have now scored 15 goals in four games.

It has been revealed that massimo Brambilla did not hide from the problems. He told TuttoMercatoWeb that his side struggled against Lecco’s high press. His players found it hard to keep the ball against a team pressing hard and man-to-man.

The coach also admitted that coming back became difficult after the second goal. He remarked his players must improve how they read the game and stop giving away goals so easily.

It has been revealed that the table makes the warning sharper. Brambilla’s side sit third from bottom after the defeat, having won just one of their last 12 matches.

Sources indicate that the result also matters beyond Serie C. Carnevali has put the youth sector at the centre of the club’s prepares.

Recent findings suggest that one player supporters will watch is Destiny Elimoghale, who came off the bench at Lecco. Next Gen had started in a 3-5-2, with Durmisi and Merola in attack. Elimoghale replaced Durmisi in the 40th minute of the second half. The forward was born in 2009. His new contract, announced on 3 November, runs until 30 June 2029.

Elimoghale was called up to the first-team squad for the first time on 17 September 2026. That call-up came for the opening Europa League league-phase match against NEC.

The next opponents arrive in good spirits. Treviso beat Novara 2-0 in round 13. Romeo scored in the 24th minute, and Paganini added the second in the 59th.

The next test comes rapidly. Next Gen host Treviso in round 14 on Sunday 15 November at 17:30. A trip to Giana Erminio follows on Saturday 21 November, at the same kick-off time.

Enzo Maresca is still searching for answers after Man City's draw with Napoli: There were glimpses of improvement but individual mistakes again proved their undoing, writes JACK GAUGHAN

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (956 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 17:07 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:02 EST, 25 November 2026.
  • According to recent reports, the message from Enzo Maresca ought to be clear when Manchester City convene for their meeting at the training ground this weekend before heading down to London.
  • It has been revealed that he has to say that Arsenal away must be considered the perfect game for his players at this point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 17:07 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:02 EST, 25 November 2026.

According to recent reports, the message from Enzo Maresca ought to be clear when Manchester City convene for their meeting at the training ground this weekend before heading down to London. Clear because there is no other appropriate message to impart, really.

It has been revealed that he has to say that Arsenal away must be considered the perfect game for his players at this point. The opportunity to reignite their season, to stand up, to show the Premier League they are not going anywhere just quite yet. Squads who went before them would certainly approach a fixture of this magnitude with that attitude. A squad with Kevin De Bruyne as its linchpin would.

City were still searching for answers against Napoli, a point rescued late on by Rayan Cherki. But despite the growing frustration in the stands, that unmistakable guttural desperation for just a bit more of something, it was better. More joined up thinking, at least.

An inverted full back did that for them and it perhaps should be the blueprint for the manager when they arrive at the Emirates on Sunday. City were eminently more comfortable with that; knew where they stood. Nico O'Reilly was not particularly brilliant in that position yet his presence, the safety net of somebody alongside Ayyoub Bouaddi in possession and in turn freeing up Elliot Anderson will surely make City more formidable as the weeks go by.

The set-up presented another tactical tweak for Maresca as he searches for answers and consistency. Defensively, City were twice undone by individual mistakes rather than the overarching plan, one that stifled the enduring class of De Bruyne.

A gentle hum, the half-hearted chants for a returning king, resembled an afternoon session in front of a crowd drowsy from their liquid lunches before a seesawing four-goal second half felt more befitting of City's guest for the evening, UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin – intriguingly entertained by chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak in the directors' box.

Rayan Cherki rescued a point late on but this was another difficult night for Man City.

Former Man United striker Rasmus Hojlund celebrates his goal against his old rivals.

Ayyoub Bouaddi scored his first goal for Manchester City since joining from Lille.

According to recent reports, city, sporting a fourth kit that had an unfortunate Guantanamo quality to it, certainly had more of a clue than they did here on Saturday. There were clearer patterns – noticeably Marc Guehi piercing midfield lines with one incisive pass for O'Reilly – but this is a team whose confidence has been shaken in recent weeks and that will not return overnight. 'We were aggressive off the ball,' noted Maresca, while bemoaning conceding for a tenth consecutive match. 'Defensively we were good, pressing good.'.

Regardless, City's supporters definitely demanded more caution thrown to the wind and some of their players wore those looks too. Anderson's dangerous crosses from that right-hand channel – the area presided over by De Bruyne for a decade – occasionally proved unsettling for Napoli, while Allan should have scored from a ricocheting corner as captain Erling Haaland claimed a penalty for being dragged down.

Man City (4-2-3-1): Donnarumma 6; Nunes 5, Guehi 5, Gvardiol 6, O'Reilly 5; Bouaddi 7, Anderson 6; Cherki 7, Fernandez 6 (Ndiaye 63, 6), Allan 5 (Doku 54, 7); Haaland 5.

Napoli (4-1-4-1): Milinkovic-Savic 6; Spinazzola 7, Beukema 6, Rrahmani 7, Olivera 6; Gilmour 8; Politano 6, McTominay 6, De Bruyne 6, Lang 7; Hojlund 7.

Manager: Massimiliano Allegri 7.

In a sign that Maresca was placing more players in threatening areas, O'Reilly had headed over a Matheus Nunes cross – yet chances had been at a premium, those who should be protagonists taking too many safe options rather than pushing chests out and relishing responsibility.

And when there was risk, Napoli pounced. Cherki the culprit, flicking a ball around the corner aimlessly into the middle of his own half. Billy Gilmour gave thanks, punched towards Rasmus Hojlund and he spun Guehi to flash under Donnarumma ten minutes into the second half. Hojlund celebrated by shouting 'one club in Manchester' while holding a single finger aloft. 'It's good banter,' he stated and we'll take his word for that.

City had been warned of the danger, when Noa Lang went clean through before checking back upon realising he didn't possess the acceleration to complete the job.

Maresca's assistant, Danny Walker, shook his head on the bench as they pored over the goal's replay. Enzo Fernandez was planting his boot into one of Vanja Milinkovic-Savic's posts when the goalkeeper nonchalantly plucked a floated cross from the night sky.

City had stirred somewhat though, helped by the inclusion of Jeremy Doku – ironically introduced seconds before Hojlund's opener – and it was the Belgian who made their equaliser seven minutes after the hour. He waited and waited inside Napoli's box for defenders to commit, finding Bouaddi alone and the teenager wrapped his left foot around the pass and was swiftly racing back to halfway.

There had appeared a head of steam, only for O'Reilly to be caught well out of position as Napoli countered – City carved open – and Lang thundered a volley past Donnarumma with 14 minutes left. Cherki made amends for his earlier error by hammering into the far corner but was less than pleased.

'We played good but we don't give a lot of energy,' Cherki mentioned. 'We need to do more, we need to win these games, and today I don't care (about) scoring my goal. I want to win this game. We're going to London to win.'.

In fact, maybe that is the team talk.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A government spokesman has mentioned that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A government spokesman has mentioned that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

It has been revealed that since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective.".

Kornelius mentioned talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

In a recent development, "Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place.".

Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could matter visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions presently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he mentioned.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there.".

Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.

Sources indicate that the IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.

Looking to move on from their midweek Champions League collapse against Real Madrid, PSV Eindhoven return to the bread and butter of Eredivisie football on Saturday.

The defending champions welcome Go Ahead Eagles to the Philips Stadion in gameweek 14, seeking a response to their humbling experience in the Spanish capital as they chase a fourth consecutive top-flight victory.

An Ivan Perisic goal made things interesting at the Bernabeu in midweek, but a Jude Bellingham-inspired second-half performance saw Jose Mourinho's Los Blancos run riot and eventually claim a 5-1 victory over PSV.

That loss, the Dutch giants' third in five European matches, leaves them 30th in the 36-team league-phase standings and their top-eight prospects looking increasingly remote.

However, Peter Bosz's men remain in contention for the qualification playoffs, with 24th-placed Villarreal just two points ahead of the reigning Eredivisie champions.

The Farmers will undoubtedly welcome a return to home comforts on Saturday as they seek to regain winning momentum after their chastening experience in the Spanish capital.

League football has brought greater encouragement, particularly in recent weeks, with three consecutive victories following a run of one win in four matches between late September and late October.

Scoring at least four goals in each of their victories over Willem II (7-0), Cambuur (6-2) and NEC (4-1) suggests a return to their free-scoring best, boding well for this weekend's visit from Go Ahead Eagles.

The Deventer outfit travel to Eindhoven in indifferent form, with a 1-0 away victory over SBV Excelsior coming between defeats to Cambuur and Fortuna Sittard.

Particularly notable has been the attacking decline of Joseph Oosting's men, who have scored just once across their last three league matches after averaging 2.3 goals per game over the opening 10 gameweeks.

While that sample remains too small for firm conclusions, the Pride of the IJssel's dip cannot be dismissed ahead of their trip to the Philips Stadion, where Kowet claimed a stunning 2-1 KNVB Beker semi-final victory in February 2025 en route to lifting their first domestic cup.

Paul Simonis was in charge for that historic success as Go Ahead Eagles secured their first victory in Eindhoven for 57 years, and they now seek a first Eredivisie win at PSV since 1968.

That will be easier said than done, however, as their historical struggles and recent scoring decline leave them vulnerable against hosts still reeling from their Santiago Bernabeu beatdown.

No player has scored more Eredivisie goals than Sven Mijnans, with the versatile attacking midfielder registering nine strikes and three assists in the top flight.

Guus Til is likely to lead the attack despite Pepi's availability, while Ruben van Bommel offers a dual threat after contributing five goals and three assists.

Soren Tengstedt shares Mijnans's position atop the league's scoring charts, with no player outscoring the Kowet forward this season.
