Overlaying Pcdh RNA staining on Pcdh DNA loci labelled by ORCA revealed DNA traces that colocalized with RNA puncta (Extended Data Fig. 6a). By measuring distances between Pcdh loci and Pcdh RNA puncta, we identified a data-driven distance threshold below which RNA transcripts could be classified as nascent (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c). RNA puncta within this threshold were brighter than those beyond it, consistent with nascent transcriptional bursting33 (Extended Data Fig. 6d).

In a recent development, we then examined the spatial relationship between transcribing Pcdh DNA loci and H3K9me3 STORM signal in mOSNs. Remarkably, we observed many examples of nascent transcription occurring at Pcdh loci that colocalized with H3K9me3 STORM (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 7a). Plotting the ORCA traces of these loci alongside H3K9me3 STORM localizations revealed transcribing promoters spatially residing within heterochromatin (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 7a).

It has been revealed that to assess whether STORM captured a nuclear enrichment of H3K9me3 over the Pcdh locus, we quantified the number of H3K9me3 localizations surrounding Pcdh loci relative to randomized positions within the same nuclei. The median number of H3K9me3 localizations detected around Pcdh DNA loci exceeded that of randomized positions in 999 of 1,000 simulations (empirical P = 0.002) (Fig. 2c). We performed the same analyses on Tex15 loci, which are not marked by H3K9me3 as assayed by bulk nChIP–seq (Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). We used Tex15 nascent RNA transcripts as proxies for Tex15 DNA positions (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). In contrast to Pcdh loci, Tex15 loci did not show an enrichment for H3K9me3 (empirical P = 0.292) (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Furthermore, we observed more Tex15 loci lacking any H3K9me3 signal compared with Pcdh loci (Extended Data Fig. 7e).

Sources indicate that we next asked whether Pcdh transcription was associated with reduced local H3K9me3 signal and domain compaction by first dividing loci into those with or without detectable nascent transcription, the latter of which we hereafter refer to as non-transcribing. We then measured the number of H3K9me3 STORM localizations around these loci and the Rg of their heterochromatin domains by ORCA. Surprisingly, transcribing Pcdh loci had slightly higher H3K9me3 STORM signal and slightly more compact heterochromatin domains relative to non-transcribing loci (Fig. 2d,e). Furthermore, transcription of individual Pcdh genes was associated neither with a change in H3K9me3 STORM signal around transcribing promoters, at the resolution of our assay, nor with a change in heterochromatin domain compaction (Fig. 2f,g).

Overall, these analyses indicate that transcription of Pcdh loci can occur in H3K9me3-rich nuclear territories and does not disrupt the heterochromatin domain of the locus.

In a recent development, these data prompted us to further evaluate features of a transcribing Pcdh locus. To do that, we expanded the design of our RNA probes to a total of 31 Pcdh genes that showed appreciable staining and specificity (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). We noted that nascently transcribing RNA puncta often colocalized with other Pcdh RNAs of the same cluster (Fig. 3a), and more nascent puncta were detected for progressively downstream isoforms at the Pcdha and Pcdhg, but not Pcdhb, clusters (Fig. 3b). Meanwhile, mature transcript levels measured by bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) remained relatively flat across all clusters (Fig. 3b). We reasoned that these results could reflect nascent transcription of Pcdha and Pcdhg genes that reads through downstream isoforms (Fig. 3c). Yet, the number of nascent Pcdh RNAs detected at a locus was not associated with changes in heterochromatin domain Rg (Fig. 3d), indicating that this putative transcriptional readthrough occurs without domain decompaction.

Sources indicate that to identify features of locus architecture associated with transcription, we subtracted the contact frequency maps of non-transcribing loci from the maps of transcribing loci in mOSNs. This revealed an enrichment of enhancer–promoter contacts in transcribing loci (Fig. 3e–g), which was further supported by an increase in transcription probability as a function of enhancer–promoter proximity (Extended Data Fig. 8). For Pcdha and Pcdhg genes, these enhancer–promoter contact enrichments included promoters upstream of the transcribing isoform, and the magnitude of enrichment experienced by each promoter diminished when filtering on transcription of progressively downstream isoforms (Fig. 3e,g). By contrast, Pcdhb promoters had more local enhancer-contact enrichments upon transcription (Fig. 3f).

Industry observers note that together, these data indicate that at the Pcdha and Pcdhg clusters, transcription of chosen promoters reads through downstream genes. This pattern is consistent with splicing of Pcdha and Pcdhg variable exons to three small constant exons located 3′ of these clusters34, and was not observed at the Pcdhb cluster, which lacks constant exons. Furthermore, these data indicate that Pcdh gene choice is driven by highly specific enhancer–promoter interactions across this multi-gene, multi-enhancer locus.

Recent findings suggest that we next asked where Pcdh transcription and enhancer–promoter interactions occur within the spatial architecture of the locus (Fig. 1l) and, in particular, whether transcribing promoters remain within or exit the heterochromatin domain. To assess the positioning of transcribing promoters, we measured the distances between promoters and heterochromatic locus positions in the presence and absence of transcription in mOSNs (Fig. 4a). These distances did not change during transcription (Fig. 4a). On the other hand, distances between promoters and euchromatic locus positions decreased during transcription (Fig. 4a). This effect seemed driven by decreased distances between promoters and enhancers upon transcription (Fig. 4b). These results indicate that enhancer–promoter contacts associated with transcription bring euchromatic locus positions closer to the heterochromatin domain, but neither these contacts nor transcription itself cause transcribing promoters to exit the domain. Plotting transcription probability as a function of a promoter’s distance to the heterochromatin centre supported this conclusion, as promoters were most likely to be transcribing at distances within the median Rg of the heterochromatin domain (Fig. 4c).

To further dissect the positioning of enhancers and promoters relative to the heterochromatin and euchromatin compartments of the locus during contact, we calculated the distances of each locus position to the centre of the heterochromatin domain (dHC) and the centre of the euchromatic region housing the cluster-specific enhancer(s) of that position (dEC) (Extended Data Fig. 9a). We examined Pcdhb16 as a case study. In non-transcribing traces and transcribing traces without enhancer–promoter contacts, Pcdhb16 was closer to the heterochromatin centre than the euchromatin centre, whereas its enhancer HS18-22 showed the opposite relationship (Extended Data Fig. 9a). In Pcdhb16-transcribing traces with enhancer–promoter contacts, Pcdhb16 and its enhancer HS18-22 were more equidistant to the two centres (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Further evaluation of the equidistant state showed that the dHC of both promoter and enhancer decreased during contact, but that the enhancer dHC decreased by a greater magnitude (Extended Data Fig. 9b), consistent with promoters remaining within the heterochromatin domain during contact and the enhancers approaching the domain to engage promoters (Fig. 4a,b). Extending these analyses to all other Pcdh genes stained for showed similar positionings of transcribing Pcdh promoters and cognate enhancers relative to their compartment centres: when in contact, promoters and enhancers became more equidistant to the two centres; when not in contact, promoters were closer to the heterochromatin centre than the euchromatin centre, whereas enhancers were closer to the euchromatin centre (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Quantifying the percentage of transcribing traces with and without enhancer–promoter contacts revealed the latter state to be more prevalent (Extended Data Fig. 9e), indicating that promoters transcribe at positions closer to the heterochromatin centre, and that Pcdh transcription can be sustained in the absence of enhancer engagement.

Industry observers note that individual traces reflected the above behaviours. Transcribing promoters remained within the heterochromatin domain, and enhancers approached the domain to engage promoters (Fig. 4d).

Lastly, we investigated the genome folding mechanisms that establish Pcdh locus architecture and how this architecture supports stochastic Pcdh gene choice. The wild-type (WT) locus architecture is defined by stripes corresponding to enhancer–promoter contacts and by inter-cluster contacts within the heterochromatin domain (Fig. 1e). To abolish enhancer–promoter contacts, we conditionally removed Rad21, the kleisin subunit of the cohesin protein complex, using an Omp-ires-cre;Rad21fl/fl;tdTomatofl/fl (Rad21 cKO) mouse (Extended Data Fig. 10a). To perturb heterochromatin compaction, we conditionally deleted Setdb1, the SET domain bifurcated histone methyltransferase 1, which catalyses di- and trimethylation of H3K9, using an Omp-ires-cre;Setdb1fl/fl;tdTomatofl/fl (Setdb1 cKO) mouse (Extended Data Fig. 10a). We confirmed knockout of Rad21 and Setdb1 in mOSNs by immunofluorescence (Extended Data Fig. 10b), then performed ORCA in both mouse models.

It has been revealed that rad21 deletion abolished enhancer–promoter contacts as evidenced by a loss of stripes (Fig. 5a), consistent with previous reports10,13,15,27. By contrast, Setdb1 deletion resulted in a loss of inter-cluster contacts (Fig. 5a), which was accompanied by an approximately 40% reduction of H3K9me3 over the heterochromatin domain (Fig. 5b,c and Extended Data Fig. 10c). Furthermore, separation between heterochromatic and euchromatic regions of the locus increased in Rad21 cKO but decreased in Setdb1 cKO (Fig. 5d), whereas the relative size of the heterochromatin domain increased in Setdb1 cKO but decreased in Rad21 cKO (Fig. 5e).

For d and e, distributions are shown as violin plots. Horizontal lines and numbers indicate medians. Significance was assessed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Adjusted P values for Rad21 cKO versus WT, WT versus Setdb1 cKO and Rad21 cKO versus Setdb1 cKO, respectively: P = 1.5 × 10−103, P = 3.6 × 10−101 and P < 1 × 10−230 in d and P = 1.1 × 10−23, P = 2.3 × 10−71 and P = 2.6 × 10−229 in e. **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001. f, ORCA traces from each condition with the heterochromatin domain and Pcdh enhancers labelled. g, Percentage of mOSNs expressing each Pcdh gene across genotypes. Pcdhb1 is excluded.h, Change in percentage of mOSNs expressing Pcdha genes as a function of each gene’s distance to the HS5-1 enhancer in Rad21 cKO relative to WT. i, Change in percentage of mOSNs expressing Pcdha genes as a function of each gene’s distance to the heterochromatin domain boundary determined by nChIP–seq at the Pcdha cluster in Setdb1 cKO relative to WT.

Individual traces reflected these structural changes. Single molecules showed distancing of Pcdh enhancers from the heterochromatin domain in Rad21 cKO OSNs relative to WT (Fig. 5f), which was further supported by changes in the distance of each locus position relative to the heterochromatin domain centre (Extended Data Fig. 10d). Meanwhile, the heterochromatin domain seemed less compact and more intermixed with euchromatin in Setdb1 cKO OSNs relative to WT (Fig. 5f), which was further supported by an increase in the entropy of each locus position in Setdb1 cKO (Extended Data Fig. 10e). These data suggest that Pcdh enhancers require cohesin to approach the heterochromatin domain and contact target promoters, whereas heterochromatin keeps the promoters in a compact and ordered environment.

Sources indicate that to evaluate how these changes in Pcdh locus architecture affect stochastic Pcdh gene expression, we performed single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq). Ablation of Rad21 resulted in widespread downregulation of Pcdh expression in favour of Pcdhac2, the Pcdha gene most proximal to the HS5-1 enhancer, which also resides in euchromatin (Fig. 5g,h and Extended Data Fig. 10f,g). This gain in expression of enhancer-proximal Pcdh genes was not observed at the Pcdhg cluster, suggesting distinct enhancer–promoter specificities at the two clusters (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 10f,g). By contrast, ablation of Setdb1 resulted in upregulation of Pcdha10–12 and Pcdhgb6–b7, the genes closest to the heterochromatin–euchromatin boundaries at the locus (Fig. 5g,i and Extended Data Fig. 10f,h). Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies reflected these expression changes in both genotypes (Extended Data Fig. 10i,j).

These results indicate that DNA loop extrusion and heterochromatin compaction cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote an unbiased enhancer–promoter search space at the locus. While cohesin is required for Pcdh enhancers to gain access to the heterochromatin domain housing Pcdh promoters, the compaction of the domain expands the ability of the enhancers to find target promoters. Thus, although generally viewed as antagonistic processes35, both cohesin and heterochromatin-driven chromatin compartmentalization are indispensable for proper Pcdh expression.

Here we show that heterochromatin spatially partitions the Pcdh locus into a compacted domain housing Pcdh promoters and multiple open regions housing Pcdh enhancers. Transcription from chosen promoters occurs within the heterochromatin domain, and enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters (Extended Data Fig. 10k). Counterintuitively, Pcdh transcription can read through hundreds of kilobases without dissolving the compacted state of the locus (Extended Data Fig. 10k). We further demonstrate that Pcdh locus architecture and proper Pcdh expression are achieved through cooperation between heterochromatin-mediated compaction and cohesin-mediated DNA loop extrusion.

Our findings challenge the prevailing view that heterochromatin is a physically inaccessible chromatin structure. Heterochromatin compaction was initially proposed to sterically hinder the transcriptional machinery and thereby repress gene expression36,37. However, rather than acting as an impenetrable barrier, our data indicate that heterochromatin can support active transcription while retaining a compact 3D organization. These findings add to a growing body of evidence suggesting that heterochromatin is not intrinsically inaccessible and can support transcription. For example, 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)-dense centromeric and pericentromeric heterochromatin are actively transcribed and accumulate abundant RNA despite their highly condensed appearance38. Furthermore, transcription can stabilize H3K9me3-modifying enzymes39,40,41, and dense heterochromatin nonetheless allows passage of transcription factors42 and large macromolecules43, including RNA polymerase II (ref. 44).

According to recent reports, these observations have motivated an alternative model of heterochromatin organization, wherein domain-scale compaction emerges from frequent intra-domain interactions that serve to reinforce the epigenetic state of the domain rather than directly silence the underlying DNA through steric exclusion. By this model, distal genomic loci are brought into proximity by the activity of heterochromatin reader and writer proteins, as readers bound to heterochromatin marks on one chromatin fibre might promote deposition of the same modification by writers on another fibre. This 3D reader–writer activity establishes a positive feedback loop that reinforces the heterochromatic state of the domain. Heterochromatin compaction thus functions to concentrate this feedback, ensuring it acts primarily back on the existing heterochromatin to stabilize its epigenetic state, rather than spreading or diluting to neighbouring euchromatin45,46.

Although heterochromatin has been proposed to be important for epigenetic memory at the Pcdh locus11,12, we found that chosen Pcdh promoters do not segregate from flanking promoters retaining the silent state, contrasting with the behaviour of chosen promoters in H3K27me3 heterochromatin29,47. This unexpected organization argues against domain-scale spatial segregation as a primary mechanism for heterochromatin-mediated memory of Pcdh gene choice. Instead, these data suggest that a more local compartmentalization of active and inactive genes might develop, with biophysically distinct microcompartments, or ‘pockets’, of active chromatin containing expressed genes forming within the heterochromatin domain. This model is consistent with the presence of both highly dynamic and more stable HP1 populations within the same heterochromatin environment48 and structural heterogeneity of heterochromatin compartments, as revealed by recent single-molecule footprinting49 and chromatin tracing46 studies.

Lastly, beyond classical examples of heterochromatic genes, such as the lt and rl genes in Drosophila3,4,5, the intermixed spatial organization of active and inactive genes within H3K9me3-enriched chromatin domains discussed here may reflect a more general property of gene regulation within heterochromatic territories—with particular relevance to genes arranged in clusters, such as OR6 and KZFP genes7. We propose that domain-scale spatial segregation of active and inactive genes might not be required at these clusters to accommodate and maintain expression of subsets of genes within a more broadly repressive chromatin domain. Furthermore, as we have shown here for Pcdh genes, these loci might also require the coordinated integration of genome folding mechanisms across scales—from higher-order heterochromatin compartmentalization to enhancer–promoter interactions mediated by various looping factors50—to achieve genomic architectures required for precise and selective gene activation.

In summary, our findings illustrate how seemingly silent chromatin domains can coordinate gene expression and invite a reconceptualization of heterochromatin from a singularly repressive chromatin environment to one that can, when properly configured, permit active transcription.

It has been revealed that mice were treated in compliance with the rules and regulations of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the University of California, San Francisco under the IACUC protocol AN-170364-03F. Rad21 cKO mice were generated by crossing Rad21 conditional allele mice51 to Omp-ires-cre mice (Omptm1(cre)Jae) harbouring a Cre-inducible tdTomato allele (ROSA26-tdtomato, Gt(ROSA)26Sortm14(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J). For the nChIP–seq experiments, cells were sorted from Krt5–GFP (labelling HBCs), Ngn1–GFP (labelling INPs) and Omp-ires–GFP (labelling mOSNs) mice. Primers used for genotyping mice are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Industry observers note that mice were perfused with 30 ml of ice-cold PBS followed by 30 ml of freshly prepared, ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Tissue from the mouse OE was dissected and incubated in 4% PFA with gentle rocking at 4 °C for 6 h. Tissue was then transferred to 30% sucrose in 1 × PBS, incubated with gentle rocking at 4 °C until sunk, then embedded in OCT. For ORCA experiments, OE tissue was sectioned coronally at 6 μm onto glass coverslips (Biooptechs, 40-1313-03191) coated with chromium potassium gelatin. Slides were coated as described previously52. For immunohistochemistry experiments, OE tissue was sectioned coronally at 20 μm onto Superfrost Plus slides (Fisherbrand, 1255015). ORCA coverslips were stored at −80 °C until use; immunohistochemistry slides were stored at −20 °C until use.

In a recent development, for a breakdown of all ORCA-related experiments in the present study, see Supplementary Table 4. The genomic coordinates of the ORCA barcodes tiling the Pcdh locus are listed in Supplementary Table 5.

Sources indicate that RNA and DNA probes were designed and hybridized as previously described52, with minor modifications as follows. Briefly, for combined RNA/DNA imaging experiments, RNA probes were hybridized and imaged first. Tissue sections mounted on coverslips were fixed in freshly prepared 4% PFA at room temperature for 10 min, followed by three washes in 1 × PBS. Sections were then permeabilized for 10 min at room temperature in 1% Triton X in 1 × PBS, followed by two washes with 1 × PBS. Next, sections were incubated for 5 min at room temperature in a protease solution consisting of 0.1 mg ml−1 pepsin (Sigma Aldrich, 501784863) in 10 mM HCl and washed twice in 0.1 M glycine in 1 × PBS to improve RNA hybridization efficiency. Sections were then cleared in 8% sodium dodecyl sulfate at room temperature for 10 min and washed three times in 2 × SSC, reducing background fluorescence. Following clearing, sections were incubated in Hybridization Buffer (2 × SSC, 50% formamide, 0.1% Tween) for 35 min at room temperature. Then, 2,500 ng of primary RNA probes diluted in Hybridization Solution (2 × SSC, 50% formamide, 10% dextran sulfate, 0.1% Tween) were added to the sections, covered with coverglass and incubated overnight (12–20 h) at 42 °C. The following morning, samples were washed twice for 10 min in 2 × SSC at 42 °C, washed once in 2 × SSC at room temperature, then imaged. After RNA imaging, samples were re-fixed in 4% PFA for 5 min at room temperature, washed three times in 2 × SSC, re-permeabilized for 10 min in 1% Triton X-100 at room temperature and washed three times in 2 × SSC. Sections were subsequently incubated for 5 min in 0.1 M HCl and washed three times in 2 × SSC. Pre-hybridization was performed for 35 min as for RNA, then 5,000 ng of DNA probes diluted in Hybridization Solution were added to sections and covered with coverglass. Sections were then incubated on a 90 °C hotplate for exactly 7 min and transferred to 42 °C overnight. The following morning, samples were washed twice in 2 × SSC for 10 min at 42 °C, once in 2 × SSC at room temperature, then incubated in a post-fix solution (2% glutaraldehyde, 8% PFA in 1 × PBS) for 30 min. Samples were then washed three times in 2 × SSC and imaged.

For ORCA experiments not involving RNA imaging, samples were fixed, permeabilized, cleared, treated with HCl, pre-hybridized and hybridized as described above, but omitting the protease step. Inclusion of the protease step was found to substantially improve RNA staining and was therefore used only for experiments that included RNA imaging. For ORCA experiments involving fluorescent protein labelling (for example, tdTomato signal in Rad21 cKO and Setdb1 cKO), samples were first fixed and washed, imaged for the fluorescent protein and then processed for DNA ORCA as described above. Throughout all procedures, care was taken to prevent sections from drying at any point in the protocol to minimize tissue shrinkage between RNA or protein imaging rounds and subsequent DNA imaging rounds.

Samples hybridized with primary probes were imaged on a previously described custom microscopy and microfluidics setup29,52. RNA and DNA readout barcodes were labelled sequentially with a 750 dye complementary to the readout barcodes on primary probes. All RNA and DNA probes share a common sequence that was labelled with a Cy3 dye complementary to this sequence, referred to as the fiducial. Fiducial probes were added before the first imaging round and imaged alongside each barcode. Fiducial signal was subsequently used for drift correction and alignment across imaging rounds. For RNA imaging, the fiducial signal captures all stained RNAs, whereas for DNA imaging it appears as discrete puncta, with each punctum representing one Pcdh locus.

It has been revealed that OE tissue was first stained for H3K9me3 as follows. Tissue on glass coverslips was fixed for 10 min in 4% PFA, washed twice in 1 × PBS, quenched for 5 min in PBS containing 0.1 M glycine and washed again in PBS. Tissue was permeabilized with three 5-min washes in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100, then blocked in PBS containing 1% BSA and 200 U ml−1 RNase inhibitor (New England Biolabs, M0314L). Primary antibody incubation was performed overnight at 4 °C using rabbit anti-H3K9me3 antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Abcam, ab8898). The following morning, tissue was washed three times for 5 min each in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100, then incubated with donkey anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 647 secondary antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen, A31573). Tissue was then washed three times for 5 min each in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100. Samples were stored at 4 °C in PBS protected from light until imaging. To image OE tissue with STORM, an imaging buffer was prepared immediately before use as follows. A dilution buffer was first prepared containing 50 mM NaCl and 200 mM Tris pH 8.0. A glucose oxidase/catalase oxygen-scavenging solution was prepared by combining 700 μl of dilution buffer, 49 mg of glucose oxidase and 175 μl of catalase, centrifuging at maximum speed for 1 min and collecting 800 μl of supernatant. STORM imaging buffer was prepared by adding 800 μl of glucose oxidase/catalase oxygen-scavenging solution, 8 ml of 50% glucose and 400 μl of β-mercaptoethanol to 32 ml of dilution buffer.

For each field of view, fresh STORM imaging buffer was flowed onto the sample immediately before imaging. H3K9me3 STORM videos were acquired at five axial positions using the 635-nm laser at maximum power and an exposure time of 0.5 s per frame. The first and fourth videos contained 3,000 frames, whereas the remaining videos contained 2,500 frames. Fresh STORM imaging buffer was flowed onto the sample after the third video to maintain fluorophore blinking during prolonged imaging. Further frames were acquired after addition of fresh buffer because extra illumination time was required for photobleaching before robust fluorophore blinking could be observed.

STORM videos were acquired across multiple axial planes rather than using astigmatism-based 3D STORM with a cylindrical lens53, because high tissue background made accurate fitting of astigmatic spot widths unreliable. The five axial planes were separated by 750 nm and sampled a 3.0-μm axial range centred on the plane with strongest H3K9me3 signal. Subsequent ORCA imaging of the same samples was acquired using Z-stacks containing matched axial planes to those imaged by STORM.

Fluorescently tagged WGA, which labels cell membranes, was used to align fields of view across imaging sessions (for example, to align H3K9me3 STORM, RNA and Pcdh DNA images). First, 3 μl of 1 ng μl−1 WGA was diluted in 600 μl of 2 × SSC, added to samples for 15 min, then washed off with 2 × SSC immediately before imaging. For RNA and Pcdh DNA imaging, the fiducial channel was imaged alongside the WGA signal at the end of each imaging session. For H3K9me3 STORM, WGA images for each field of view were taken immediately following completion of STORM acquisition. For imaging of fluorescent proteins tagging mOSNs, WGA was imaged simultaneously in a different channel alongside the fluorescent protein. When aligning images across RNA and DNA imaging rounds, images from each field of view were first aligned to the fiducial signal acquired with WGA, and fields of view were subsequently registered across imaging modalities using the WGA signal. The WGA signal additionally enabled 3D cell segmentation (described below).

In a recent development, all imaging was performed on a custom microscopy and microfluidics setup as previously described29,52. The details of the microscopy setup are also listed on the 4DN data portal and Mirco-Meta App54 under Stanford-Boettiger_lab_ORCA_Nikon_Eclipse_Ti2-U_Scope3.

Sources indicate that three-dimensional cell segmentations were generated from the WGA signal acquired during RNA imaging. We trained a Cellpose55 algorithm to identify cell outlines in individual sections of WGA images. This algorithm was then run on every section of WGA Z-stack images for each field of view. To connect the resulting two-dimensional (2D) cell segmentations into 3D cell segmentations, we applied ultrack56, an algorithm initially designed to track cells over time in time-series data, to the 2D segmentations for each stack, effectively treating the Z dimension as time. Ultrack produced 3D cell segmentations that matched WGA staining (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We used ultrack, as we found Cellpose’s performance with 2D images to be superior to its performance with 3D images for OE sections stained with WGA.

Segmented cells were classified into distinct cell types on the basis of RNA transcripts within each segmentation as follows. RNA puncta were first identified from 3D stacks using storm-analysis (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7679267), which identifies their X, Y position in each frame and is robust to overlapping spots. The Z position of each punctum was computed by fitting the axial fluorescence intensity profile to puncta with a common X, Y position (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7698979). RNA puncta were then mapped to cell segmentations and segmentations were classified by cell type as follows: for each cell, counts of Icam1, Ascl1, Tex15, Gap43 and Omp transcripts were log-transformed, Z-scored and combined into marker-specific scores corresponding to HBCs (Icam1), GBCs (Ascl1), INPs (Tex15), iOSNs (Gap43) and mOSNs (Omp high, Gap43 low). Cells were assigned to the cell type with the highest score, subject to further marker-based rules (Tex15+ cells were forced to INP and not allowed to be mOSN; HBC labels were forbidden in Gap43+ or Omp+ cells). A confidence score was defined as the difference between the top two scores, and cells with low confidence or ambiguous profiles were labelled ‘undetermined’. To map DNA loci to each segmentation, the X, Y, Z coordinates of DNA loci were transformed by the image alignments computed between WGA images. Each locus was then mapped to a classified cell from its respective field of view and assigned that cell’s label.

Recent findings suggest that for ORCA experiments involving protein rather than RNA staining, DNA loci were classified as belonging to a particular cell type (namely, mOSNs) on the basis of the fluorescent signal of tdTomato. Apart from Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e, data in all figures come from cells classified as mOSNs.

After aligning images from RNA and DNA imaging rounds, the X, Y, Z positions of RNA puncta and DNA loci were registered into a common coordinate system. For each DNA locus, we computed the 3D Euclidean distance to every RNA punctum in the same field of view in voxel units, where X–Y coordinates are in pixels and Z is in imaging planes. A locus was classified as ‘transcribing’ for a given gene if at least one RNA punctum for that gene lay within a 3D distance of 8 voxel units, and as ‘non-transcribing’ otherwise. This threshold corresponds to 1.23–1.60 μm in physical space, depending on how the separation between DNA and RNA puncta is distributed across the X–Y and Z axes. The threshold of 8 voxel units was chosen on the basis of the distribution of nearest RNA distances across all DNA loci for each Pcdh RNA, which was consistently bimodal, with one population less than 8 voxel units and another greater than or equal to 8 voxel units.

Sources indicate that STORM videos were processed frame by frame using the 2dfixed multi-emitter-fitting algorithm from storm-analysis (https://github.com/ZhuangLab/storm-analysis). Initial frames dominated by saturated fluorescence before photobleaching were excluded. Single-molecule localizations in each frame were identified using a 10-sigma detection threshold and fit with a fixed-width 2D Gaussian model using an initial Gaussian sigma of 1.3 pixels. Drift correction was not applied during fitting. Localizations were fit independently for each axial imaging plane, and each localization was assigned the Z position of its corresponding imaging plane for downstream analysis.

H3K9me3 STORM signal around Pcdh loci in mOSNs was quantified as the number of STORM localizations within a 324-nm radius, corresponding to 3 pixels, of the X–Y position of the fiducial signal of each locus. Similar results were obtained using different radius sizes. For each locus, localizations were counted from the STORM imaging plane or planes nearest to the locus in Z. If the locus was located in the same Z plane as a STORM video, only localizations from that plane were used. If the locus was located between two STORM imaging planes, localizations from both planes were included and linearly weighted according to their proximity to the locus Z position. For example, for a locus located at Z plane 26 between STORM videos acquired at planes 25 and 28, localizations from plane 25 were weighted by 2/3 and localizations from plane 28 were weighted by 1/3. For the analyses in Fig. 2f, the same quantification was performed using the X, Y and Z position of the ORCA barcode containing the Pcdh gene being analysed, rather than the fiducial position of the locus.

For the simulations in Fig. 2c, randomized positions were used to compare H3K9me3 STORM signal at observed Pcdh loci with signal expected at other positions within the same nuclei. For each of 1,000 simulations, one random position was selected for each observed Pcdh locus from the same cell and Z plane, thereby controlling for non-uniform axial distribution of H3K9me3 STORM signal within individual cells. H3K9me3 STORM signal was quantified at each randomized position using the same 324-nm radius and Z-plane weighting scheme described above. The median STORM signal from each simulation was used to generate a null distribution, which was compared with the observed median STORM signal around Pcdh loci to calculate an empirical P value. The same randomization and quantification procedure was performed for putative Tex15 transcription sites in INPs for Extended Data Fig. 7d. Putative Tex15 transcription sites were identified from Tex15 RNA FISH z-stacks by detecting bright 3D regional maxima. For each field of view, the Tex15 stack was smoothed with a 3D Gaussian filter and thresholded to identify local maxima corresponding to candidate nascent RNA puncta. The intensity threshold was empirically chosen by visual inspection across fields of view to retain bright Tex15 transcription sites while excluding dimmer spots probably corresponding to mature transcripts.

For visualization of H3K9me3 STORM localizations together with ORCA traces in three dimensions (Extended Data Fig. 7a), STORM localizations from each axial imaging plane were shown with a randomized Z position drawn from a truncated Gaussian distribution centred on the corresponding STORM imaging plane. The Gaussian had a standard deviation of 1.2 imaging-plane units and was truncated to ±3.5 imaging-plane units around the plane centre. This jittering was used only to create smooth 3D renderings of STORM signal across the sparsely sampled axial planes and was not used for quantitative analyses.

Image processing (drift correction and localization of spots) was performed as described previously29,52 using ORCA analysis tools (https://github.com/BoettigerLab/ORCA-public).

Industry observers note that before downstream analyses, ORCA traces were quality filtered on the basis of barcode detection. For each experiment, we computed the number of detected barcodes per trace. Median barcode detection per trace was calculated to be around 40–60 barcodes, and we restricted our analysis to traces with ≥25 detected barcodes. We further filtered out traces with unnaturally high barcode detection, keeping only traces with ≤86 barcodes detected. For each retained trace, the 3D positions of detected barcodes were ordered by genomic position. Next, barcodes with consistently poor detection or abnormal labelling (for example, failed strand displacement) were assigned estimated positions by linear interpolation in traces for which the immediately flanking barcodes were detected. This selective interpolation was applied to 2–5 barcodes per experiment. For contact frequency map analyses, such as those presented in Figs. 1e and 3e–g, we further interpolated missing barcodes using a maximum gap length of three consecutive missing barcodes. This interpolation preserved the major features of contact frequency maps while improving their smoothness. Different maximum gap lengths were tested. Gap lengths greater than three did not produce measurable further smoothing, whereas allowing larger interpolations produced abnormally short adjacent-barcode distances. For all other analyses, raw detected barcode positions were used, with only the selective interpolation of poorly labelled barcodes described above.

For contact frequency analyses, we chose contact thresholds near the average distance between adjacent barcodes in a spatially contiguous region of the locus. These thresholds ranged from 170 to 220 nm across experiments. We also conducted a threshold parameter sweep to verify that observed contact patterns were robust to a range of thresholds around the selected value, and varying the contact threshold within a reasonable range did not qualitatively alter any within-experiment effects. Thresholds were used to call contacts between all barcode pairs in an experiment. The thresholds used for each experiment are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

Industry observers note that enhancer–promoter barcode pairs were assigned on the basis of previously reported regulatory relationships between Pcdh cluster enhancers and their target promoters13,15,25,57, together with the ORCA locus positions containing the corresponding genes and enhancers. All Pcdha genes were assigned the HS5-1 enhancer (barcode 27), whereas Pcdhb genes were assigned the HS18-22 enhancer (barcode 78) and Pcdhg genes were assigned the HS16-17 enhancer (barcode 76). Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies were extracted from contact frequency matrices generated from max-gap-3 interpolated polymer coordinates, as described above. For ORCA barcodes containing multiple Pcdh promoters, combined gene labels were used.

According to recent reports, we defined the geometric centre of an ORCA trace as the median X, Y, Z position of all detected barcodes in that trace. For the distance-to-centre profiles in Fig. 1i, we computed the Euclidean distance between each barcode and this centre on a per-trace basis, then plotted, for each position, the median distance across all traces. When distances to the centre of the heterochromatin domain were measured in Fig. 4c and Extended Data Figs. 9a–d and 10d, the heterochromatin centre was defined as the median X, Y, Z position of barcodes assigned to the heterochromatin domain (barcodes 2–14 and 29–67), and the distances of relevant locus positions to this centre were measured. When distances to the centre of a euchromatin region were measured in Extended Data Fig. 9a–d, the centre was defined as the median X, Y, Z position of barcodes assigned either to the euchromatin stretch between the Pcdha and Pcdhb clusters (barcodes 15–28) or to the euchromatin stretch downstream of the Pcdhg cluster (barcodes 68–90), depending on the specific locus position being analysed.

Radius of gyration (\({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\)) was used as a single-number measure of the spatial spread of a set of barcodes around its geometric centre47. For a set of \(N\) barcodes with 3D coordinates {\({r}_{i}\)}, we first calculated the centre \(c\) as the coordinate-wise median position, then defined \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) as \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}{\sum }_{i=1}^{N}{||}{r}_{i}-c{{||}}^{2}}\). The \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) of the heterochromatin domain was primarily evaluated. In Fig. 5e, the heterochromatin domain \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) was calculated as a fraction of the trace-wide \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\).

For each isoform measured in Fig. 4a, the promoter barcode was assigned on the basis of the ORCA locus position containing the respective Pcdh gene. The heterochromatin compartment was defined as barcodes 2–14 and 29–67. The euchromatin compartment was defined on the basis of the cluster of the promoter being analysed: barcodes 15–28 for Pcdha promoters, and barcodes 68–90 for Pcdhb and Pcdhg promoters. The promoter barcode itself was excluded from the compartment to which it belonged. For each trace, a promoter-to-heterochromatin centre distance was calculated as the median Euclidean distance between the promoter barcode and all heterochromatin compartment barcodes. Promoter-to-euchromatin centre distances were calculated analogously as the median Euclidean distance between the promoter barcode and all barcodes in the corresponding euchromatin compartment.

In Extended Data Fig. 10e, entropy was calculated for the distance distributions between pairs of locus positions as described previously58. For each barcode pair, we pooled 3D distances across all traces within each genotype separately, then normalized each genotype’s distances by that genotype’s own median distance for the pair to account for length-scale differences between experiments. We then pooled the normalized distances from both genotypes together and set common histogram bin edges (50 bins) using the 1st and 99th percentiles of this pooled, normalized distribution, so that entropy values were computed on the same scale for both genotypes. Using these shared bin edges, we separately estimated each genotype’s distribution, normalized bin counts to probabilities pk and computed Shannon entropy as \(S=-{\sum }_{k}{p}_{k}{\log }_{2}({p}_{k})\), such that higher S reflects broader, more variable distances and lower S indicates more narrowly peaked, reproducible distances. For each locus position, we calculated its entropy with respect to all other positions, averaged these pairwise entropies per position and compared the resulting mean entropies between Setdb1 cKO and WT.

It has been revealed that to quantify spatial segregation between heterochromatic and euchromatic regions of the Pcdh locus, we calculated a separation score as follows. For each polymer, we designated heterochromatin locus positions (barcodes 2–14 and 29–67) as region A and euchromatic locus positions (barcodes 15–28 and 68–90) as region B, computed all pairwise 3D distances and took the median distance between A and B (heterochromatin–euchromatin) and the median distance within A (heterochromatin–heterochromatin). The separation score was defined as the ratio of these two medians (medianA–B/medianA–A), such that higher values indicate that the heterochromatin domain is more spatially separated from neighbouring euchromatin. This score was computed per trace for WT, Rad21 cKO and Setdb1 cKO and compared across genotypes.

To validate the specificity of RNA probes targeting Pcdha and Pcdhg isoforms, plasmids encoding Pcdha and Pcdhg variable exons fused to mCherry under control of a CMV promoter were generated through FastCloning59. Plasmid sequences were validated using Plasmidsaurus. Plasmids were transfected into Cath.a-differentiated cells grown in eight-well Ibidi glass-bottom plates (Ibidi, 80827). Cells were seeded at a density of 40,000 cells per well in 220 μl of media and transfected after 24 h of growth using lipofectamine (Invitrogen, L3000001). Each well was then stained with primary RNA probes according to the procedure described above. For 12 plasmids across each of the Pcdha and Pcdhg clusters, three wells were transfected, with each well stained by a different ORCA readout barcode. Only wells that were labelled with a readout barcode mapping to the Pcdh isoform they were transfected with produced signal.

Industry observers note that FACS isolation of mouse OSNs was performed as previously described15. In brief, mice were euthanized with CO2 followed by cervical dislocation and OE tissue was immediately dissected. Cells were then dissociated into a single-cell suspension by incubating freshly dissected tissue with papain for 30–40 min at 37 °C according to the Worthington Papain Dissociation System. After dissociation and filtering through a 35-μm cell strainer, cells were resuspended in 1 × PBS with 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS), DNase (0.0025% final concentration) and DAPI. Fluorescent cells were sorted on a FACS Aria Fusion cell sorter (BD Biosciences) with BD FACSDiva 9.0.1 software. Cells were sorted into 1 × PBS + 2% FBS. FACS gating strategies used to isolate GFP+ and tdTomato+ mOSNs are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1.

In a recent development, scRNA-seq experiments were performed as previously described15. In brief, cells were dissociated from OE tissue from 4- to 5-week-old mice as described above. About 70,000 mOSNs were FACS-isolated. Complementary DNA and library preparation were performed using the 10x Genomics Single Cell 5′ Gene Expression workflow, and libraries were sequenced using a NovaSeq SP100 PE50 and a NextSeq 2000 P2 200 through the UCSF Gladstone Genomic Core and the UCSF Center for Advanced Technology. Sequencing data were processed using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger 6.0.1. Data analysis was performed using Seurat60,61 and custom scripts. Cells were filtered to retain cells with 1,000–10,000 detected genes and less than 5% mitochondrial reads. Counts were then normalized using Seurat’s NormalizeData with log normalization and a scale factor of 10,000. See Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 for further details on scRNA-seq analysis and statistics.

According to recent reports, for analyses in Fig. 5 and Extended Data Fig. 10, Pcdh isoform choice was analysed in mOSNs defined by detected Omp expression and no detected Gap43 expression using raw unique molecular identifier counts. A Pcdh isoform was considered detected in a given mOSN if one or more unique molecular identifier-corrected reads were assigned to that gene. For each condition, the percentage of mOSNs expressing each Pcdh isoform was calculated as the fraction of mOSNs with detected expression of that isoform. Changes in Pcdh choice across genotypes were calculated as percentage-point differences relative to WT. Data for single-cell experiments represent one biological replicate per condition.

Industry observers note that nChIP–seq was performed as previously described62. Briefly, live cells were sorted from papain-dissociated mouse OE; in experiments for which spike-ins were included to enable quantification of ChIP signal across conditions, HEK293T cells at around 70% confluency were trypsinized, washed with PBS and added at a ratio of 0.75% to the sorted mouse cells. (HEK293T cells were grown in RPMI or DMEM media supplemented with 10% FBS and 1 × penicillin-streptomycin, incubated at 37 °C and 5% CO2, and tested for mycoplasma (ATCC Universal Mycoplasma Detection Kit) before use in experiments.) Live sorted cells were pelleted in a swinging bucket centrifuge (800g, 15 min, 4 °C) and then resuspended in Buffer 1 (0.3 M sucrose, 60 mM KCl, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 15 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Cells were lysed on ice for 10 min by adding an equal volume of Buffer 2 (0.4% Igepal CA-630, 0.3 M sucrose, 60 mM KCl, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 15 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Nuclei were pelleted (1,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in MNase buffer (0.32 M sucrose, 4 mM MgCl2, 1 mM CaCl2, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Resuspended nuclei were treated with MNase (Sigma) at 37 °C, and the reaction was quenched with the addition of EDTA to a final concentration of 20 mM. Two fractions of solubilized chromatin were collected; nuclei were pelleted (10,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and fraction S1 was collected and stored at 4 °C overnight. Nuclei were resuspended in Dialysis Buffer (1 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM PMSF, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors) and rotated overnight at 4 °C. Insoluble material was pelleted (10,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and fraction S2 was retained. MNase treatment was optimized to yield predominantly mono-nucleosomes in the S1 fraction and predominantly di-nucleosomes, tri-nucleosomes and some larger chromatin fragments in the S2 fraction. S1 and S2 DNA concentrations were measured by HS DNA Qubit after RNase A treatment. Equal volumes of S1 and S2 fractions were pooled, and total yields were estimated. In spike-in experiments, chromatin input was not always equalized across immunoprecipitations, as spike-in normalization accounts for differences in input.

MNase-digested chromatin was diluted in Wash Buffer 1 (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 10 mM EDTA, 125 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween-20, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and 5% inputs were reserved. Histone H3 lysine 9 tri-methyl antibody (H3K9me3, Abcam ab8898) was added, and the binding reaction was rotated overnight at 4 °C. For each immunoprecipitation, 20 μl of Dynabeads Protein G (Invitrogen) were blocked overnight with 2 mg ml−1 yeast transfer RNA and 2 mg ml−1 BSA in Wash Buffer 1. The next day, blocked beads were added to antibody-bound chromatin and rotated for 1–3 h at 4 °C. Chromatin-bound beads were washed at 4 °C a total of four times with Wash Buffer I, three times with Wash Buffer II (5 mM Tris pH 7.5, 17.5 mM NaCl, 0.01% NP-40, 1 mM EDTA, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and one time with Tris-EDTA buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1 mM EDTA). Two 15-min elutions were conducted at 37 °C in Elution Buffer (1% SDS, 250 mM NaCl, 2 mM DTT). ChIP DNA and input DNA were column purified using Zymo ChIP DNA columns (Zymo Research, D5205 or D5201).

Libraries were prepared using the Ovation Ultralow V2 DNA-Seq Library Preparation Kit (Tecan Life Sciences). The quality of the libraries was assessed by Bioanalyzer and quantified using a combination of Bioanalyzer and Qubit. Libraries were pooled and sequenced on a NextSeq 2000 (Gladstone Institutes), NextSeq 500/550 (UCSF Center for Advanced Technology) or NovaSeq X (Chan Zuckerberg Initiative Biohub San Francisco).

Data processing and analysis was conducted in accordance with previous literature63,64. For spike-in experiments, adapters were trimmed with cutadapt with --minimum-length 18 and checked for sequencing quality control with FastQC. Reads were aligned with Bowtie2 to a concatenated mouse and human genome (mm10 + hg38) in which the spike-in chromosomes were pre-labelled with a ‘_hg38’ suffix. Alignments were split by chromosome using bamUtil’s splitChromosome function, and samtools’ merge command was used to collect mouse and human alignments separately. Then, duplicates were marked and removed using Picard MarkDuplicates, and the spike-in chromosome suffix was stripped. Alignments with mapping quality < 30 were removed using samtools, and read counts aligning to the mouse and human genomes were used to calculate spike-in scaling factors.

As in the original ChIP-Rx method describing quantitative spike-in normalized ChIP followed by sequencing, our spike-in corrections normalized for the number of spike-in reads in the immunoprecipitation63. We sequenced every input as well, allowing us to adjust for the variability in spike-in read fraction in each input64,65. The spike-in adjusted coverage signal, \({z}_{i}\), was calculated from counts per million (CPM)-normalized coverage values, \({x}_{i}\), with the equation \({z}_{i}={x}_{i}\cdot \frac{{S}_{\mathrm{in}}}{{T}_{\mathrm{in}}}\frac{{T}_{\mathrm{ip}}}{{S}_{\mathrm{ip}}}\), where \({S}_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \({T}_{\mathrm{in}}\) are the number of spike-in (human) and target (mouse) reads in the inputs, respectively, and \({S}_{\mathrm{ip}}\) and \({T}_{\mathrm{ip}}\) are the number of spike-in (human) and target (mouse) reads in the immunoprecipitations, respectively. Bigwig files were generated from Deeptools bamCoverage using --scaleFactor of \(\frac{{S}_{\mathrm{in}}}{{T}_{\mathrm{in}}}\cdot \frac{{T}_{\mathrm{ip}}}{{S}_{\mathrm{ip}}}\), --binSize 10, --minMappingQuality 30 and --normalizeUsing CPM. In Fig. 5c, to compare spike-in-normalized nChIP–seq values from different experiments, we batch-corrected using the average of the scale factors from the WT samples within each experimental batch. Significance was assessed and confirmed using both a Welch’s unpaired t-test and a two-way ANOVA (main effects only).

Sources indicate that for experiments without spike-ins, adapters were trimmed and the first 4 nucleotides of each read removed with cutadapt (v1.9.1; -u 4, --minimum-length 18). Reads were aligned to mm10 with Bowtie2. BigWig files were generated with deepTools bamCoverage in 10-base-pair bins from unextended reads, normalized to 1 × genome coverage (reads per genomic content; effective genome size 2,407,883,318; chr. X, chr. Y and chr. M excluded from normalization).

Immunohistochemistry for RAD21 was performed as described previously15. A similar staining protocol was performed for SETDB1, with minor modifications to the blocking buffer composition to improve signal. Sections were removed from −20 °C, washed in 1 × PBS for 5 min at room temperature, then washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min. Sections were incubated in blocking solution (3% BSA, 0.2% Tween in 4 × SSC) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary antibody incubation proceeded overnight (12–16 h) at 4 °C in a humidified chamber. The following morning, sections were washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min at room temperature, then incubated in secondary antibody at room temperature for 1 h. Samples were then washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min at room temperature and mounted under coverslips with antifade mounting medium with DAPI (Vector Laboratories, H-2000-2). For RAD21 staining, primary antibody was added at 1:100 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen, PA5-28344). For SETDB1 staining, primary antibody was added at 1:250 in blocking buffer (Thermofisher, MA5-47120). For both RAD21 and SETDB1, secondary antibody was added at 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen donkey anti-rabbit 647, A31573).

Arsenal eye Serie A’s 11-goal striker: Should they pay £26m?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Footballtransfertavern

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, arsenal transfer news from Italy centres on Monza striker Gustavo Varela, with Gianluca Di Marzio reportingthat the Gunners are very interested.
  • Sources indicate that the interest makes sense.
  • FotMob‘s data has him scoring well above his expected goals for a Monza side that won only two of its first 10 league games, and he averages around three shots per 90 minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, arsenal transfer news from Italy centres on Monza striker Gustavo Varela, with Gianluca Di Marzio reportingthat the Gunners are very interested. The 21-year-old Portugal forward has scored 11 goals in 11 Serie A games since joining from Benfica B in July. Barcelona are equally keen, Inter watch him live at every match, and Napoli are reported as his strongest Italian suitor.

Sources indicate that the interest makes sense. Viktor Gyokeres, signed for £64m in 2025, has two goals in 15 appearances and none in the Premier League, while Kai Havertz has started 10 of 11 league games for three goals. Arsenal’s results haven’t suffered, but their number nine position has produced little.

Finishing is the selling point. FotMob‘s data has him scoring well above his expected goals for a Monza side that won only two of its first 10 league games, and he averages around three shots per 90 minutes. The weaknesses are just as clear: he wins 34% of his duels, completes 41% of his dribbles and ranks in the ninth percentile among forwards for defensive contribution, which clashes with the pressing Arteta wants from his striker.

Di Marzio says Monza will listen at around £22m to £26m, with the money earmarked for other signings, after paying about £3m including bonuses. Flashscore reports Benfica hold a 20% sell-on and a right to match offers, and Varela’s agents meet Monza this week.

Recent findings suggest that yes, but in the summer and only if Gyokeres leaves. Arsenal’s results are strong, so a January rush for a 21-year-old would add risk without fixing a crisis. A fee near £26m looks modest beside the £64m Gyokeres cost, and Varela’s goals-per-game record argues for the gamble far more than Gyokeres’ two in 15 does.

The real risk is suitability. He also scores for a struggling side, so his chances come in games unlike most of the Premier League games Arsenal play. Arteta needs a number nine who presses and wins duels, and Varela does neither well, so Arsenal would be buying a finisher and building the rest of his game themselves.

Sources indicate that that is workable if Varela arrives as competition for Havertz rather than the first choice. Arsenal should also expect resistance beyond the price, because Benfica’s matching right and Inter’s summer aims complicate any early bid.

Watching him until June costs Arsenal nothing, and another 20 league games will show whether this form is real or a hot streak.

Como beat Cagliari 2-0 with two headers from Yan Couto crosses, moving back into fourth place on 26 points. Juventus visit next and trail the side holding the last Champions League place by eight points.

Recent findings suggest that como beat Cagliari 2-0 at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia on Saturday, 21 November 2026. Both goals were headers, and Yan Couto crossed for both of them. The result lifted Fàbregas’ side back into fourth place. That is the last Champions League place, and Juventus are the next visitors.

Ramón opened the scoring after 24 minutes. He met Couto’s cross from the right and headed past goalkeeper Caprile. Da Cunha, the captain, doubled the lead in the 56th minute. He headed in another Couto delivery from the centre of the area.

In a recent development, fàbregas left Nico Paz and Perrone on the bench. The two Argentinians had rejoined the squad only hours before kick-off after international duty. Como play AEK in the Champions League on Tuesday. Even without the pair from the start, the hosts kept Cagliari out. Both men entered in the 57th minute, with Liberali and Milla making way respectively. It was Como’s first win since a defeat to Inter before the international break.

For Fàbregas, the performance was not perfect, but he was very pleased. Perrone had a minor problem, the coach explained, which ruled out a full 90 minutes for the midfielder.

Sources indicate that como have now won three Serie A home games in a row without conceding, which they last did in October and November 1984, according to Sportmediaset. Da Cunha has three goals in his last four games across Serie A and the Champions League. Fàbregas has never lost to Cagliari in five Serie A matches as a coach. He has won three of them and drawn two. Cagliari have lost each of their last four away league games. That is their first run of four straight away defeats in Serie A since November–December 2023.

Recent findings suggest that como have eight wins, two draws and two defeats from 12 games, according to Como 1907. They have scored 20 goals and conceded 10.

In a recent development, in that table, Juventus’ record reads five wins, three draws and three defeats. They have scored 15 goals and conceded 12. The gap to Como stood at eight points before Juventus’ game against Venezia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea transfer news around Cole Palmer has flared again, with Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival at Manchester United reviving the noise. Reporter Dean Jones insists the England playmaker’s future at Stamford Bridge is not in doubt, but he admits the sentiment around it is becoming harder to ignore.

Sources indicate that palmer, a boyhood United supporter, has been linked with Old Trafford before. United appointed Pochettino on 18 November after sacking Michael Carrick following one win in ten league games. The Argentine made Palmer one of his most used players at Chelsea, where the pair built a positive relationship, and Palmer scored 22 league goals in 2023/24.

In a recent development, jones rates the chances of Palmer joining United as extremely low. United’s January budget stands at roughly £50m, and they want a left-back, a centre-back and a striker. A player FotMob values at €100m, roughly £87m, sits outside both the money and the shopping list. Jones also sees no sign that Palmer wants to leave, and claims relations at Stamford Bridge would need to break down badly first.

In a recent development, palmer has started all 11 of Chelsea’s Premier League games this season, playing 970 minutes for three goals, one from the penalty spot, and three assists. His 23 chances created include six massive chances, and his 2.58 expected goals backs up the output. Xabi Alonso claims, “The better Cole we have, the better Chelsea we have”.

Only ten of Palmer’s 31 shots have hit the target; he wins 46.9% of his dribbles, and he has collected two yellows and a red. Fitness worries more after an injury-hit 2025/26 that ended with him missing the World Cup.

Industry observers note that no, but Chelsea should treat Jones’s condition as the real warning. Palmer’s contract runs to 2034, and United’s budget does not reach his valuation, so the danger lies in a deteriorating relationship, not a bid. That puts the onus on Alonso, Chelsea’s seventh permanent manager since 2021.

Industry observers note that morgan Rogers’ £117m arrival from Aston Villa creates the obvious flashpoint. If Palmer feels crowded out of the number ten role, or pushed wide right too often, the homesickness talk will return. Clear roles and managed minutes will protect him better than another forward.

Recent findings suggest that the money belongs elsewhere. Alonso’s side beat United 2-0 on 31 October, then lost 1-0 at Sunderland eight days later, and defensive brittleness and thin squad depth keep undermining a front line that already scores. A back line that leaks goals will not.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool transfer news from Goal says Ajax teenager Abdellah Ouazane is a January target as attacking cover for Florian Wirtz. Julian Ward, Liverpool’s recruitment chief, has reportedly sped up aims to support the £116m playmaker, and Ouazane has become a serious option before the winter window opens. Wael Mohya and Gilberto Mora sit on the same shortlist.

The 17-year-old grew up supporting Liverpool and badly wants to play at Anfield. Ajax hold the leverage, though: his contract runs to 2028, and persuading them to sell a prized academy graduate mid-season will take careful negotiation. De Telegraaf also reported earlier this season that sporting director Jordi Cruyff wants to give him a new deal when he turns 18 on 15 January.

Ouazane is mainly an attacking midfielder who also plays wide or up front. FotMob‘s 2026/27 numbers show two goals and one assist in 12 Eredivisie games, only four of them starts, across 441 minutes. His goals and shot attempts rank in the 88th and 86th percentiles among comparable attackers.

In a recent development, the gaps are just as clear: he sits in the 19th percentile for defensive contributions and the 15th for aerial duels won, and a 45.7% dribble success rate suggests he still loses the ball too often against senior opponents. Real Madrid pulled out of a 2025 deal after his medical, though Ajax’s own checks cleared him.

  • Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a newly introduced study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons.".

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

Sources indicate that the study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters noted. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%.".

Sources indicate that it is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

According to recent reports, and even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

Recent results have seen Inter slip behind both Rome clubs, but they gained a vital European victory in midweek; meanwhile, their visitors have surged into the top half after recovering from a rocky start.

Having exited at the first knockout round last season, Inter started this term's Champions League campaign by taking nothing from their first two fixtures - but​ things have improved dramatically since then.

Three straight wins without conceding have moved them up the table, and Cristian Chivu's side now occupy a playoff place - in fact, finishing inside the top eight cannot be ruled out.

After defeating Shakhtar Donetsk and Feyenoord, the Nerazzurri beat Stuttgart 2-0 on Wednesday night, as captain Lautaro Martinez scored his first goal since returning from injury.

That partly made amends for throwing away two Serie A points three days beforehand, when Inter played out a chaotic 4-4 draw with local rivals Atalanta BC.

Despite Pio Esposito's first top-flight hat-trick, they let in a couple of avoidable late goals that left them three points behind surprise leaders Lazio, with Roma sandwiched between.

Such has been their dominance, Inter have won all of the last 12 league meetings at San Siro, keeping 10 clean sheets and only conceding two goals.

Either home or away, Genoa have won none of their last 14 clashes with Inter, so they may be dreading an upcoming double-header.

Just days after this league game, the Grifone must return to Milan for a cup tie, as the sides vie for a place in the Coppa Italia quarter-finals.

Though their past record makes for grim reading, present form suggests Genoa can at least give the Italian champions a scare, as they have won five of their last seven Serie A matches.

Since Daniele De Rossi swerved the sack during the October international break, his rejuvenated side have shot up the table, swapping the drop zone for the top half.

Last weekend, the Rossoblu beat lowly Sassuolo 2-0 thanks to a Milutin Osmajic brace, posting back-to-back away wins for the first time since 2024.

Some 12 years have passed since Genoa recorded three successive away wins at Italy's elite level, and few would expect them to do so on Saturday.

Bastoni was substituted before half time against Stuttgart, and it remains to be seen if he will recover from a muscular problem in time to play.

After scoring as a substitute in midweek, Martinez must vie with Marcus Thuram and in-form Esposito to feature up front.

It has been revealed that level with the latter pair in the Capocannoniere race, Genoa striker Osmajic has scored six goals in his first 12 Serie A appearances. The Montenegrin is almost certain to start, as fellow forward Lorenzo Colombo suffered an ACL injury last weekend, probably curtailing his 2026-27 campaign.

Leo Ostigard was recently hospitalised with a high fever, but he is still expected to lead the visitors' three-man defence in Milan.

Key midfielder Morten Frendrup has been struggling with an ankle issue, meaning he faces a race against time.

This was hardly “the Battle of the Bridge”, but Chelsea blew up during a ridiculous 10-minute spell towards the end of a game in which Tottenham had bossed possession but not looked like scoring.

Palmer was lucky to stay on the pitch in the 70th minute, when he shoved his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes after the Tottenham midfielder had stopped him racing through with a foul and a handball.

Christopher Kavanagh, the referee, let him off with a yellow card, but 10 minutes later Palmer inexplicably gave Kavanagh no choice but to book him again and send him off, following a late challenge on substitute Conor Gallagher.

Alonso had said he was confident his players could keep calm ahead of the game, but he got that wrong – along with his team selection and substitutions.

It’s Xabi Alonso’s first taste of the bitter rivalry and has hyped up the atmosphere ahead of the clash. “We are expecting a good atmosphere,” he said. “Electric, with good energy, knowing that in a derby this passion is really in the air in the stadium.

No bans after matchday 12: Juventus and Como at full strength for the Sinigaglia

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (482 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Juvefc

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Serie A disciplinary judge suspended no players after matchday 12, so neither Juventus nor Como lose anyone for Sunday's game.
  • Juventus travel to Como on Sunday with no suspension worries.
  • In a recent development, the decisions covered the games of 21, 22 and 23 November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Serie A disciplinary judge suspended no players after matchday 12, so neither Juventus nor Como lose anyone for Sunday's game. Como were fined again for a slow restart, and Juventus head to Lake Como five points behind them.

Juventus travel to Como on Sunday with no suspension worries. Nor do their hosts. Serie A disciplinary judge Gerardo Mastrandrea banned nobody after matchday 12 in a ruling published in Milan on 24 November.

In a recent development, the decisions covered the games of 21, 22 and 23 November. Nobody was sent off across the round. No player one booking from a ban picked up a yellow card either.

In a recent development, juventus had no cards from their own fixture. The club’s match sheet for the 4-0 win over Venezia at the Allianz Stadium lists no bookings, with Arena as referee.

Recent findings suggest that all four goals came after the break. Woltemade (53′), Koopmeiners (59′) and Cabal (65′) scored before Kolo Muani converted a penalty (71′).

Two Lecce players, Danilo Veiga and Jamil Siebert, picked up their fourth booking of the season and are now one caution from a ban, Virgilio Sport reported. No Juventus or Como player reached that threshold this round.

Como did not escape the judge entirely. The €8,000 fine was imposed under strict liability for delaying the start of the second half by about four minutes without good reason. The judge treated it as a repeated repeat offence.

Industry observers note that it was the largest of the round’s penalties for late restarts. Fiorentina and Milan were also fined as repeat offenders. Genoa received €3,000 for a two-minute delay to kick-off.

The problem is not new for Como. In the previous round, the communiqué of 10 November fined them €10,000, again as repeated repeat offenders. On that occasion the second half started about two minutes late.

According to recent reports, juventus were not blameless that week. The same 10 November ruling fined them €5,000 for holding up the start of the first half by the same margin as Como’s latest delay.

It has been revealed that the match carries weight in the race for the top four. Como have 8 wins, 2 draws and 2 defeats from their 12 games. They have scored 20 goals and conceded 10.

Industry observers note that juventus have 6 wins, 3 draws and 3 defeats. Their attack, with 19 goals, has almost kept pace with Como’s. The difference lies at the back, where Juventus have conceded 12.

A win on Lake Como would narrow the gap to their hosts. Defeat would push Juventus further from the top four.

Como host Juventus at the Sinigaglia on 29 November.
