According to recent reports, we next examined whether Pik3caH1047R affects this developmental trajectory. To address this, we jointly analysed WT and Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells. Integrated analysis resolved seven endothelial populations: tip (C1), metabolic angiogenic (C2), proliferative 1 (C3), proliferative 2 (C4), venous (C5), arterial capillary (C6) and arterial (C7) endothelial cells (Fig. 3b,c, Extended Data Fig. 7i and Supplementary Data 1). GFP expression revealed a marked redistribution of Esm1-traced cells (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 7j,k). Whereas WT GFP+ cells predominantly localized to arterial capillary and arterial clusters (C6 and C7), Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells were instead enriched within angiogenic, proliferative and venous clusters (C2, C3, C4 and C5) (Fig. 3d,e and Extended Data Fig. 7k). Quantification confirmed selective expansion of mutant GFP+ cells in proliferative, angiogenic and venous clusters, but not arterial clusters (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 7k). Importantly, Pik3ca expression was comparable across all endothelial clusters (Extended Data Fig. 7l).

Recent findings suggest that to determine whether this redistribution also reflected altered endothelial transcriptional identity, we performed cluster-specific differential expression analysis comparing GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R endothelial populations. We identified transcriptional alterations between WT and mutant cells in all clusters, with only limited changes in arterial cells (C7), consistent with the resistance observed in differentiated arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7m). The tip cluster (C1) contained too few cells for robust differential expression analysis (Extended Data Fig. 7k). Affected clusters indicated a consistent shift towards venous-associated gene expression, accompanied by reduced tip, arterial, guidance and capillary-specialization programmes (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 7n). This pattern remained after correcting for differences in cluster size (Supplementary Fig. 1). Hierarchical clustering further showed the greatest genotype-dependent divergence in angiogenic and venous populations (Extended Data Fig. 7o). We next performed RNA velocity analysis on subclustered GFP+ cells, which revealed altered cell-state dynamics in Esm1-traced mutant endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7p,q and Supplementary Data 1). Whereas WT GFP+ cells displayed coherent trajectories toward capillary and arterial states, mutant cells showed altered cell-state trajectories, with prominent progression toward proliferative and venous-associated populations and reduced progression toward the arterial lineage (Extended Data Fig. 7r). Together, these findings indicate that Pik3caH1047R promotes endothelial proliferation while diverting differentiating endothelial cells away from the arterial programme towards venous-associated cell states.

To determine whether this programme is initiated rapidly after Pik3caH1047R expression, we analysed cultured sister endothelial cells derived from Pik3caH1047RPdgfb-creERT2 mice using scRNA-seq (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b and Supplementary Data 2). Endothelial identity across clusters was confirmed by uniform Pecam1 expression, and Pik3ca expression was comparable between clusters (Extended Data Fig. 8c,d). Acute Pik3caH1047R expression recapitulated the in vivo transcriptional changes, with expansion of proliferative and venous-like populations and reduction of tip/arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 8e–g). Mutant cells also expressed higher levels of venous markers (that is, Nr2f2 and Nrp2) and lower levels of tip markers (that is, Esm1 and Angpt2) (Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). These data indicate that Pik3caH1047R rapidly and cell-autonomously initiates a programme of proliferation and loss of arterial identity.

Recent findings suggest that we next examined how this transcriptional transition unfolds during arterial differentiation in vivo by staining tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas at P4 and P6 for UNC5B and NR2F2. Control GFP+ cells expressed UNC5B by P4 while remaining NR2F2 negative at both timepoints (Fig. 3g–j and Extended Data Fig. 8j–l). Mutant GFP+ cells were similar to controls at P4 but, by P6, showed reduced UNC5B expression at the sprouting front and near arteries, along with ectopic NR2F2 expression (Fig. 3g–j and Extended Data Fig. 8j–n). These findings validate the scRNA-seq data and demonstrate that Pik3caH1047R progressively disrupts arterial differentiation in vivo.

Industry observers note that to establish the temporal relationship between hyperproliferation and arterial differentiation defects, we examined the proliferative behaviour of Esm1-traced cells at P4 and P6. EdU incorporation showed that Esm1-traced cells normally retain proliferative capacity at P4, with proliferation beginning to diminish by P6 (Fig. 3k–m). Pik3caH1047R mutant Esm1-traced cells exhibited the same temporal pattern, although proliferation remained markedly higher at both timepoints, indicating that hyperproliferation precedes ectopic NR2F2 induction (Fig. 3k–m). The absence of a further increase in proliferation after NR2F2 induction at P6 argues against NR2F2 driving endothelial hyperproliferation.

Industry observers note that to test whether hyperproliferation accounts for defective arterial differentiation, we treated tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R mice with the CDK4 and CDK6 inhibitor palbociclib. Palbociclib partially reduced endothelial proliferation and vascular hyperplasia in tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas but did not restore arterial differentiation or suppress NR2F2 expression (Fig. 4a–h). Similar results were obtained with mitomycin C, which robustly inhibited endothelial expansion without restoring arterial incorporation or reducing NR2F2 expression in mutant GFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 9a–i). Consistently, palbociclib inhibited cell cycle progression in vitro but did not prevent Pik3caH1047R-driven NR2F2 upregulation (Fig. 4i–k and Extended Data Fig. 9j–m). Together, these findings show that suppressing proliferation does not prevent NR2F2 induction or restore arterial differentiation, supporting distinct effects of Pik3caH1047R signalling on proliferation and arterial specification. Consistent with this interpretation, scRNA-seq analysis revealed no association between Nr2f2 expression and cell cycle status in mutant GFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 10a).

As Pik3caH1047R induces NR2F2 expression in pre-arterial endothelial cells, and NR2F2 suppresses arterial identity23,24,25,26, we hypothesized that NR2F2 mediates the arterial differentiation defect downstream of Pik3caH1047R. To test this hypothesis, we crossed the Nr2f2flox/flox allele with tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R mice (tip-cell-specific Nr2f2 deletion; hereafter, tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC mice) and optimized 4-OHT dosing to maximize recombination of both alleles (Fig. 5a). NR2F2 expression was efficiently reduced in tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC retinas (Extended Data Fig. 10b,c). Deletion of Nr2f2 alone neither impaired mobilization of Esm1-traced Nr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC-GFP+ cells into arteries nor altered vascular density (Fig. 5b–d and Extended Data Fig. 10d). Importantly, Nr2f2 deletion restored the ability of Pik3caH1047R cells to contribute to arteries (Fig. 5b,c), whereas endothelial hyperproliferation and vascular expansion remained essentially unchanged compared with tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R mice (Fig. 5d–f and Extended Data Fig. 10d).

We confirmed these findings using the complementary tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R clonal tracing model (Extended Data Fig. 11a–i). Whereas Cherry+ and Cherry+ Nr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC endothelial cells contributed similarly to arteries, eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells were detected in 35% of arteries, compared with 10% for eGFP-PIK3CAH1047R cells (Extended Data Fig. 11c,e). Moreover, most eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells that reached arteries did not form lesions, whereas eGFP-PIK3CAH1047R cells consistently generated small arterial lesions (Extended Data Fig. 11c,f). Nevertheless, eGFP-PIK3CAH1047RNr2f2ΔEC/ΔEC cells continued to overexpand within the capillary plexus (Extended Data Fig. 11g–i). Together, these findings demonstrate that NR2F2 mediates the PIK3CA-driven block in arterial differentiation but is dispensable for mutant cell hyperproliferation in non-arterial vessels.

Sources indicate that to investigate how PIK3CAH1047R activation induces NR2F2 expression, we analysed endothelial cells in culture. Nr2f2 transcript levels increased within 24 h after 4-OHT-induced recombination and remained elevated thereafter (Extended Data Fig. 12a). NR2F2 protein levels increased by 72 h (Extended Data Fig. 12b–d). To test whether Nr2f2 induction depends on PI3K signalling, endothelial cells were treated with the PI3Kα-selective inhibitor alpelisib (BYL719). PI3Kα inhibition reduced Nr2f2 mRNA and protein levels in a dose-dependent manner, accompanied by reduced p-AKT levels (Extended Data Fig. 12e–h). Similarly, alpelisib reduced NR2F2 transcript and protein levels in patient-derived endothelial cells with activating PIK3CA mutations (Extended Data Fig. 12i,j).

Sources indicate that to investigate the transcriptional mechanisms underlying NR2F2 induction, we focused on FOXO transcription factors, major downstream effectors of PI3K signalling7,32, with FOXO1 the predominant family member in endothelial cells33. PI3K–AKT signalling inhibits FOXO1 through phosphorylation-dependent nuclear exclusion7,32 and, consistent with this, FOXO1 was excluded from the nucleus in vascular lesions of Pik3caH1047R mutant mice (Extended Data Fig. 12k,l). We next examined whether FOXO1 directly regulates NR2F2. Analysis of published RNA-seq, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing (ATAC–seq), FOXO1 chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) and H3K27ac ChIP–seq datasets from human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) expressing constitutively nuclear, PI3K-resistant FOXO1(A3)34,35 revealed sustained repression of NR2F2 transcripts and protein, reduced chromatin accessibility at the NR2F2 locus and FOXO1 binding to a vein-specific NR2F2 enhancer (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12m–v). FOXO1(A3) increased occupancy at this enhancer while reducing H3K27 acetylation and chromatin accessibility, consistent with direct transcriptional repression (Extended Data Fig. 12p).

Conversely, endothelial deletion of Foxo1 markedly increased Nr2f2 transcript and protein levels (Fig. 5h,i). Finally, induction of PIK3CAH1047R in HUVECs increased NR2F2 expression, whereas the PI3K-resistant FOXO1(A3) suppressed this response (Fig. 5j). Together, these findings establish FOXO1 as a transcriptional repressor of NR2F2 and define a PI3K–FOXO1–NR2F2 axis through which oncogenic PIK3CA disrupts arterial differentiation.

Using the vasculature as a model, we show that the consequences of PIK3CAH1047R are dictated by endothelial cell context. Depending on the differentiation state of the affected endothelial cell, the mutation promotes pathological proliferation, remains phenotypically silent or disrupts differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 13). This context-dependent model provides a mechanistic explanation for the marked predominance of capillary and venous lesions, and the rarity of arterial lesions, in PIK3CA-driven vascular disease. More broadly, it may also help to explain why PIK3CA-associated overgrowth preferentially affects mesoderm-derived tissues and suggests that similar principles probably apply to other pathogenic PIK3CA variants, which exhibit comparable lesion distributions in patients3.

In a recent development, genetic lineage tracing revealed that endothelial cells expressing endogenous Pik3caH1047R persist in mature arteries without eliciting a detectable phenotype. Consistently, embryonic expression of Pik3caH1047R in Tie2+ cells does not give rise to arterial lesions32. This finding is unexpected given the broad endothelial expression of Pik3ca and the prominent role of PI3Kα signalling in all endothelial cells33. However, basal PI3K signalling is comparatively low in arteries and is not increased by endogenous Pik3caH1047R expression. By contrast, forced overexpression, enhances PI3K signalling and induces mild overgrowth in arterial endothelial cells that have not yet completed differentiation, suggesting that these cells require higher signalling levels to mount a pathological response than venous or capillary endothelial cells. Nevertheless, increased PI3K signalling does not induce overgrowth or NR2F2 expression in fully differentiated arteries. Likewise, reducing shear stress or Notch signalling, key pathways in the acquisition and maintenance of arterial identity30,34,35, does not restore responsiveness to Pik3caH1047R. These findings suggest that arterial endothelial cells possess multiple layers of protection that may also underlie their broader resistance to other mutations36. Future studies are needed to determine how microenvironmental cues, including extracellular matrix composition and mural cell interactions, contribute to this resistance.

In a recent development, we also find that PIK3CAH1047R disrupts arterial differentiation at early developmental stages. During angiogenesis, a subset of tip cells acquires a pre-arterial identity by expressing canonical arterial markers (such as CXCR4, UNC5B, HEY1 and DLL4)30,37,38 and migrates retrogradely into nascent arteries to support arterial expansion. Pik3caH1047R disrupts this transition by inducing an early hyperproliferation response followed by Nr2f2 upregulation and loss of arterial identity. Supporting a causal role for NR2F2, Nr2f2 deletion restored the ability of Pik3caH1047R tip cells to contribute to arteries, consistent with previous studies demonstrating that NR2F2 antagonizes pre-arterial specification26. More broadly, our findings align with evidence that PI3K signalling promotes venous specification39,40, suppresses arterial differentiation41 and favours a stemness state42. Similar effects have been reported in other tissues, where PIK3CAH1047R biases ageing oesophageal progenitor cells towards self-renewal and induces dedifferentiation during mammary tumorigenesis14,15. In parallel, we show that proliferation blockade in Pik3caH1047R-expressing pre-arterial cells limits lesion formation, but neither reduces NR2F2 expression nor restores arterial contribution of mutant cells. These findings indicate that impaired arterial differentiation cannot be explained solely by proliferative exclusion43,44. Conversely, NR2F2 depletion did not block lesion growth or endothelial proliferation, despite previous reports implicating NR2F2 in cell cycle regulation25,45. Together, these findings indicate that PIK3CAH1047R-driven endothelial proliferation and the NR2F2-mediated arterial differentiation defect are functionally separable downstream outputs.

Industry observers note that our findings identify a transcriptional mechanism linking PI3K activation to NR2F2 induction. Previous studies showed that TIE2–PI3K signalling stabilizes NR2F2 protein during venous specification39 and that NR2F2 is elevated in PI3K-driven prostate tumours46. We show that PI3K signalling also promotes NR2F2 transcript and protein expression by inhibiting FOXO1. This is consistent with the established role of FOXO factors as nuclear effectors of PI3K signalling, including in PIK3CA-related vascular malformations47, and with the vascular overgrowth caused by endothelial FOXO1 loss48. Notably, FOXO1 has been reported to promote NR2F2 transcript and protein expression in pancreatic β cells49, whereas our data identify FOXO1 as a direct NR2F2 repressor in endothelial cells. Although the molecular basis of this difference remains to be determined, it is consistent with the context-dependent transcriptional activity of FOXO factors and NR2F2 regulation50,51 and may reflect differences in enhancer use and FOXO1 occupancy. Given that additional transcription factors regulate endothelial NR2F2 expression52,53,54, defining how they cooperate with or compete with FOXO1 will help to explain this context-dependent regulation.

Industry observers note that together, our findings show that the pathological consequences of oncogenic PIK3CA activation depend not only on signalling strength but also on developmental state and endothelial identity. Differentiated arterial cells resist pathological overgrowth, whereas pre-arterial cells undergo an NR2F2-mediated differentiation defect alongside increased proliferation. These functionally separable responses help to explain the vessel-type specificity of PIK3CA-driven vascular malformations.

According to recent reports, the in vivo experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines and legislation of the Catalan Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock, Fisheries and Food (Catalonia, Spain), following protocols approved by the local animal experimentation ethics committee (CEEA) of the Institut Germans Trias i Pujol (IGTP) and local animal authorities of the State of Berlin (Landesamt für Gesundheit und Soziales Berlin). Mice were housed in individually ventilated cages under specific-pathogen-free conditions. All mice were crossed onto the C57BL/6J genetic background. Both male and female pups were used for retinal experiments.

The following mouse strains were used in this study. Pdgfb-creERT2-eGFP (pan-endothelial Cre line)55 mice were provided by M. Fruttiger. Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2 (pan-endothelial Cre line)56, Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 (arterial-endothelial Cre line)57 and Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 (tip-endothelial Cre line)58 mice were obtained from R. Adams. The R26-mTmG59 mice express membrane-targeted Tomato in the absence of Cre activity and this switches to membrane-targeted GFP expression after Cre activation, enabling cell lineage visualization and tracking. Pik3catm1.1Waph/+ mice, which harbour a Cre-inducible H1047R point mutation in the endogenous Pik3ca locus, were provided by W. Phillips60. In this allele, loxPsites flank exon 20, which is replaced after Cre recombination by a downstream version containing a CAT-to-AGG substitution at codon 1047. The two loxPsites are only 419 bp apart, making this region highly recombinogenic. Consistent with this, robust phenotypes are observed even at low doses of 4-OHT19. We occasionally observed vascular overgrowth in regions lacking GFP labelling, suggesting the presence of mutant cells in which the reporter allele had not recombined. Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R mice (hereafter iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R) overexpress the human PIK3CAH1047R cDNA along with H2B-eGFP-V5 (details are provided in the next section and Extended Data Fig. 5). The Nr2f2flox/flox mouse line61, provided by S. Y. Tsai, was used for conditional deletion of Nr2f2. The Foxo1flox/flox mouse line62 was used for conditional deletion of Foxo1. A list of all mouse lines and genotyping primer sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Sources indicate that to induce CreERT2 activity in pups, 4-OHT (Sigma-Aldrich, H7905) was dissolved in ethanol to prepare a 10 mg ml−1 solution. The stock solution was aliquoted and stored at −20 °C. Pups received intragastric injections in volumes adjusted to deliver the doses specified in the figures. To achieve the desired recombination pattern (such as sparse mosaic recombination, efficient recombination or recombination of multiple alleles), the 4-OHT dose was titrated for each CreERT2 line and experimental configuration (Supplementary Table 2).

To inhibit proliferation, pups received palbociclib (70 mg kg−1 in distilled H2O; Selleckchem S1116; intraperitoneal (i.p.), P3–P5) or mitomycin C (10 mg kg−1 in PBS, Sigma-Aldrich, M4287, i.p., P4–P5). To modulate blood flow and inhibit the Notch signalling pathway, pups received captopril (4.125 mg kg−1 in PBS; Sigma-Aldrich, C4042; i.p., P4–P5) or DAPT (100 mg kg−1 in DMSO/peanut oil; Calbiochem, 565770; subcutaneous, P4–P5). DAPT stock (10 mg ml−1) was prepared by dissolving 5 mg in 50 µl DMSO at 40 °C for 10 min and diluting in 450 µl peanut oil. To assess endothelial cell proliferation, pups were injected i.p. with 100 μg of EdU and euthanized 2 h later. EdU incorporated into the retina was detected using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor 594 Imaging Kit (Invitrogen, C10339).

To generate the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R) mouse line, we introduced the DNA insert containing the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-humanPIK3CAH1047R gene by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated homologous-dependent repair, in the previously targeted iChr2-Mosaic mouse embryonic stem (ES) cell line31. To generate the donor construct of interest, we first obtained the HA-huPIK3CAH1047R sequence from the plasmid pBabe-puro-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R (Addgene, 12524) and cloned it into plasmid SO107 (Addgene, 99617)31, which contained the LoxP2-H2B-eGFP-V5-2A cassette. We then inserted the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R cassette into the donor vector JP6 (Addgene, 99627), which contains the hygromycin-resistance gene. This resulted in the generation of the donor vector NA453, containing the complete donor construct of interest (Extended Data Fig. 5). ES cells of the G4 genetic background63 were cultured in standard ES cell medium consisting of DMEM supplemented with GlutaMax (31966-047, Gibco), 15% FBS (tested for germline transmission), 1× non-essential amino acids (Hyclone, SH3023801), 0.1% β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma-Aldrich, M7522), 1× penicillin–streptomycin (Lonza, DE17-602E) and leukaemia inhibitory factor. ES cells were maintained on dishes coated with a feeder layer of mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs). For each nucleofection, 2.5 × 106 ES cells were resuspended in 100 µl nucleofection solution containing 1.5 µg of circular px330 plasmid (NA505), encoding the guide RNA sequence (Guide3, GTTGCCTATGAGAGGCTAGAC), and 3.5 µg circular donor plasmid (NA453) containing the H2B-eGFP-V5-2A-HA-huPIK3CAH1047R sequence and the PGK-hygromycin resistance cassette (Extended Data Fig. 5). After nucleofection, 5 µl or 30 µl of the cell suspension was plated into separate wells on a six-well plate containing MEF feeder layers. Then, 7 days after hygromycin selection, 24 isolated ES cell colonies were picked for cryopreservation and subsequent screening. PCR with the flanking primers identified clones with correct homologous recombination and targeted insertion. After identifying correctly targeted ES cell clones, the functionality of the targeted allele was validated by transient transfection of a Cre-expressing plasmid. Positive clones were expanded and microinjected into C57BL/6J host blastocysts. Chimeric mice with a high degree of agouti coat colour were subsequently bred to achieve germline transmission of the targeted allele.

Mice were euthanized by decapitation, and their eyes were isolated and incubated on ice in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA; Sigma-Aldrich, 158127) in PBS for 1 h. Retinas were dissected and fixed for an additional 1 h in 4% PFA on ice, washed three times in PBS and incubated overnight at 4 °C in blocking buffer (1% BSA, 3% donkey serum and 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS) with gentle agitation. For NR2F2 staining, retinas were subjected to antigen retrieval by boiling for 20 min in 0.01 M citrate buffer (pH 6, Sigma-Aldrich, W305600) before permeabilization. Retinas were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with specific primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. In iFluMosaic-PIK3CA retinas, the antigen-retrieval step required for NR2F2 staining abolished the GFP signal and prevented detection with anti-GFP antibodies; therefore, the retinas were incubated overnight with anti-GFP antibodies before antigen retrieval. After washing three times in PBST (0.1% Tween-20 in PBS), the retinas were incubated for 30 min at room temperature in PBLEC buffer (1% Triton X-100, 1 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM MnCl2 in PBS (pH 6.8)). Secondary Alexa-Fluor-conjugated antibodies or isolectin GS-B4 (IB4) were incubated with retinas in PBLEC buffer for 2 h at room temperature or overnight at 4 °C. After three additional washes with PBST, retinas were flat-mounted onto microscope slides with Mowiol (Calbiochem, 475904), supplemented with the anti-fade reagent DABCO (1.4-diazabicyclo-(2.2.2)octane; Sigma-Aldrich, D27802) or Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech, 0100-01). For FOXO1/ERG co-immunostaining, an additional blocking step was included because both primary antibodies were raised in the same species, thereby preventing cross-reactivity. After the incubation with the anti-FOXO1 antibody and its corresponding secondary antibody, retinas were incubated with AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragments donkey anti-rabbit IgG (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 711-006-152, 1:100) in PBS for 1 h at room temperature. The retinas were then washed, briefly fixed with 4% PFA, blocked again and incubated with the primary Alexa-Fluor-647-conjugated anti-ERG antibody. A list of all of the primary and secondary antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Mouse endothelial cells were isolated from the lungs of adult mice (both female and male) aged 3 to 6 weeks. Under sterile conditions, lungs were minced and digested in 4 U ml−1 dispase II (Roche, 04942078001) in Hanks’ balanced salt solution (Gibco, 14170-112) for 1 h at 37 °C with constant agitation. Tissue was further dissociated by pipetting to obtain a single-cell suspension, and digestion was stopped with Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; Corning, 10-013-CV) supplemented with 10% FBS (Biowest, S1810-500) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco, 15140-122). Cells were resuspended in PBS and incubated for 30 min at room temperature with rat anti-CD144 (Cdh5; BD Biosciences, 55289) antibody-coated magnetic Dynabeads (Invitrogen, 11035). CD144+ cells were washed in PBS containing 0.5% BSA and sorted by magnetic separation. CD144+ cells were plated on 0.5% gelatine-coated 12-well plates (Sigma-Aldrich, G1890) and cultured in complete DMEM/F12 (PromoCell, C-30140) supplemented with 20% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and two vials of endothelial cell growth supplement/heparin (ECGF/H; PromoCell, C-30120). Once confluent, a second selection with CD144-antibody-coated magnetic Dynabeads was performed for 1 h at room temperature. Cells were trypsinized, magnet-sorted, resuspended in F12 complete medium and cultured in a six-well format. Cells were maintained at 37 °C under a 5% CO2 atmosphere and used for experiments up to passage 5. Primary cells were not tested for mycoplasma contamination. Mouse endothelial cells used in Fig. 5i,j were isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2Foxo1flox/flox lungs as described previously64.

To induce CreERT2-mediated recombination in vitro, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice were treated with 5 μM 4-OHT for 6 h, with ethanol-treated cells as controls, and cultured for a further 72 h. Then, 1 day before immunofluorescence analysis, cells were replated at low confluency onto gelatine-coated coverslips in 12-well plates. At 4 h before collection, the culture medium was replaced with starvation medium, after which cells were processed for immunofluorescence. For mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2-Pik3caH1047R/+ mice, recombination was induced by treatment with 2 μM 4-OHT for 6 h, with ethanol-treated cells as controls, followed by the indicated experimental conditions before collection for immunoblot or qPCR analysis. For mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2Foxo1flox/flox mice, recombination was induced with 250 nM 4-OHT or vehicle control (DMSO), and cells were analysed 72 h after treatment.

Pooled HUVECs were purchased from Lonza (CC-2519) and cultured in EBM endothelial cell growth basal medium (EBM, Lonza, CC-3121) supplemented with EGM endothelial cell growth medium SingleQuots kit (Lonza, CC-4133) and 10% FBS (Life Technologies). Human embryonic kidney (HEK293FT) cells were used to produce lentiviruses and purchased from Life Technologies (R70007). HEK293FT cells were cultured in DMEM (Gibco, 31966-021) supplemented with 10% FBS (Life Technologies) and gentamicin (500 µg ml−1, Lonza, 17-518L). Cells were purchased from commercial suppliers, visually inspected for expected morphology and used for a limited number of passages. No further authentication was performed in-house. All cells were tested negative for mycoplasma and maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2.

For doxycycline-inducible lentiviral expression of PIK3CAH1047R, a V5-PIK3CAH1047R-encoding cDNA was cloned into the pLVX-TetOne-Puro vector (Takara, 631847). For CRISPR–Cas9-mediated genome editing, gene-specific gRNA sequences (Supplementary Table 4) were cloned into a plentiCRISPRv2 plasmid co-expressing Flag-tagged Cas9 nuclease and a puromycin-selection marker (Addgene, 52961). Lentivirus production was performed by co-transfection of HEK293FT cells with pMD2.G (Addgene, 12259), psPAX2 (Addgene, 12260) and transfer plasmids. Transfections were performed using the Lipofectamine 2000 transfection reagent (Life Technologies, 11668027) as previously described65. Viruses were collected 48 and 72 h after transfection and filtered through a 0.45-μm filter. HUVECs were transduced with lentiviruses for 16 h in the presence of 8 μg ml−1 polybrene (Santa Cruz, sc-134220) and selected with 1 μg ml−1 puromycin (InvivoGen, ant-pr-1). Lentiviral expression of PIK3CAH1047R was induced by stimulating HUVECs with 600 ng ml−1 doxycycline (Sigma-Aldrich, D9891) for 72 h.

It has been revealed that subconfluent HUVECs were transduced with custom-made adenoviruses (Vector Biolabs) to overexpress constitutively nuclear human FOXO1 (FOXO1A3-Flag) or control (CMV-null) adenoviruses (Vector Biolabs, 1300). For adenoviral transductions, HUVECs were incubated in EBM medium (Lonza, CC-3121) containing 0.1% (v/v) BSA (Sigma-Aldrich, 1595) for 4 h and transduced with the respective viruses for an additional 4 h in the presence of 8 µg ml−1 polybrene (Santa Cruz, sc-134220). HUVECs were then washed five times with Hank’s balanced salt solution (Gibco, 14175095) and cultured for the indicated times in EBM basal medium supplemented with 10% FBS and EGM SingleQuots.

Industry observers note that gene-specific gRNA sequences to target the NR2F2-1345 enhancer were designed using CHOPCHOP66. For each target gene, we used three independent gRNAs and co-transfected them with packaging vectors for lentivirus production. After transduction, puromycin was used to select a pool of CRISPR–Cas9-mediated mutant HUVECs. The knockout efficiency was confirmed by PCR analysis of gDNA isolated from transduced cells. Single guide RNA sequences and genotyping primers are provided in Supplementary Table 4.

In a recent development, cells were washed with warm 1% PBS containing Mg2+ and Ca2+ (Gibco, 14080-055), fixed for 15 min in 4% PFA and washed again with warm PBS. For staining, cells were permeabilized for 5 min with 0.4% Triton X-100 in PBS, followed by a 1 h incubation in blocking buffer (2% BSA in PBS). After washing with PBS, cells were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. Subsequently, secondary AlexaFluor-conjugated antibodies were diluted in blocking buffer and added to the cells for a 1 h incubation at room temperature. After additional washes with PBS, cells were incubated with DAPI (Invitrogen, D1305; 1:500) for 1 min and then mounted on microscope slides with Fluoromount-G (Southern Biotech, 0100-01). A list of all of the antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

In a recent development, human endothelial cells were isolated from patient biopsies of vascular malformations. These biopsies were obtained during therapeutic surgical resection, with informed consent and approval from the Biomedical Committees at Hospital Sant Joan de Déu, Hospital Santa Creu i Sant Pau, Hospital Universitari de Bellvitge and Hospital Universitario Germans Trias i Pujol (codes PR264/16, PIC-96-16 and PI-21-171). Experiments adhered to the WMA Declaration of Helsinki and the Belmont Report. Data were stored in a secure database maintained by Hospital Sant Joan de Deu. Biopsies were homogenized and digested in dispase II (Roche, 04942078001) and collagenase A (Roche Diagnostics, 10103586001) for up to 1.5 h at 37 °C, with continuous movement. The tissue was dissociated by pipetting into a single-cell solution, then inactivated with DMEM (10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin). Cells were resuspended in 0.5% BSA in PBS and incubated with CD31-antibody-coated (Agilent Dako, M0823, JC70A) magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11041) for 1 h at room temperature. The CD31+ fraction was magnetically sorted, resuspended and cultured in 0.5% gelatine-coated wells in EGM2 medium (PromoCell, C-39211) supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin (EGM2 complete) at 37 °C and 5% CO2 until confluency. Cells were then subjected to a second CD31-based magnetic selection. Mycoplasma testing was not performed on primary cells. To validate the presence of the mutation in isolated endothelial cells, genomic DNA was extracted according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Thermo Fisher Scientific, K182001) and detected by next-generation sequencing. For the vascular malformation (VM) 64, we obtained from 1,572 reads, c.3140A>G (H1047R) with a 45.86% variant allelic frequency and for the VM90 from 461 reads, c.2740A>G (E545G) with 48.37% variant allelic frequency.

Cells were lysed in ice-cold lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 5 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl and 1% Triton X-100, supplemented with protease (Roche, 11836153001) and phosphatase (Sigma-Aldrich, 4906837001) inhibitors. The protein concentration was measured using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Total cell lysates were resolved on 10% SDS–polyacrylamide gels using a Mini-Protean Tetra Vertical Electrophoresis Cell (Bio-Rad, 1658004) and subsequently transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes using a Mini Trans-Blotcell system (Bio-Rad, 1703930). Membranes were blocked with 5% milk in TBST (TBS containing 0.1% Tween-20) and incubated with appropriate primary antibodies diluted in 2% BSA in TBST. Secondary antibodies were diluted in 5% milk in TBST. Immunoblots were visualized using ECL (0.1 M Tris-HCl, pH 9.35, 2.2 mM luminol, 2.2 mM p-coumaric acid and 0.06% H2O2). Western blots shown in Fig. 5i,j and Extended Data Fig. 12o,s were performed as described previously65. Information on all antibodies is provided in Supplementary Table 3. Uncropped western blot images are provided in Supplementary Fig. 2.

Industry observers note that RNA was extracted using the Maxwell RSC SimplyRNA Cells Kit (Promega, AS1390) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and RNA quality was assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Reverse transcription was performed using 500 ng of RNA from cell lysate samples with the High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems, 4368814). qPCR was performed using a QuantStudio 7 Flex system with SYBR Green real-time PCR master mix (Applied Biosystems, A46110). RNA isolation, cDNA synthesis and qPCR for Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 12n,r,u were performed as previously described65. Primer sequences and TaqMan assay IDs are provided in Supplementary Table 4.

To inhibit PI3Kα activity, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were treated with ethanol or 4-OHT for 6 h, followed by vehicle or the PI3Kα-selective inhibitor alpelisib (BYL719; at 1 or 5 µM) for an additional 66 h. Patient-derived endothelial cells isolated from venous malformations were treated with vehicle or BYL719 (1 µM or 5 µM) for 72 h before downstream analysis. To inhibit proliferation in vitro, mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were cultured for 24 h in DMEM/F12 supplemented with reduced growth factors (10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and endothelial cell growth supplement/heparin (ECGF/H)) to limit baseline proliferation and achieve approximately 40% confluency. Cells were then treated with palbociclib (2 μM) or vehicle (PBS), followed 6 h later by the addition of 4-OHT (2 μM) or ethanol while maintaining palbociclib treatment. Cells were collected 24 h after 4-OHT treatment for western blot, qPCR analysis and flow cytometry.

For EdU incorporation assays, EdU (10 μM) was added 2 h before collection. Cells were processed using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor 647 Flow Cytometry Assay Kit (Invitrogen, C10634) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Data were acquired on a BD FACSymphony A1 cell analyser and analysed using FlowJo (v.10.1, BD Biosciences). Cells were gated based on forward and side scatter to exclude debris and doublets before analysis as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 3.

Imaging was performed with Leica Stellaris 8, Leica TCS SP5, Zeiss LSM 980 and Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscopes, operated with LAS X v.4.8.2, LAS AF v.2.7 and Zen v.3.9 software, respectively. Adobe Photoshop (v.25.12.0), Adobe Illustrator (64-bit, v.29.0.1), ImageJ v.1.54b, CellProfiler v.4.2.6 and Imaris v.10.1 were used for image processing and quantification. All images shown in the figures are maximum intensity projections. Images were taken from at least three retinal areas in each retina and are representative of at least four retinas analysed for each genotype unless otherwise stated. The identification of retinal vascular lesions and their locations was performed by observing IB4 in ×10 images. Vascular malformations were defined based on abnormal vessel morphology and GFP+ clonal expansion. In capillary beds, lesions were identified as focal regions displaying abnormal vessel enlargement compared with the surrounding capillary plexus and associated clusters of GFP+ endothelial cells. In veins and arteries, malformations were defined by the presence of GFP+ endothelial cell clusters indicative of clonal expansion, together with abnormal vessel enlargement compared with control vessels. Retinal vascularity was measured using the IB4 channel by adjusting the threshold to select IB4+, followed by quantification of the percentage of IB4+ area relative to the total retinal surface. Vessel width was determined by measuring the average diameter at three different points along each vessel. GFP+ cell expansion was quantified by calculating the percentage of GFP+ area within the IB4+ area. For capillary analysis, images containing only capillary beds were used. To quantify GFP+ cells in veins and arteries, IB4 staining was used to delineate the vascular area, and vessel-specific regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to arteries or veins were manually selected. For quantification of aEC-GFP+ endothelial cells, the analysed area was defined by a fixed ROI (200 × 550 μm (P6 retinas), 200 × 630 μm (P9 retinas) and 500 × 1,200 μm (P12 retinas)) to maintain consistent arterial length across replicates and to avoid including other vascular types. In P21 retinas, aEC-GFP+ cells were spread across various vessel types, so the ROI for quantification included the entire vascular plexus. To quantify vascular p-S6 intensity, a manual threshold was set to obtain the GFP+ area and define the ROI. The integrated density of p-S6 was then measured within the GFP+ area. In iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice, p-S6 integrated density was quantified separately in Cherry+ (WT) or eGFP+ (PIK3CAH1047R) cells after manual delineation of IB4+ areas containing each recombinant cell population. In both cases, the background signal (mean grey values) was measured in adjacent IB4-negative regions. The corrected total fluorescence (CTF) was calculated using the following equation: CTF = integrated density – (vascular area × mean grey background value). αSMA, CX37 and UNC5B expression in endothelial cells was quantified by measuring the mean intensity within GFP+ areas. Endothelial cell proliferation was quantified as the percentage of ERG+ endothelial cell nuclei co-immunostained positive for Ki-67 or EdU relative to the total number of ERG+ nuclei within the GFP+ area. In the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model, proliferation was quantified separately for Cherry+ and eGFP+ nuclei as the percentage of Ki-67+ nuclei relative to the total number of Cherry+ or eGFP+ nuclei, respectively. Nuclear FOXO1 positivity was quantified as the percentage of FOXO1+ERG+ nuclei relative to the total number of ERG+ nuclei within the GFP+ area. NR2F2 levels were assessed by manual scoring of nuclear immunofluorescence intensity in ERG+ endothelial cells. Endothelial nuclei with strong and unequivocal nuclear signal were classified as NR2F2high, nuclei with weak but discernible nuclear signal as NR2F2low and nuclei lacking detectable nuclear signal were classified as NR2F2negative, including after a substantial increase in display intensity during image visualization. Scoring was performed using identical acquisition settings across samples. Quantification of Cherry+ and eGFP+ endothelial cells in iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas was performed manually, differentiating their presence in capillaries, veins and arteries. Vascular lesions were classified based on size as small (<10 PIK3CAH1047R cells), medium (between 10 and 35 PIK3CAH1047R cells) or large (>35 PIK3CAH1047R cells) based on manual counting of PIK3CAH1047R mutant cells. The incidence of arteries populated with PIK3CAH1047R cells was determined as a percentage in relation to the total number of arteries containing any recombinant cell. The relative arterial vessel width in iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas was assessed by comparing vessel diameter in a central region containing recombinant cells with adjacent regions of the same vessel lacking recombinant cells.

In a recent development, in cultured endothelial cells, maximum-intensity projections of confocal images were analysed using CellProfiler (v.4.2.6). DAPI, eGFP, Cherry and Ki-67 signals were defined as primary objects. Nuclei were identified based on DAPI staining and used to generate secondary objects for p-S6 quantification. CellProfiler assigned p-S6 intensity to individual nuclei and classified cells as p-S6+ or p-S6−. WT and PIK3CAH1047R endothelial cells were quantified by identifying Cherry+DAPI+ and eGFP+DAPI+ cells, respectively.

Sources indicate that FOXO1-bound Nr2f2 enhancer identification was performed according an approach described previously67. In brief, enhancer marks from three published datasets were used to identify putative enhancers: (1) open chromatin as assessed by ATAC–seq in mouse P6 retina endothelial cells (MRECs)68; (2) enriched EP300 binding in Tie2-cre+ cells from embryonic day 11.5 mouse embryos69; and (3) binding of the ETS factor ERG, which marks all known endothelial cell enhancers, in HUVECs70. Putative enhancer regions were then assessed for FOXO1(A3) binding47,65, identifying the FOXO1-bound NR2F2-1345 enhancer. For in vivo validation, the NR2F2-1345 enhancer sequence was cloned into the E1b-GFP-Tol2-Gateway vector71 using the Gene Synthesis service from Genewiz (part of Azenta Life Sciences). F0 mosaic transgenic zebrafish embryos were generated using Tol2-mediated integration72. All animal procedures were approved by a local ethical review committee at Oxford University, licensed by the UK Home Office and conducted in accordance with ARRIVE guidelines. All zebrafish (KLC strain) were maintained in groups. Embryos were maintained in E3 medium (5 mM NaCl, 0.17 mM KCl, 0.33 mM CaCl2, 0.33 mM MgSO4) at 28.5 °C. To image, all embryos were dechorionated and anaesthetized with 0.01% tricaine methanesulfonate in E3 medium. For analysis of transgenic zebrafish, single embryos were transferred into a flat-bottom 96-well plate, mounted in 0.1% TopVision low-melting-point agarose (Thermo Fisher Scientific, R0801) in E3 medium with tricaine methanesulfonate (Merck, A5040). GFP reporter gene expression was screened with a Zeiss LSM 980 (Carl Zeiss) confocal microscope at 32–72 h post-fertilization. Whole zebrafish were imaged using the ‘tile scan’ command, combined with z-stack collection, at 488 nm excitation and 510 nm emission for eGFP.

To target tip endothelial cells, recombination was induced with 25 mg kg−1 4-OHT at P1 and P2 in Esm1(BAC)-creERT2R26-mTmG (control) and Esm1(BAC)-creERT2R26-mTmG;Pik3caH1047R (mutant) mice. Retinas were collected at P6 and processed fresh for enzymatic dissociation using the Neural Tissue Dissociation Kit (P) (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-092-628). After dissociation, the cell suspension was incubated with CD31 MicroBeads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-097-418) and subjected to two consecutive rounds of magnetic separation using MS columns (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-042-201) and an OctoMACS Separator (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-042-109). Cells were resuspended in 0.04% BSA in PBS and processed for scRNA-seq using the 10x Genomics platform. Two independent experiments were performed on separate days using independent cohorts of control and mutant mice, with retinas pooled per genotype (Exp1: n = 5 control, n = 3 mutant; Exp2: n = 4 control, n = 4 mutant).

Mouse lung endothelial cells isolated from Pdgfb-creERT2Pik3caH1047R/+ mice were treated in vitro overnight with 2 μM 4-OHT to induce recombination and expression of Pik3caH1047R, while ethanol-treated cells were used as a control (WT cells for Pik3ca). The medium was then changed to F12 complete, and cells were collected 48 h post-induction. Cells were detached with trypsin, centrifuged, subjected to debris removal (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-109-398) and finally resuspended in 0.04% BSA in PBS. For the scRNA-seq, three independent biological replicates were pooled for each treatment condition.

Sources indicate that single cells were encapsulated into emulsion droplets using the Chromium Controller (10x Genomics) with the 3′ Next GEM kit (v3 chemistry) or the Chromium GEM-X Single Cell 3′ Kit v4 for in vitro and in vivo samples, respectively. Libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s protocol, targeting a recovery of around 10,000 cells per sample. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq X 25B platform using 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads. Raw sequencing data were processed using Cell Ranger (v.7.0.1 or v.8.0.1) and aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10) using the default parameters. For the in vivo datasets, raw UMI count matrices were corrected for ambient RNA contamination using CellBender (v.0.2.1)73. This approach models background RNA from empty droplets and infers corrected expression counts for cell-containing droplets using a probabilistic framework. Corrected matrices were used for downstream analyses.

All scRNA-seq datasets (in vivo and in vitro) were processed using a unified analytical pipeline in R (v.4.2.2) with the Seurat package (v.4.9.9)74. CellBender output count matrices were imported using a custom function designed to read H5AD files in R. Each sample was initially processed independently. tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R samples were initially analysed separately to prevent the pronounced transcriptional changes associated with the mutation from dominating the global data structure and obscuring the physiological organization of the tEC-GFP retina. After independent quality control, dimensionality reduction and clustering, endothelial cells were identified within each genotype based on canonical marker expression. The endothelial subsets from tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R samples were subsequently combined and jointly reanalysed to enable direct comparison of endothelial states across genotypes while retaining an accurate representation of the WT retinal vasculature. Within each condition, control filtering was applied to remove low-quality cells and uninformative genes. Cells were excluded if they contained fewer than 250 detected genes, more than 20% mitochondrial transcripts or exhibited a complexity index greater than 0.8. Genes with zero counts across all cells were removed. Potential doublets were estimated using DoubletFinder (v.2.0.3) on a per-sample basis75. Although doublets were not removed from the dataset, they were excluded from downstream differential expression analyses. Data normalization was performed using Seurat’s NormaliseData function with the LogNormalise method and a scale factor of 10,000. Highly variable genes (HVGs) were defined based on the distribution of non-zero gene expression counts, selecting a threshold corresponding to the third quartile plus 100 genes. Data were then scaled using ScaleData, and then a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using RunPCA. To correct for batch effects across biological replicates, datasets were integrated using the Harmony algorithm (v.1.2.3)76, applied to PCA embeddings. The sample identity (ID) was used as the batch variable, enabling alignment of cells across replicates while preserving biological variability. Harmony-corrected principal components were used for downstream analyses. Graph-based clustering was performed by constructing a shared-nearest-neighbour graph using FindNeighbours, followed by community detection with the Louvain algorithm implemented in FindClusters. To specifically analyse the vascular compartment, endothelial cells were identified based on canonical marker expression (Pecam1 and Cdh5) and computationally subsetted. A secondary, endothelial-focused analysis pipeline was then applied, including re-identification of highly variable features, normalization, scaling, PCA and Harmony integration76. Multiple clustering resolutions (0.1, 0.3 and 0.5) were evaluated, with a resolution of 0.3 selected as it best recapitulated known endothelial cell subpopulations (for example, tip, arterial, venous and proliferative endothelial cells). Cluster annotation was performed using a one-versus-all differential expression approach with Seurat’s FindAllMarkers function, applying the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing.

In a recent development, in the in vivo retinal endothelial cell dataset, GFP expression was used to identify recombined endothelial cells. To enable GFP quantification, the GFP coding sequence was appended to the standard mouse reference genome (mm10), and raw sequencing reads were aligned against this modified reference using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger v.8.0.1. This allowed simultaneous quantification of endogenous transcripts and GFP expression. To identify GFP-expressing cells, GFP transcript levels were examined across the dataset. Density plots of log-normalized GFP expression revealed a bimodal distribution, which enabled the application of a stringer classification threshold (log-normalized expression > 1.5). Cells with log-normalized GFP expression of greater than 1.5 were classified as GFP+, whereas cells with expression at or below this threshold were classified as GFP−.

Recent findings suggest that differential expression analysis was performed by comparing mutant (GFP+ Pik3caH1047R) and WT (GFP+ WT) cells within defined endothelial cell populations using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test implemented in Seurat (FindMarkers). To enhance robustness and account for sparsity inherent to single-cell data, a complementary pseudobulk approach was applied. Raw counts were aggregated at the sample level (grouped by ID and phenotype) using AggregateExpression, treating each mouse as an independent biological replicate. The resulting count matrix was analysed using DESeq2 (v.1.38.3)77, applying a generalized linear model based on the negative binomial distribution. Concordance between single-cell and pseudobulk approaches was assessed by correlating log2[FC] values across clusters and evaluating overlap of significantly regulated genes (adjusted P < 0.05). A high level of agreement in both magnitude and direction of gene regulation was observed. Based on this consistency, Wilcoxon-derived results were used for downstream visualization and functional analyses due to their higher sensitivity, while pseudobulk results served as an independent validation of biological signal.

It has been revealed that average expression profiles were calculated for each endothelial population using Seurat’s AverageExpression function and HVG. The 1,500 most variable genes were scaled by gene and hierarchically clustered using Pearson correlation distance and average linkage. Analyses included either all endothelial cells from tEC-GFP retinas, irrespective of GFP status, or only traced GFP+ endothelial cells from tEC-GFP and tEC-Pik3caH1047R retinas. In the latter, populations were additionally stratified by genotype. Heat maps were generated using ComplexHeatmap (v.2.15.4).

To control for potential biases from unequal cell numbers between conditions (GFP+ Pik3caH1047R versus GFP+ WT), we implemented a bootstrapped downsampling strategy. For each endothelial cell subtype, 1,000 iterations of random subsampling were performed. In each iteration, the condition with more cells was downsampled to match the size of the smaller group, thereby generating balanced datasets. Differential expression was recalculated in each iteration using the Wilcoxon test (FindMarkers, with logfc.threshold = 0 and min.pct = 0). For each gene, the frequency of significance (adjusted P < 0.05) and the consistency of log2[FC] direction were recorded across iterations. This approach confirmed that the identified transcriptional signatures were stable and reproducible, supporting their interpretation as robust biological features of the mutant phenotype rather than artefacts driven by differences in cell numbers.

It has been revealed that the expression of Nr2f2 and proliferation scores across GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells were estimated. Cell cycle and proliferation scores (the sum of S and G2/M phases) were computed using ccAFv278. Biological thresholds were established: the Nr2f2 threshold was set at the 99th percentile of reference WT arterial and artery capillary cells, and proliferation status used a cut-off of 0.1. Cells were categorized into Nr2f2 status, proliferation status and a joint status (double high, Nr2f2 high, proliferation high or low/basal).

In a recent development, RNA velocity was inferred with scVelo in GFP+ endothelial cells and further analysed using CellRank v.2. GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R cells were analysed independently using identical parameters. For each genotype, 2,000 highly variable genes were selected, and genotype-specific neighbourhood graphs and expression moments were calculated using 30 principal components and 15 neighbours. Transcriptional dynamics and velocities were estimated using the dynamical model. CellRank was subsequently used to construct a velocity-based transition matrix using the VelocityKernel and to identify macrostates using GPCCA. Velocity vectors were projected onto the shared integrated UMAP and visualized as streamlines and cell-level arrows.

In a recent development, statistical analysis was performed using Prism 10 (GraphPad). Data are presented as the mean ± s.e.m. For in vivo experiments, each retina was considered an independent experimental unit. At least three mice from at least two independent litters were used per condition, except for in Extended Data Fig. 11i (n = 2). For the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model, only retinas containing identified recombined cells were included. Experiments using mouse endothelial cells included biological replicates, whereas those using human endothelial cells were performed as independent experimental repeats. Sample sizes are indicated in the figure legends. Statistical significance between two groups was assessed using either an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests or the two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test or two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s test was used. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample sizes; sample sizes were based on previous experiments. Reproducibility was confirmed through multiple independent experiments. The experiments were not randomized, and the investigators were not blinded during the experiments or data analysis.

In a recent development, a, Experimental timeline using the Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 mouse line. b, Confocal images of P6 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red) and GFP (cyan). c, Quantification of GFP+ areas in IB4+ areas in capillaries, veins, and arteries of P6 retinas (n = 14, 11, 14, 11, 14 and 12 retinas, left to right). d, Confocal images of P4 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red) and GFP (cyan). e, High-magnification confocal images of P4 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan), ERG (blue), and Ki-67 (yellow). f, Quantification of endothelial cell proliferation within GFP+ capillary areas, expressed as ERG+Ki-67+ nuclei relative to total ERG+ nuclei, in P4 retinas (n = 5 and 10 retinas, left to right). g, Confocal images of P6 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R capillary areas, stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan), and p-S6 (Ser235/236) (yellow/grey). h, Quantification of p-S6 (Ser235/236) fluorescence intensity within the GFP+ capillary areas in P6 retinas (n = 6 and 5 retinas, left to right). i, Confocal images of P21 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red) and GFP (cyan/grey). j, Confocal images of P21 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R capillaries, veins and arteries stained for IB4 (red) and GFP (cyan). k, Quantification of vessel width (left) and GFP+ area in IB4+ area (right) in P21 retinas (n = 4, 6, 4, 5, 4 and 6 retinas, left to right in both graphs). l, Quantification of GFP+ area within IB4+ area in capillaries (left, n = 14, 11, 8, 8, 4 and 6 retinas, left to right), veins (middle, n = 14, 11, 8, 8, 4 and 5 retinas, left to right) and arteries (right, n = 14, 11, 8, 8, 4 and 6 retinas, left to right) of P6, P8, and P21 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas (n = 14, 12, 8, 8, 4 and 6 retinas, left to right in each graph). Recent findings suggest that a, Details of construct generation are provided in Methods. PGK-hygro-pA, resistance marker for selection; WPRE-pA, viral sequence that enhances transgene expression by promoting mRNA stability and nuclear export; CAG, strong and ubiquitous promoter; PGK-Neo-pA, resistance marker for ES cell selection; 2 A, viral peptide enabling equimolar expression of multiple proteins from a single open reading frame (ORF); HA, V5, and His, epitope tags for antibody detection; H2B, histone tag targeting proteins to chromatin; N-PhiM, non-fluorescent protein that is used as a reporter of promoter expression; INS, insulator sequence that prevents inappropriate enhancer-promoter interactions. b, Schematic illustrating the mouse strategy combining the pan-EC (pEC) tamoxifen-inducible Cre allele (Cdh5(PAC)-creERT2) with the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R allele. c, Mouse lung ECs isolated from pEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice were treated with 4-OHT for 6 h, expanded for 72 h and then replated. Samples were collected at 24, 48 and 72 h after replating, following 4 h of serum starvation immediately before each collection. d,e, Confocal images of primary mouse lung endothelial cells (ECs) isolated from pEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice collected at 24, 48, and 72 h after seeding. Cells were stained with DAPI (blue, nuclei) and for eGFP (yellow, PIK3CAH1047R-expressing ECs), Cherry (cyan, wild-type ECs for Pik3ca), and Ki-67 (magenta, proliferating cells) (d) or and p-S6 (Ser235/236, grey) (e). f, Percentage of Cherry+ (cyan) and eGFP+ (yellow) cells among total Cherry+ and eGFP+ cells at 24, 48 and 72 h post-seeding (n = 6 biological replicates). g,h, Quantification of Ki-67+ cells (g) and p-S6 (Ser235/236) fluorescence intensity (h) within Cherry+ (cyan) and eGFP+ (yellow) cell populations at 24, 48, and 72 h after seeding (n = 6 biological replicates). Data are mean ± SEM. Two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test (f–h). Scale bars, 200 μm (d,e).

It has been revealed that a, Experimental timeline for studies using the tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model. b, Pie chart showing lesion categories, defined by the number of EGFP-PIK3CAH1047R-expressing endothelial cells per lesion in P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas (n = 14 retinas). c,d, Confocal images of P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (magenta), Cherry (cyan), eGFP (yellow), and Ki-67 (c, red/grey) or p-S6 (Ser235/236) (d, grey). e, Confocal images of an arterial lesion (top) and capillary regions (bottom) in P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas, stained for IB4 (magenta), Cherry (cyan), eGFP (yellow) and ERG (blue). No Cherry+ cells were detected in these areas. f,g, Confocal images of P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (left), P9 aEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (middle) and P12 aEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (right) arteries stained for IB4 (magenta), Cherry (cyan) and eGFP (yellow) with additional staining for p-S6 (Ser235/236, white/grey) in g. The schematic below illustrates the degree of arterial differentiation according to the targeted endothelial cell population and timing of Cre induction. h, Stacked bar graph showing the percentage of Cherry+ wild-type and eGFP+ PIK3CAH1047R Bmx-derived progeny in arteries following Cre induction at P4–P6 or P7–P9, analysed at P9 and P12, respectively (n = 14, n = 27 retinas, left to right). i, Quantification of relative arterial width (fold change) in arterial regions containing Cherry+ and eGFP+ cells (n = 7, 7, 14, 14, 14 and 14 retinas, left to right). j, Quantification of p-S6 fluorescence intensity (fold change) in Cherry+ and eGFP+ cells within arteries (n = 8, 8, 5, 5, 7 and 7 retinas, left to right). k, Confocal images of P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (left), P9 aEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (middle) and P12 aEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (right) arteries stained for IB4 (magenta), Cherry (cyan), eGFP (yellow) and NR2F2 (white). Yellow arrows indicate eGFP+ cells. Representative of 3 retinas per condition analysed across 2 independent experiments. Data are mean ± SEM. Two-tailed Mann-Whitney test (i,j). ns, non-significant. Scale bars, 40 μm (c,d), 50 μm (e), 30 μm (f,g), and 20 μm (k).

a, UMAP projection of all endothelial cells from P6 tEC-GFP retinas. b, Violin plot of log-normalised Pecam1 expression across endothelial cell clusters. c, Dot plot of markers used for cluster annotation; dot size indicates the percentage of expressing cells and colour indicates average expression. d, Heatmap of scaled average expression profiles across endothelial populations, with hierarchically clustered rows and gene-wise z-scores. e, Density plot of log-normalised GFP expression across all endothelial cells. GFP+ cells were defined using a log-normalised GFP expression threshold of 1.5. f, Absolute numbers of GFP+ cells across clusters identified in P6 tEC-GFP retinas. g, UMAP highlighting GFP+ (green) and GFP- (grey) cells. h, Distribution of wild-type (WT) GFP+ endothelial cells across endothelial clusters, expressed as a percentage of total GFP+ WT endothelial cells. i, Violin plot of log-normalised Pecam1 expression in the merged dataset (P6 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinal endothelial cells) shown in Fig. 3b. j, Density plot of log-normalised GFP expression in the merged dataset; GFP+ cells were defined using the same threshold as in e. k, Absolute numbers of GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells in each cluster of the merged dataset. l, Violin plot of log-normalised Pik3ca expression in the merged dataset. m, Proportions of significantly upregulated (log2FC > 0) and downregulated (log2FC < 0) genes in GFP+ Pik3caH1047R versus GFP+ WT endothelial cells within each cluster, relative to all detected genes. n, Differential gene expression between GFP+ endothelial cells from tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas across clusters C2-C7. o, Heatmap of average gene expression in GFP+ endothelial cells for each cluster-genotype group, shown as gene-wise z-scores with hierarchically clustered rows. p, UMAP projection of subclustered Esm1-traced GFP+ endothelial cells from the merged dataset (P6 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinal endothelial cells). q, Dot plot of marker genes used for annotation of GFP+ clusters shown in p. r, RNA velocity streamlines projected onto the integrated UMAP of subclustered GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells. RNA velocity was inferred independently for each genotype, and streamline direction indicates the predicted transcriptional progression between cellular states.

a, Strategy for in vitro induction of Pik3caH1047R in mouse lung endothelial cells (ECs; three biological replicates pooled per condition). b, UMAP projection of the merged scRNA-seq dataset of ethanol-treated and 4-OHT-treated pEC-Pik3caH1047R mouse lung ECs. c,d, Violin plots showing the distribution of log-normalised Pecam1 (c) and Pik3ca (d) expression in the in vitro EC scRNA-seq dataset. e, Bar plot showing the distribution of wild-type (ethanol-treated) and Pik3caH1047R (4-OHT-treated) ECs across clusters. f, UMAP of wild-type and Pik3caH1047R cells, highlighting cluster 1 in wild-type cells (red, tip/arterial-like ECs) and cluster 2 in the Pik3caH1047R cells (green, venous-like ECs). g, Dot plot of marker gene expression used to annotate in vitro EC populations. h, Violin plots showing the expression of Nr2f2, Nrp2, Esm1, and Angpt2 in in vitro ECs. Data are shown separately for control and mutant cells. Boxes indicate the median and interquartile range (IQR; 25th–75th percentiles); whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR. Dots represent individual cells (Pik3caWT, n = 6,443 ECs. Pik3caH1047R, n = 7,514 ECs). i, Density plots showing the distribution of Nr2f2, Nrp2, Esm1, and Angpt2 expression in in vitro ECs. Data are split between control and mutant cells. j, High-magnification confocal images of P4 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and UNC5B (yellow). White arrows indicate representative GFP+UNC5Bhigh endothelial cells. k, Quantification of UNC5B mean fluorescence intensity in GFP+ cells within the sprouting front area (fold change) (n = 7 and 4 retinas, left to right). l, Confocal images of P4 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan), ERG (blue) and NR2F2 (yellow). No NR2F2+ GFP+ ECs were detected in either genotype. m, Confocal images of P6 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and UNC5B (yellow) in the capillary plexus. Mario Hermoso was Roma’s man of the match at PSG.

The Spanish center-back never feared the team that has won the last two Champions Leagues and scored the goal that temporarily led 0-1.

The former Atlético Madrid player delivered a performance worthy of a total leader: high recoveries, intercepted balls, quality with the ball at his feet, and constant support for the attack, even finding himself consistently in the French team’s penalty area.

Hermoso, after the match, commented with a hint of bitterness on the 2-2 draw against PSG: “An vital point. It’s a shame not to take home three points, but one is good. We want to fight for everything, we have the mentality to do so, and we also have the quality.”.

In a recent development, roma fans have fallen in love with Mario Hermoso. In a very tough match, the Spanish defender showcased his leadership skills with a near-perfect performance.

Sources indicate that as reported by Corriere dello Sport, the 1995-born defender won 11 possessions, won 6 duels, and took 5 shots, 4 of which were from inside the opponent’s penalty area. A complete player.

Recent findings suggest that wesley reveals: “I told Endrick to come to Roma. He would be given a special welcome”.

De Roon praises team effort: “We put in a great performance.”.

Recent findings suggest that joao Neves: “Roma are one of the best teams we’ve faced. They press really hard and have lots of quality.”.

Marquinhos greets Roma fans in away section.

Luis Enrique: “This was by far the hardest game so far.”.

Gasperini after PSG draw: “I will rewatch it, we were great. Soule is becoming a top player.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Punditry work is the lucrative alternative to management for retired ex-footballers and some earn more than a pretty penny for their time.

TV companies want ex-pros to front their coverage and for some audiences, watching the after-match debate has become as entertaining as watching the actual football.

As was the case when they were playing, the best ones get paid the significant bucks but who are the biggest earners in football?

Industry observers note that we’ve done our best to put together an accurate list but it is worth noting a couple of things. First off, the BBC’s Royal Charter means that they have to declare anyone who receives over £178k so anyone earning below that will not feature in this list.

Another crucial point to note is that the salaries of TNT pundits like Peter Crouch and Joe Cole are far more secretive than those at Sky.

But with those caveats in mind, here are the top earners in the UK.

Scott is the closest thing we have to Gary Lineker now that the former Match of the Day host has left in that player-turned-pundit-turned-presenter mould.

She has worked with the BBC since 2017, covering her first tournament at the 2018 World Cup, but was not picked as one of the hosts of Match of the Day.

Instead, she has branched out away from sport and also presents The One Show.

Some reports have Redknapp’s salary as high as £750k a year but that seems a little unrealistic.

Redknapp is on the B-tier of Sky Sports pundits, you will rarely see him on the Sunday 4:30pm game but he might be there for a Saturday 5:30.

He has been at Sky for a long time now having joined in 2006, he was even there in the Keys and Gray era, and is also a team captain on A League of Their Own.

Richards has fingers in many pies and so it is hard to nail down exactly what he earns.

What we do know is that he took home £205k from the BBC in their 2022 accounts but he was missing from the 2025/26 report so it must have dipped below £178k.

If we presume that it is still similar, Richards also appears on Sky and CBS, further inflating his pay packet.

To top it off, Richards is also one of the main faces on Gary Lineker’s Stick to Football podcast.

Recent findings suggest that alan Shearer took a 50k pay cut from 2025 to 2026 but still remains one of the best-paid pundits. With the departure of Gary Lineker, he became the highest-earning sports-related pundit in the BBC but has since lost that accolade.

He’s Match of the Day’s main pundit and was co-commentator for the BBC’s coverage of the World Cup Final this summer.

Rooney became a regular Match of the Day pundit in August 2025 after numerous attempts to stay in the managerial game failed.

Signing for the BBC, he reportedly put pen to paper on a two-year £800k deal.

He was one of the key pundits for the BBC’s World Cup coverage, most memorably calling the extended half-time break “crap”, and has defied doubters to actually be a decent pundit.

He’s at the moment on a hiatus from his BBC deal as he is being paid a reported £800k to appear on I’m a Celeb.

Would Wayne Rooney have worked in Pep Guardiola’s Barcelona?

“It’s your job,” he famously once mentioned, and his job pays very well.

Keane’s exact contract details are not known but he is rumoured to be earning anywhere from £500k to £1m.

That comes from both his Sky work but also his regular appearances for ITV.

The main man for Monday Night Football ranks second in the best-paid pundits.

Carragher reportedly takes home £1m a year from his Sky deal which sees him feature on every big game as well as plenty of others.

Unlike his partner in crime Neville, Carragher does branch out away from Sky though and is part of CBS Sports’ coverage of the Champions League for US audiences.

Neville is the face of Sky Sports’ football coverage.

He reinvented the punditry role following his retirement in 2011 and if his early Monday Night Football performances were a little too high-pitched and awkward, he soon transformed into the perfect pundit.

These days, he has jumped the shark somewhat and is becoming increasingly depressed at Manchester United but his Stick to Football podcast has been backed by Global and Disney+.

For his Sky contract alone he is reported to be taking home £1.1m a year, making him the best-paid pundit in the UK.

#129927. Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1460 w)
