Industry observers note that A structural model of the TnsA/B STC with target and donor DNA was generated using AlphaFold 321 and used as input for structure-based sequence design. Protein and DNA substrate sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 3.

In a recent development, the AlphaFold 3-generated TnsA–TnsB STC model was used as input for structure-based protein design. A total of 74 TnsA residue positions were fixed during design based on five structural criteria: (1) residues predicted to participate in primary or secondary interactions with the active site; (2) residues within contact distance of the DNA; (3) residues predicted to form protein–protein interfaces with TnsB; (4) residues predicted to contribute to a binding pocket engaging the TnsB or TnsC hook regions; and (5) N- and C-terminal residues with low predicted confidence (pLDDT), indicative of structural disorder. The full set of designable positions is listed in Supplementary Table 4.

Sequences were generated using three graph neural network-based protein design methods that sample amino acid probabilities from local structural context: LigandMPNN22, SolubleMPNN40 and HyperMPNN41. Because these models are trained on structural rather than functional information, and because design was performed on an AlphaFold 3 model rather than an experimentally determined structure, a bias towards TnsA sequences was introduced to restrict sampling to structurally favourable substitutions and improve the likelihood of recovering functional variants. Bias was applied by modifying per-residue logits prior to softmax normalization, such that increasing bias values progressively shifted the amino acid probability distribution towards the native identity without fully enforcing it. Bias strengths of 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 were applied to each of the three models using the flag bias_AA_per_residue. In a parallel strategy, an additional sampling bias was introduced towards residues conserved in a multiple sequence alignment of TnsA homologues.

It has been revealed that all designed sequences were folded as monomers and as part of the STC using Chai-142. Designed sequences were clustered using MMseqs243, and final designs were selected from each strategy based on threshold criteria across six metrics: backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD) of monomeric TnsA relative to input structure (<0.9–1.2 Å, depending on design strategy), backbone RMSD of predicted STC complex (<1.5–1.7 Å), predicted TM-score of the monomer (>0.918–0.928), predicted interface TM-score of the STC (>0.839–0.845), predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) of the monomer (>0.893–0.910), and pLDDT of the STC (>0.834–0.840).

In total, 499 designed TnsA variants were selected for experimental screening. One additional sequence was independently generated using PROSS44, yielding a final library of 500 sequences (Supplementary Table 1).

It has been revealed that A TnsA entry vector was constructed by replacing the TnsAWT region of the VchCAST TnsABC pHelper (Addgene #130633) with BsaI flanking sites. Nucleotide sequences of TnsA designs (693 bp) were fragmented into 300 bp oligonucleotides containing BsaI flanking sites, unique primer-binding sites, and unique per-design barcodes using the OMEGA program45 and purchased from Twist Bioscience. The oligonucleotide pools were PCR-amplified and inserted into the entry vector by Golden Gate assembly at a 20:1 insert-to-vector molar ratio. The assembled TnsA library was purified and electroporated into NEB 10-beta electrocompetent E. coli (NEB, #C3020K). Cells were plated on agar plates containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin after 1 h recovery at 37 °C. Colonies were collected at greater than 100× coverage per variant to ensure adequate library representation, and the TnsA library plasmid pool was extracted using the ZymoPURE II Plasmid Midiprep Kit (Zymo Research, D4201).

cJP003 cells were transformed with a Cascade–TniQ pHelper plasmid encoding TniQ, Cascade, a ccdB-targeting guide RNA, and a chloramphenicol resistance marker. Transformed cells were rendered electrocompetent by three successive washes with ice-cold 10% glycerol. The TnsA library was electroporated into the prepared cells at a 0.5:1 plasmid-to-cell ratio to ensure that each cell received a unique TnsABC pHelper variant. Cells were recovered at 37 °C for 1 h and plated on agar containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin and 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol. Colonies were collected at greater than 100× coverage per variant and cultured at 37 °C in LB medium supplemented with 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin and 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol.

Industry observers note that upon reaching OD600 ≈ 0.6, cells were collected and washed 3 times with 10% glycerol to prepare electrocompetent recipient cells. At this step, pHelper plasmids from a subset of recipient cells were extracted as input reference samples using the Monarch Spin Plasmid Miniprep Kit (NEB, T1110L). Recipient cells were electroporated with the non-replicable VchCAST pDonor at a 5:1 plasmid-to-cell ratio, immediately resuspended in 1 ml SOC medium, and recovered at 37 °C with shaking for 1 h. Cells were subsequently incubated overnight at 30 °C without shaking. The following day, cells were plated on agar containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin, 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin, and 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol for the activity screen, or on the same agar additionally supplemented with 0.1% (w/v) L-arabinose for the specificity screen. pHelper plasmids were extracted from selected colonies collected at greater than 100× coverage per variant using the ZymoPURE II Plasmid Midiprep Kit. All steps were performed in biological duplicate.

Barcode regions from the input reference and screened plasmid pools were PCR-amplified and indexed using the Nextera XT Index Kit v2 Set A (Illumina, FC-131-2001). Primers used for NGS are provided in Supplementary Table 5. Indexed amplicons were sequenced on an in-house MiSeq instrument. Activity and specificity scores for each design were calculated using an Enrich2-based pipeline23,46 on a log2-fold change basis and normalized to the score of TnsAWT.

Recent findings suggest that E. coli cells that had undergone in vivo transposition assays were plated on agar containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin, 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin and 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol to select for all integration events. More than 1,000 colonies were scraped for gDNA extraction using the Wizard Genomic DNA Purification Kit (Promega, A1125). Tagmentation-based transposon insertion sequencing (TagTn-seq)11 was performed on the extracted gDNA. Libraries were prepared by fragmenting gDNA with the Nextera XT DNA Library Kit (Illumina, FC-131-1024), followed by PCR amplification using an i7 primer and VchCAST right-end (RE)-specific primers, and indexing prior to sequencing on the in-house MiSeq. Reads mapping to the intact VchCAST pDonor were filtered from the resulting sequencing data using BBMap (v39.80), and RE-adjacent sequences were mapped to the cJP003 genome to profile integration site distribution.

TnsA activity is assessed through the formation of simple insertion products, as TnsA-mediated DNA cleavage results in cleavage of the 5′ end of donor DNA and lack of cleavage results in integration of the donor DNA backbone, otherwise referred to as co-integrates. We used long-read sequencing to distinguish between these two products, as previously established8.

E. coli cells that had undergone in vivo transposition assays were plated on agar containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin, 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin, 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol, and 0.1% (w/v) l-arabinose to select specifically for on-target integration events. More than 1,000 colonies were scraped and gDNA was extracted using the Wizard Genomic DNA Purification Kit (ProMega, A1125). Whole-genome sequencing was performed by Plasmidsaurus. Sequencing reads were analysed to identify integration products by detecting reads containing both target-site and left-end (LE) sequences, which define the boundaries of the integrated region. Reads containing pDonor backbone sequence were classified as co-integrates, while reads lacking pDonor backbone but containing the downstream target-site sequence were classified as simple insertions. Reads lacking both features were classified as ambiguous.

Far-UV circular dichroism spectra were collected using a JASCO CD spectropolarimeter. WT-TnsA and D1A were buffer exchanged into 10 mM potassium phosphate (pH 7.4) and analysed at a final concentration of 15 µM using a 0.1 cm path length quartz cuvette. Spectra were recorded from 195 to 280 nm at room temperature in continuous scanning mode with a 1.0 nm bandwidth and a scan speed of 200 nm min−1. Eight accumulations were collected for each sample and averaged to improve the signal-to-noise ratio. A buffer-only spectrum was recorded under identical conditions and subtracted from each protein spectrum.

The corrected circular dichroism signal was converted to mean residue ellipticity according to the manufacturer’s instructions:.

In a recent development, where θobs is the buffer-subtracted ellipticity, n is the number of amino acid residues, c is the protein concentration (M), and l is the cuvette path length (cm). WT-TnsA and D1A were normalized using 229 and 236 amino acid residues, respectively. For plotting, mean residue ellipticity values were divided by 1,000 and are reported as [θ] ×10−3 (deg cm2 dmol−1).

The DNA substrate used was designed based on in vivo genomic profiling experiments, synthesized as single-stranded DNA, and annealed to form a strand-transfer product substrate which was used for complex reconstitution, following our previously described strategy12,13. The left end spans LE1 through LE3 (positions 1–109) and the right end spans RE1 through RE3 (1–72), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 4. The native arrangement of left and right ends are identical up to position 30 (encompassing the 8 bp terminal sequence and LE1/ RE1). Past the first binding site, the placement and spacing of LE2–LE3 and RE2–RE3 differ, additionally there is a IHF binding site between LE1 and LE2 (Supplementary Fig. 4).

In a recent development, two double-stranded DNA substrates were independently assembled for the STC and transpososome reconstitution: a LE fragment and a RE fragment, each designed to recapitulate the relevant structural elements of the VchCAST RNA-guided transposition product, including the transposon terminal repeat sequences, the 5 bp target site duplication, and flanking target and gDNA regions (Supplementary Table 6). A diagram of the substrates can be found in Supplementary Fig. 4.

The LE fragment was assembled from three oligonucleotides: LE–TGS, which contains the transposon LE and flanking gDNA, Target-RC, which completes the double-stranded target genomic region, and LE–HFR, which provides the complementary LE region to LE–TGS along with a host flanking region for TnsA binding.

The RE fragment was assembled from four oligonucleotides: RE–TGS, which contains the RE and the target strand for guide RNA binding, NTGS–Scramble, a non-target strand oligonucleotide contained a scrambled sequence to facilitate bubble formation, RE–HFR, an oligonucleotide that complements the RE sequence of RE–TGS and contains a flanking HFR region, and DTB–LUEGO, a desthiobiotinylated oligonucleotide incorporated at the 5′ end of the RE fragment to enable streptavidin-based affinity capture of the assembled complexes during pull-down experiments47.

It has been revealed that prior to annealing, all oligonucleotides were purified by HPLC using an Agilent 1260 Infinity II system equipped with an AdvanceBio Oligonucleotide column (Agilent Technologies) to ensure incorporation of only full-length species. The LE and RE fragments were each assembled independently by combining their respective oligonucleotides at equimolar concentrations in annealing buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA), heating to 95 °C for 5 min, and gradually cooling to 50 °C at 1 °C per min using a thermal cycler (Bio-Rad). The annealed fragments were stored separately until used in STC and transpososome reconstitutions.

Industry observers note that STC assembly reactions were prepared using an annealed DNA substrate (0.5 µM in 100 µl) and containing TnsB together with D1A using the same 1:5:10 stoichiometry. Complex assembly was initially carried out under high-salt conditions in a buffer containing 26 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 5 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 20 mM KCl, 750 mM NaCl, 0.2 mM MgCl2, 15 mM magnesium acetate, 2% glycerol, 1 mM DTT and 0.1% Tween-20. Following assembly, samples were dialysed overnight at 4 °C from high-salt buffer into an identical low-salt buffer in which the NaCl concentration was reduced to 150 mM to promote stable complex formation.

Recent findings suggest that for affinity capture of assembled complexes, Streptavidin Mag Sepharose magnetic beads (Cytiva) were washed 3 times with 500 μl of low-salt buffer prior to use. Dialysed samples were incubated with the equilibrated streptavidin beads for 1 h at room temperature with continuous rotation to allow binding of biotinylated DNA substrates and associated protein complexes.

Following incubation, the beads were washed 3 times with 500 μl of low-salt buffer to remove unbound proteins and nonspecific material. Bound complexes were subsequently eluted using low-salt buffer supplemented with 10 mM biotin. Elution was performed in 2 sequential rounds using 50 µl buffer per step, with each incubation carried out for 30 min at room temperature under rotation before collection of the eluate. Elution fractions were analysed by SDS–PAGE to confirm the presence of protein components within the assembled complexes. Sample quality, homogeneity and the presence of assembled STCs were further evaluated by negative-stain electron microscopy prior to cryo-EM grid preparation and vitrification.

According to recent reports, sequential on-bead assembly of the HIC was performed by first capturing the desthiobiotinylated RE substrate (0.5 µM in 100 µl) on Streptavidin Mag Sepharose magnetic beads (Cytiva). Binding was carried out for 1 h at room temperature with gentle rotation in binding buffer comprising 26 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 5 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 20 mM KCl, 750 mM NaCl, 0.2 mM MgCl2, 15 mM MgOAc, 2% glycerol, 1 mM ATP, 1 mM DTT, and 0.1% Tween-20, followed by 3 washes with 500 µl of the same buffer.

It has been revealed that cascade–TniQ was subsequently introduced at a 1:2 DNA:protein molar ratio and incubated for 1 h at room temperature, followed by 3 washes. The LE substrate (0.5 µM), pre-complexed with E. coli IHF at a 1:8 DNA-to-protein molar ratio, was then added alongside TnsB (1:5 DNA:protein) and designed TnsA (1:10 DNA:protein), and the assembly was allowed to proceed for 1 h at room temperature. Beads were washed 3 times with 500 µl binding buffer. In the final step, TnsC was introduced at a 1:10 DNA-to-protein ratio in binding buffer supplemented with equimolar concentrations of ATP and ATPγS (1 mM each) and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. Unbound proteins were removed by 3 washes with 500 µl of ATP/ATPγS-containing binding buffer.

In a recent development, the assembled HIC was released from the beads by two sequential elution steps, each using 50 µl of elution buffer (binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM biotin) incubated under rotation for 30 min. Eluted fractions were resolved by SDS–PAGE to verify the presence of all HIC components. Prior to cryo-EM grid preparation, samples were evaluated by negative-stain electron microscopy to confirm the presence of assembled HIC particles and to assess sample homogeneity.

It has been revealed that graphene sheets with a poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) support layer (ACS Material, TTG100BB,25 ×25 mm) were stored at 4 °C until use. Graphene transfer onto cryo-EM grids was performed based on a previously described protocol with minor modifications48. Ultrafoil grids (Au R1.2/1.3, Quantifoil) were placed on a 3D-printed grid transfer tool immersed in deionized water. Excess support material from the graphene pad was trimmed, and the PMMA/graphene pad was placed gently onto the water surface to avoid overflow onto the graphene layer. After positioning, the water level was gradually lowered by syringe withdrawal, allowing the graphene sheet to settle onto the grids. Grids were left overnight at room temperature to anneal, then baked at 150 °C for 30 min to promote firm adhesion. Grids were transferred to a Petri dish, and PMMA was removed by three successive acetone washes. Graphene-coated grids were individually transferred to a grid box and stored at room temperature until use.

In a recent development, STC samples were prepared for cryo-EM either directly from pull-down elution fractions or following two- to four-fold dilution in low-salt buffer. Graphene-coated grids were prepared as described above. Prior to sample application, grids were plasma-cleaned using a Solarus II Plasma Cleaner (Gatan) under an Ar/O2 atmosphere at 10 W for 10 s (s), with the graphene-coated surface oriented upward.

Sources indicate that for vitrification, 4 µl of STC sample was applied to the carbon side of a graphene-coated grid and incubated for 60 s inside a Vitrobot Mark IV chamber (Thermo Fisher Scientific) maintained at 4 °C and 100% relative humidity. Grids were blotted for 3.5 s at a blot force of −7 and immediately plunge-frozen into liquid ethane cooled by liquid nitrogen.

HIC samples were prepared for cryo-EM from either undiluted pull-down eluates or two- to four-fold dilutions thereof. Graphene-coated grids were prepared as described above and plasma-cleaned using a Solarus II Plasma Cleaner (Gatan) under an Ar/O2 atmosphere at 10 W for 10 s with the graphene-coated face oriented upward.

Recent findings suggest that for vitrification, 4 µl of HIC sample was applied to the carbon side of a graphene-coated grid and incubated for 60 s inside a Vitrobot Mark IV chamber at 4 °C and 100% relative humidity. Grids were blotted for 3.5 s at a blot force of −7 before plunge-freezing into liquid ethane cooled by liquid nitrogen.

Industry observers note that ni-NTA affinity grids were prepared as previously described49. Quantifoil Au R1.2/1.3 grids were coated with a Ni-NTA lipid monolayer composed of 20% 18:1 DGS-NTA(Ni) (Avanti Polar Lipids) diluted with DOPC (18:1; Avanti Polar Lipids). Grids were incubated with 3 µl of His-tagged HIC diluted in 2 µl of elution buffer (26 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 5 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 20 mM KCl, 750 mM NaCl, 0.2 mM MgCl2, 15 mM MgOAc, 2% glycerol, 1 mM ATP, 1 mM DTT, 0.1% Tween-20) for 1 h at 4 °C in a humidity chamber to allow affinity capture. Unbound material was removed by three brief washes with elution buffer, after which grids were blotted and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane using a Vitrobot operated at 4 °C and 100% relative humidity with a blot force of −7 and blot time of 3.5 s.

Vitrified STC samples were initially screened on a Talos Arctica transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated with fringe-free illumination at 130,000× magnification (0.63 Å per pixel) and 200 kV, equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector and a BioQuantum imaging filter (20 eV slit width). Data were collected using the EPU software package (Thermo Fisher Scientific). This screening step was used to assess grid quality and particle distribution prior to large-scale data collection. Grids of sufficient quality were subsequently imaged on a Titan Krios G3i transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated with fringe-free illumination at 130,000× magnification (0.745 Å per pixel) and 300 kV, equipped with a Falcon 4i (4k × 4k) direct electron detector, a BioQuantum imaging filter, and a 20 eV energy-selecting slit. Data collection employed the aberration-free image shift and multi-shot-per-hole acquisition modes of EPU. For the STC dataset, 7,724 movies were collected using EPU with image shift, with nominal defocus ranging from −1.5 to −2.5 µm at 0.2 µm intervals. Each movie was acquired with a 3.1 s exposure and a total dose of 60 e− Å−2, fractionated into 60 frames. Frames were aligned using MotionCor250, and CTF estimation was performed in cryoSPARC v4.7.151. The full data processing workflow is presented in Supplementary Fig. 4.

Particles were initially picked using blob picker, and approximately 290,000 extracted particles were subjected to 2D classification. Classes representing the STC were identified and used as templates for a second round of template-based particle picking, yielding approximately 1,000,000 particles that were re-subjected to 2D classification. The resulting 22,000 particles were used to train a Topaz neural network picking model (v0.2.5)52. After confirming model performance, additional particles were extracted from all micrographs using the trained model. The latest particle set underwent 2D classification, and selection of high-quality classes yielded 97,972 particles that were used for ab initio reconstruction. Heterogeneous refinement separated the dataset into two classes: 70,006 particles representing the STC complex and the remainder classified as non-particles. Non-uniform refinement of the STC class produced an initial map at 2.9 Å resolution. The particle stack was then subjected to 3D classification using principal component analysis with a 13 Å resolution cut-off, separating 18,831 particles lacking target DNA from 51,169 particles with target DNA bound. Both subsets were independently subjected to non-uniform refinement, yielding a 3.2 Å map for the STC without target DNA and a 2.9 Å map for the STC with target DNA. Both maps were further processed with DeepEMhancer v12132253 prior to model building.

In a recent development, initial cryo-EM data collection on graphene grids revealed a strong preferred orientation bias, limiting the angular coverage of the dataset. To improve particle orientation distribution and enable higher-quality three-dimensional reconstructions, Ni-NTA lipid monolayer grids were subsequently prepared49.

It has been revealed that A total of 144,294 movies were collected at a pixel size of 0.848 Å and processed using Patch Motion Correction and Patch CTF Estimation with a CTF-fit cut-off of less than 10 Å. Initial particle picking was performed by blob picking on approximately 2,600 micrographs, yielding ~570,000 extracted particles (binned 3×), which were subjected to two rounds of 2D classification to generate ~5,000 representative particles for training a Topaz neural network picking model (v0.2.5)52. The trained model was applied across all ~22,000 micrographs, extracting 2,722,447 particles (binned 3×). Following two rounds of 2D classification, 897,848 particles were retained for further analysis. The complete data processing workflow is described in Extended Data Fig. 4.

Single-particle analysis revealed substantial compositional heterogeneity within the reconstituted sample. Two-dimensional class averages resolved density for all expected components in multiple orientations (Extended Data Fig. 4). Heterogeneous refinement (n = 4) partitioned the dataset into 4 populations: 2 HIC classes (131,242 particles, 14.6%; and 462,255 particles, 54.8%), 1 STC–TnsC class (127,845 particles, 14.2%) and 1 Cascade class (146,705 particles, 16.4%). These populations enabled classification of the following assemblies: a Cascade–TniQ sub-complex (3.3 Å), a STC (2.9 Å) an STC–TnsC assembly (4.3 Å) and the complete HIC (4.5 Å) (Extended Data Fig. 4). Each population was further processed by sub-classification and homogeneous refinement. For the HIC, signal subtraction of the STC–TnsC region followed by 2D slice projection-guided particle sorting enabled focused local refinement, yielding a map at 4.5 Å resolution (Fourier shell correlation (FSC) = 0.143). Non-uniform refinement of the Cascade region within the full complex achieved 3.5 Å (FSC = 0.143). Free Cascade and Cascade–TniQ populations were resolved to 2.8 Å, 3.0 Å (closed) and 3.1 Å (open), respectively (FSC = 0.143). The HIC exhibits variable local resolution (3.7–9.0 Å, Supplementary Fig. 9), and focused refinements were combined into a composite map.

For the STC maps, PDB 9Y7B was used as a starting model. The structure was initially docked into the STC-without-target-DNA map and manually rebuilt in Coot (v0.9.8.96)54 where required. DNA sequences were modified manually and fitted into the density using ISOLDE as a ChimeraX plugin (v1.11.1). The TnsA subunit was modelled using AlphaFold 3 and docked into the corresponding density. This assembled STC model was subsequently used as the starting model for the STC-with-target-DNA map. Structural rearrangements in TnsB required individual domains to be docked independently into the density before rejoining in Coot.

It has been revealed that for the Cascade–TniQ complex structures, individual Cas subunits were modelled using AlphaFold 3 and docked into the map. The DNA scaffold was derived from PDB 6PIJ and mutated to match the designed substrate sequence. The target recognition complex was assembled, and manual adjustments were performed in Coot.

Industry observers note that both the Cascade–TniQ and STC complex structures were used as starting models for modelling the HIC. TnsC protomers were individually modelled using AlphaFold 3 and docked into the density. The STC–TnsC portion of the HIC was used as the starting model for the off-pathway complex, with minor adjustments applied to the TnsC ring.

Industry observers note that for all structures, real-space refinement of DNA substrates was performed in Phenix (v2.0rc1-5690)55 with base-pair and secondary structure restraints enforced. Model validation was carried out by computing map-model FSC at a 0.5 cut-off. The masked cross-correlation coefficient (CCmask) from refinement output was reported as the representative model-map cross-correlation. All validation statistics are summarized in Extended Data Table 1.

Sources indicate that helical rise and twist were measured from docked protomers in the HIC (PDB: 36AU) and VchTnsC structures (PDB: 7UFI) using a script from the Rosetta software suite: make_symmdef_file.pl56. Rise values (in Å) were extracted from the output and plotted using Python.

Iranian activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi shares her story in memoir

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.
  • "A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.
  • The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.

"A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.

The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.

It has been revealed that mohammadi wrote the autobiography in prison: "She was constantly writing," states Claren, whose own mother, activist Nahid Taghavi, shared a cell with Mohammadi for two and a half years, in Iran's notorious Evin prison. "Then, in 2020, Narges was forcibly moved to another prison. All her documents were gone. And she had to start all over.".

But she managed to rewrite it all, and her texts were smuggled out of prison in fragments by fellow prisoners and visitors who risked their own safety.

In her memoir, Mohammadi recounts pivotal moments in her life, including her childhood and youth, how she started taking action against gender discrimination, political repression, the death penalty and human rights abuses, and the personal and emotional toll of her activism.

Recent findings suggest that the human rights activist has been sentenced to a combined total of more than 44 years in prison and 154 lashes. For more than a decade, she has been separated from her twin children, who are now 19 years old and live in exile in France for their own protection.

Born on April 21, 1972, in Zanjan, Iran, Narges Mohammadi became politically active while studying in physics at Imam Khomeini University of Qazvin in the 1990s.

In "A Woman Never Stops Fighting," she describes how she started mountain climbing as a student, and organized mixed-gender groups dedicated to mountaineering — a controversial initiative at the time. She also helped establish an independent student organization and advocated for political reform. Her activities led to repeated harassment and arrests by authorities.

In a recent development, she began her journalism career in 1996, writing about Iran's student and women's movements. As her public profile grew, she became increasingly involved in Iran's civil society and human rights community.

According to recent reports, in 1998, she married political activist Taghi Rahmani. The couple's twins, Ali and Kiana, were born in 2006.

Over the course of her career, Mohammadi worked with some of Iran's most prominent human rights organizations and became a leading figure in the Defenders of Human Rights Centre, founded by 2003 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi.

In a recent development, she played a key role in initiatives promoting free elections, peace and the abolition of the death penalty, especially for juvenile offenders. She also helped establish organizations supporting political prisoners and advocating for women's rights.

According to recent reports, her first major prison sentence related to her human rights activities came in 2011. It marked the beginning of a cycle of arrests and prosecutions that would define much of her adult life.

Sources indicate that in her memoir, she describes an arrest that took place in front of her young children. At one point during her imprisonment, she lost the right to call them for several months.

She also details the brutal treatment she experienced in prison, with constant interrogations, beatings and denial of medical care.

Another central focus of her activism is denouncing the psychological effects of solitary confinement, which she had previously documented with fellow inmates in her book and documentary project "White Torture.".

"When someone is subjected to physical torture, the scars, blood and infections — dreadful as they may be — serve as visible witnesses," she writes in her memoir. But, she adds, "when someone is subjected to psychological torture, no visible traces remain, and the victim cannot justify the trauma — neither to themselves nor to others. In fact, it becomes virtually impossible to even accept that one has been tortured at all, which causes the suffering to continue indefinitely.".

"This is also the goal of solitary confinement: to bring the imprisoned person to the very edge of nothingness — to strip them of their identity and of everything that makes them human," she writes.

Through her relentless campaigning against executions and state violence, she helped bring these complications to the forefront of public debate among Iranian activists.

International recognition of her work culminated in October 2023 when she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all.".

As Mohammadi was unable to attend the ceremony because she remained imprisoned in Tehran's Evin Prison, the award was accepted on her behalf by her teenage twins, who delivered her message to the world.

Following the Nobel Prize, Iranian authorities continued to pursue new legal cases against her, restrict her communications and intensify pressure on her from prison.

She became the target of a systematic smear campaign, including widespread defamation, gender-based harassment and explicit death threats.

"We are firmly convinced that the Islamic Republic of Iran has deployed its cyber army — which is the second-largest, after Russia's — to this end," states Claren of the Narges Mohammadi Foundation. Conspiracy theorists even started claiming she might be working for the regime, she adds: "And what is truly terrible about this is that when a lie is repeated over and over again and spread over the course of years, it eventually leads even ordinary people to start believing it.".

In late 2024, following surgery, Mohammadi was granted a temporary medical release. Doctors warned at the time that a return to prison could seriously endanger her health.

Nevertheless, Mohammadi was brutally arrested again in December 2025, while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi, a lawyer and human rights activist who died in suspicious circumstances.

Industry observers note that in prison, she was held in solitary confinement for an extended period and her health continued to deteriorate, Claren reports. But "thanks to a public campaign, she has now been granted what is known as an interruption of detention for medical reasons.".

But "that doesn't mean she is free," adds Claren, who notes that she still suffers from serious health problems — as do many Iranians who have been tortured in prison.

In February, an Iranian court ordered additional prison sentences for Mohammadi, along with a travel ban.

Recent findings suggest that mohammadi lives in constant fear of having to return to prison any day, notes Claren, and "this all comes with the pressure to which Iranian civil society — including, of course, people like Narges — is right now subjected, with questions like: Will Trump launch an attack, yes or no? Will there be another war?".

Sources indicate that despite this uncertainty, Mohammadi continues her activism. Her international profile also helps her supporters keep addressing publicly the issue of human rights in Iran in the public eye, states Claren: "It is incredibly vital that, alongside the individual Narges Mohammadi, the focus also remains consistently on the struggle of the people in Iran for freedom, dignity, and fundamental rights — for the right to sing and dance.".

Man Utd the masters of self-destruction as pressure piles on Carrick

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that so where do Manchester United go from here?
  • After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.
  • It has been revealed that as the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that so where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

It has been revealed that as the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, noted he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

According to recent reports, equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

The problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

Take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

Michael Carrick stated he expects to be in charge of Manchester United next week despite Lisandro Martinez’s moment of madness leaving the club mired in a relegation battle and on their worst run for 38 years.

United were urged to sell Martinez after the controversial Argentina defender was sent off for elbowing Wesley Fofana as Carrick accused his side of “unravelling” as they slumped to a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea.

Sources indicate that it left United without a win in nine matches, their worst run since 1988, and at risk of being sucked into the relegation zone. They have won just two of 13 games this season.

Sources indicate that the Old Trafford hierarchy gave Carrick a stay of execution in midweek and, when asked if he expected to still to be at the helm when United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, the head coach replied: “Yes. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”.

Having been booked moments earlier for a foul on Morgan Rogers, Martinez was sent off for a second yellow. The incident came less than three weeks after the Argentinian was fined and publicly apologised for attacking United director of football Jason Wilcox and the board over transfer policy and was the latest in a series of mistakes from him on the pitch this season.

Joe Cole, the former Chelsea and England forward, believes United must get rid of Martinez.

“Whatever the next Manchester United looks like, Lisandro Martinez has run his course,’ Cole noted on TNT Sports. “He’s at the scene of the crime too often for Manchester United and is at fault for moments and goals like that. So that’s probably his time done.”.

Carrick refused to publicly criticise Martinez but admitted his dismissal was a “huge moment” and felt his team “unravelled” in the second period.

“Things have gone against us in a big way,” the United manager said. “It’s unravelled quickly. There’s a lot of emotion right now. It’s a huge moment in the game. Sometimes you get setbacks in games and you’ve got to deal with that better. I’ve not seen it [the Martinez incident] back so I don’t know if it was [a red card] or not. He’s gone to it and the referee gave that decision, but it’s a big moment.”.

Asked if there would be a stigma attached to United potentially dropping into the relegation zone, Carrick added: “Not for me, no.”.

And when asked how his players would deal with a relegation battle, Carrick added: “We’ve got to keep moving forward and winning games. There’s no words I’m going to explain to you now that makes any difference, it’s not going to change it. We’ve got to move forward and win matches.”.

What do football fans actually want from their club owners? The model for most has been Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan and friends at Manchester City, owners whose hands are put frequently into pockets of unlimited depth, have made vast improvements to every aspect of the club and its community and are rarely ever seen, let alone heard from.

That view may have to evolve after certain verdicts about certain charges, but few envious glances from around the country have been cast towards the owners of Manchester’s other major club.

Manchester United’s accounts for last season suggest that ownership could be changing in the next three years, with a route to Sir Jim Ratcliffe assuming full control by 2029. But who would actually be the better custodians for United?

I’m good. It’s one of them – when you’ve had a result like we have, maybe a spell like we have, it definitely makes you hungry to push on and improve things. That’s what we have done this week.

Sources indicate that we know it’s not been good enough. It’s obvious to say that. But it’s something we can flip and we are the ones who can control that. That’s the beauty of it for me. We are in control of it and know there’s something we can do about it.

I don’t need any assurances [from the board]. I totally understand what’s needed here. I’m just focused on winning games.

Industry observers note that if there’s anything I take about beyond these four walls it’s how the supporters are thinking. That’s all that matters to me. I’m not interested [in external noise in the media etc], my only focus is on making us better.

[Do you think the players are behind you?] One hundred per cent, for sure.

Industry observers note that good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the new year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

“Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

As for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.
